surveys.label: language-choice
surveys.summary: I verified the cross-compilation matrix empirically on this exact box rather than trusting folklore, and the result is decisive. Rust cross-compiles a *realistic* editor dependency set (339 crates: tokio, tree-sitter 0.27 + three C grammars, ratatui, ropey, arboard, nucleo) from this headless Linux container to x86_64/aarch64 Linux (gnu + musl), Windows x86_64, macOS arm64, macOS x86_64 AND a universal2 fat Mach-O — all four succeeded, with tree-sitter's C runtime emitting real Mach-O arm64 and Windows COFF objects. Go cannot match this: `go env CGO_ENABLED` silently returns 0 for any cross target, and Go+cgo to macOS fails even with `zig cc` as CC because Go's runtime demands `-lresolv` and `-framework CoreFoundation` from a real macOS SDK — which means Go + tree-sitter simply cannot be cross-built to macOS here. The classic "GC pauses kill editors" argument, however, does NOT survive testing: Go's STW pauses were 0.094ms median / 0.182ms max on a pointer-heavy 1.76M-object live heap, far under a frame budget. The real Rust advantages are elsewhere: Unicode currency (unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 and unicode-width 0.2.2 are at Unicode 17.0.0 with Indic conjunct-break GB9c; Go's rivo/uniseg v0.4.7 is stuck at Unicode 15.0.0 and I proved they disagree — हिन्दी segments to 2 clusters in Rust, 3 in Go), a production rope (ropey 1.6.1 built a 125MB/1.77M-line buffer in 137ms and sustained 1.91µs random inserts), and purpose-built editor infrastructure (termina 0.4.0, which Helix adopted specifically to get ConPTY/VT on Windows). Electron/Node SEA is disqualified on size alone — a hello-world SEA is 124.8MB. Tauri is disqualified because its Linux webview is a system webkit2gtk dependency and it cannot be exercised headlessly at all. Zig is disqualified by churn: 0.16.0 landed 2026-04-13 with a std.Io rewrite that nearly deleted std.posix, and Ghostty still has an open migration issue. I also confirmed the repo is public, so macOS and Windows GitHub-hosted runners are free and unmetered — and that wine 9.0 plus qemu-user-static give a local Windows/aarch64 smoke-test loop, so only macOS is truly CI-only.

findings.claim: Rust cross-compiles a REALISTIC editor dependency set (339 packages incl. tokio, tree-sitter 0.27.0 + tree-sitter-rust/python/json C grammars, ratatui, ropey, arboard, nucleo) from this headless Linux box to musl, windows-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin AND universal2-apple-darwin. All four succeeded.
findings.evidence: Built in /tmp/.../scratchpad/realed. Output: '--- musl --- OK / --- win-gnu --- OK / --- macOS arm64 --- OK / --- macOS universal2 --- OK'. Artifacts: `file` reports 'Mach-O 64-bit arm64 executable', 'Mach-O universal binary with 2 architectures', 'PE32+ executable (console) x86-64', 'ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable ... static-pie linked'.
findings.implication: jio in Rust can produce every release artifact except windows-msvc directly from this container. macOS is NOT a CI-only build target for Rust — only a CI-only *test* target.

findings.claim: Proof the C code really cross-compiled: tree-sitter's C runtime and grammars produced genuine Mach-O arm64 and Windows COFF object files, and 173 rlibs were built for the darwin target.
findings.evidence: `file -b .../aarch64-apple-darwin/release/build/tree-sitter-python-*/out/*-parser.o` -> 'Mach-O 64-bit arm64 object, flags:<|SUBSECTIONS_VIA_SYMBOLS>'. Windows: 'Intel amd64 COFF object file ... 1107 sections, 2613 symbols'. `ls target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/deps/*.rlib | wc -l` = 173.
findings.implication: The hardest case for cross-compilation (a C library with build.rs codegen) works. Rust's `cc` crate + zig linker handles the whole tree-sitter stack without a Mac.

findings.claim: Go SILENTLY disables cgo when cross-compiling, and Go+cgo to macOS FAILS even with `zig cc` as CC because Go's runtime links -lresolv and -framework CoreFoundation from a real macOS SDK.
findings.evidence: `GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go env CGO_ENABLED` -> `0`. With CC=zig cc -target aarch64-macos: "error: unable to find dynamic system library 'resolv' using strategy 'paths_first'. searched paths: none". Reproduced identically with the real github.com/tree-sitter/go-tree-sitter v0.25.0.
findings.implication: DECISIVE against Go. Both maintained Go tree-sitter bindings are cgo. Choosing Go means either abandoning tree-sitter, betting on an unproven pure-Go/wasm reimplementation, or making macOS builds strictly CI-only with zero local reproduction.

findings.claim: Go+cgo to Windows DOES work via zig cc, unlike macOS.
findings.evidence: `CGO_ENABLED=1 GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 CC='zig cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu' go build` -> 'PE32+ executable (console) x86-64, for MS Windows, 14 sections'; ran under wine printing 'cgo: 42'.
findings.implication: Go's cgo cross problem is macOS-specific, not universal. Honest framing: Go loses on macOS+tree-sitter, not on Windows.

findings.claim: Rust's Unicode stack is two major versions ahead of Go's, and they measurably disagree on Indic text.
findings.evidence: unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 tables.rs: `UNICODE_VERSION: (u64,u64,u64) = (17,0,0)` and contains explicit Indic_Conjunct_Break/InCB (GB9c) code. unicode-width 0.2.2: `UNICODE_VERSION = (17,0,0)`. rustc `char::UNICODE_VERSION` -> `(17, 0, 0)`. rivo/uniseg@v0.4.7 (latest per `go list -m -versions`) source: '// Unicode version 15.0.0.' Live test on हिन्दी: Rust graphemes=2, Go graphemes=3.
findings.implication: A cursor moving through Devanagari lands in different places depending on language choice. Rust is correct per UAX#29 with GB9c (Unicode 15.1+). This is exactly the CJK/combining-mark correctness the project requires.

findings.claim: Go's standard library has NO grapheme cluster segmentation at all; it ships only unicode/utf8, unicode/utf16 and x/text/unicode/norm.
findings.evidence: `go list std | grep -iE 'unicode|text'` returns text/scanner, text/tabwriter, text/template, unicode, unicode/utf16, unicode/utf8, vendor/x/text/unicode/{bidi,norm}. `go doc unicode | grep -ci grapheme` = 0.
findings.implication: Go forces a third-party dependency (rivo/uniseg, last released at Unicode 15.0.0) for the single most safety-critical operation in a text editor. Rust's is equally third-party but current.

findings.claim: ropey 1.6.1 handles a 125MB / 1.77M-line mixed CJK+emoji file with editor-grade latency: rope construction 137ms, 100k scattered single-char inserts in 191ms (1.91 µs/edit), full line iteration 160ms, 2000 line_to_char lookups in 2.64ms.
findings.evidence: Ran /tmp/.../scratchpad/bench on /tmp/big.txt (125,000,232 bytes, 1,765,540 lines, 107,697,940 chars). Peak RSS 258MB after load, 320MB after 100k edits.
findings.implication: 1.91µs/edit is ~8000x under a 16ms frame budget. Large-file handling is a solved problem in Rust with an off-the-shelf crate; no custom piece-table needed for v1.

findings.claim: The 'GC pauses kill editors' argument does NOT hold for Go at editor scale. Max STW pause was 0.182ms with a 1.76M-pointer live heap under heavy allocation churn.
findings.evidence: gobench: 1,765,541 live strings + 1,765,541 live *string, GOGC=50, 3M undo-record allocations. runtime.MemStats PauseNs: p50=0.182ms MAX=0.182ms; earlier run p50=0.094 max=0.094, GCCPUFraction 0.0033–0.02.
findings.implication: I must be honest: this is the standard anti-Go argument and it is largely obsolete (Go 1.26's Green Tea GC improves it further). Reject Go for cgo/tree-sitter/Unicode reasons, NOT for GC latency.

findings.claim: Go's memory footprint for the same file is worse and its naive line-splitting is 5x slower than Rust's rope construction.
findings.evidence: Go: ReadFile 79ms, strings.Split into 1.77M lines 676ms, HeapAlloc 146MB / Sys 274MB. Rust: read 139ms, Rope::from_str 137ms, peak RSS 258MB. Note Go's Sys stays ~274MB while holding a naive line slice with no rope structure at all.
findings.implication: Go would still need a real rope/gap-buffer implementation written by hand; there is no Go equivalent of ropey with comparable maturity.

findings.claim: Only the musl target produces a genuinely dependency-free Linux binary. The default linux-gnu build requires GLIBC_2.34, locking out anything older than Ubuntu 22.04 / RHEL 9.
findings.evidence: `objdump -T target/release/realed | grep GLIBC` -> GLIBC_2.28, 2.30, 2.32, 2.33, 2.34. musl build: `file` says 'static-pie linked', objdump shows 0 GLIBC symbols, `ldd` says 'statically linked'.
findings.implication: Ship x86_64-unknown-linux-musl as THE Linux release artifact. This is a concrete config decision, not a preference.

findings.claim: The macOS Rust binary links only /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib — genuinely dependency-free on every Mac.
findings.evidence: Parsed LC_LOAD_DYLIB commands from the aarch64-apple-darwin Mach-O: single entry '/usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib'.
findings.implication: 'Download and run' works on macOS with zero user setup, modulo Gatekeeper quarantine/codesigning (which is a signing problem, not a linking one).

findings.claim: The windows-gnu (mingw) binary imports msvcrt.dll — the LEGACY CRT — not the modern UCRT.
findings.evidence: `objdump -p realed.exe | grep 'DLL Name'` -> KERNEL32.dll, USERENV.dll, WS2_32.dll, api-ms-win-core-synch-l1-2-0.dll, bcryptprimitives.dll, msvcrt.dll, ntdll.dll.
findings.implication: All these DLLs are in-box on Win10+, so it runs. But msvcrt.dll has legacy locale/printf behavior and mingw has historically weaker SEH unwinding. Use windows-gnu for LOCAL wine smoke tests; ship x86_64-pc-windows-msvc built natively on a windows-2025 runner.

findings.claim: cargo-xwin (Windows MSVC cross from Linux) is blocked ONLY by this container's proxy, not by any technical limitation.
findings.evidence: cargo-xwin 0.23.1 installed fine; failure is 'HTTP GET request for https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/channel failed / CONNECT proxy failed: proxy server responded 403/403'.
findings.implication: Don't design around this. MSVC builds belong on the native windows-2025 runner anyway, where you also get real console/path/locking behavior.

findings.claim: The jio repo is PUBLIC, so GitHub-hosted macOS and Windows runners are free and unmetered — the 10x macOS multiplier does not apply.
findings.evidence: GitHub API for zhangyuxuan1999/jio: "private": false, "visibility": "public", created 2026-09-07. Public repos get unmetered standard GitHub-hosted runners; the 1x/2x/10x Linux/Windows/macOS multipliers apply only to private-repo included minutes.
findings.implication: Budget is NOT a constraint on CI validation. Run the full test suite on macos-26 (arm64), macos-15-intel (x86_64), windows-2025 and windows-11-arm on every push. This substantially de-risks the 'no Mac, no PC' problem.

findings.claim: Current GitHub-hosted runner labels give native coverage of every target: macos-26 (arm64, GA since 2026-02-26, becomes macos-latest June 2026), macos-26-intel/macos-15-intel (x86_64), windows-2025 (VS2026 since June 2026), windows-11-arm (arm64).
findings.evidence: actions/runner-images issues #13739, #14167; github.blog changelogs 2026-02-26 and 2026-05-14.
findings.implication: Pin explicit labels (macos-26, macos-15-intel, windows-2025), never macos-latest/windows-latest — those migrated in June 2026 and will silently move again.

findings.claim: A local smoke-test loop for Windows and aarch64 IS possible without those machines: wine 9.0 runs the cross-built Windows binaries with byte-identical output, and qemu-user-static runs aarch64 Linux binaries.
findings.evidence: apt-installed wine 9.0~repack-4build3 ran realed.exe ('Hello, world!'), the Go cgo exe ('cgo: 42'), and edprobe.exe printing the exact same 9-line Unicode table as the native Linux run. qemu-aarch64-static -L /usr/aarch64-linux-gnu ran the aarch64 build. No macOS emulator exists (darling unavailable).
findings.implication: You can catch most Windows logic bugs locally in seconds. wine will NOT model ConPTY, real file locking, antivirus interference, or NTFS case-insensitivity — those are genuinely CI-only. macOS is 100% CI-only for execution.

findings.claim: Helix migrated its terminal backend from crossterm to termina specifically to drop legacy Windows Console API code and use ConPTY/VT uniformly. termina 0.4.0 is on crates.io now.
findings.evidence: helix-editor/helix PR #13307, merged 2025-08-31 by the-mikedavis. `cargo add termina --dry-run` -> 'Adding termina v0.4.0'. Requires Windows 10 build 10.0.17763+.
findings.implication: For jio, take termina (or crossterm 0.29.0) and set a Windows 10 1809+ floor. This eliminates the entire dual-codepath legacy-console problem — the single biggest Windows terminal pain — for free.

findings.claim: Node/Electron is disqualified on binary size: a hello-world Node 22 SEA is 124.8 MB, and SEA injects into a platform-specific node binary so cross-building requires the target platform's node.
findings.evidence: Built with --experimental-sea-config + postject on node v22.22.2: base node binary 124,679,552 bytes, SEA 124,783,808 bytes, runs and prints 'hello jio v22.22.2'.
findings.implication: 250x larger than the Rust musl binary (541,840 bytes) for zero functionality. Also inherits V8 GC and JS string UTF-16 boundary hazards. Reject.

findings.claim: Tauri is disqualified twice over: its Linux webview is a SYSTEM webkit2gtk dependency (not a self-contained binary), and it cannot be exercised at all on a headless box with no display server.
findings.evidence: Tauri v2 uses OS-native webviews (WebView2/WebKitGTK/WebKit); Linux .deb depends on webkit2gtk, AppImage inflates ~10MB to ~100MB to bundle it. This container has no GUI/display server per the project constraints.
findings.implication: Violates both the 'download and run' requirement and the 'must be verifiable in CI' requirement. Any GUI approach is unverifiable here — jio should be a TUI editor for v1.

findings.claim: Zig is disqualified by churn, not capability. 0.16.0 landed 2026-04-13 with a std.Io interface rewrite that all but removed std.posix; Ghostty (the flagship Zig terminal) has an open 0.16 migration issue.
findings.evidence: ziglang.org 0.16.0 release notes: 244 contributors, 1183 commits, 'I/O as an Interface', std.posix 'almost completely removed', stricter dependency-loop detection breaks previously-compiling code. ghostty-org/ghostty issue #12228 'Zig 0.16 migration'. Installed ziglang 0.16.0 via pip on this box.
findings.implication: A solo dev would pay a multi-week tax on every Zig release with no editor-specific library ecosystem to show for it. Note the useful inversion: zig is far more valuable to jio as a *linker* (via cargo-zigbuild) than as its implementation language.

findings.claim: Zig IS installable here despite the stated 'no zig' constraint — `pip install ziglang` gives 0.16.0 — and this is what unlocks Rust's macOS cross-compilation.
findings.evidence: `pip install ziglang` -> 'Successfully installed ziglang-0.16.0'; wrapped as `#!/bin/sh; exec python3 -m ziglang "$@"`. cargo-zigbuild then built aarch64-apple-darwin, x86_64-apple-darwin and universal2-apple-darwin.
findings.implication: Correct the project's environment assumption. The single highest-leverage setup step for jio is `pip install ziglang && cargo install cargo-zigbuild`.

findings.claim: C++ cross-compilation is a solved problem via `zig c++` — it hit all 6 targets from here including static musl and both macOS arches — so C/C++ loses on ecosystem, not on portability.
findings.evidence: `zig c++ -target {x86_64,aarch64}-{linux-musl,macos} / {x86_64,aarch64}-windows-gnu` all produced correct ELF/Mach-O/PE binaries; musl output 'not a dynamic executable'.
findings.implication: Reject C/C++ because there is no ropey, no cargo, no crates.io tree-sitter/LSP integration, and every buffer bug is a potential memory-safety CVE — not because it can't ship binaries.

findings.claim: Build times on this 4-vCPU box are a real but acceptable Rust cost: 339-package clean release build = 71s; incremental cargo check on a small crate ≈ 5s. Go is roughly 16x faster cold (4.3s) and 33x faster warm (0.15s).
findings.evidence: Measured with bash `time` in /tmp/.../realed and /tmp/.../gouni. Rust clean release 1m11s (user 4m06s), cargo check after touch 5.7s, debug build 5.0s. Go: clean 4.3s, warm rebuild 0.15s.
findings.implication: This is Go's strongest genuine argument. Mitigate in Rust with a cargo workspace, `cargo check` as the inner loop, opt-level=1 for dev, and lld as linker. 71s cold is survivable; it is not a reason to give up tree-sitter.

findings.claim: Every editor crate jio needs is current and maintained (verified today via cargo, not memory): ropey 1.6.1 (2.0.0-beta.1 published), crop 0.4.3, crossterm 0.29.0, termina 0.4.0, termwiz 0.23.3, ratatui 0.30.2, tree-sitter 0.27.0, tree-sitter-highlight 0.27.0, regex 1.13.1, nucleo 0.5.0, async-lsp 0.2.4, lsp-types 0.97.0, tower-lsp 0.20.0, notify 8.2.0, ignore 0.4.33, grep-searcher 0.1.17, memmap2 0.9.11, arboard 3.6.1, imara-diff 0.2.0.
findings.evidence: `cargo add <crate> --dry-run` against the live crates.io index on 2026-09-07.
findings.implication: jio does not have to build a rope, a fuzzy matcher, a file watcher, a gitignore walker, a diff engine, or an LSP client. That is the whole argument: Rust lets a solo dev spend time on the editor, not on infrastructure.

findings.claim: For the owner's distributed/parallel background, Rust offers a genuine, non-gimmick learning payoff: compiler-checked Send/Sync parallelism (rayon 1.12.0, crossbeam 0.8.5, dashmap 6.2.1), the loom 0.7.2 concurrency model checker, and production CRDT crates (diamond-types 1.0.0, yrs 0.27.4, automerge 0.11.0) for collaborative editing.
findings.evidence: All versions verified via cargo add --dry-run. Zed 1.0 (released 2026-04-29) is the existence proof: its rope is a SumTree with Arc-refcounted nodes chosen precisely because concurrent buffer access was a hard requirement, and text::Buffer is a CRDT layer.
findings.implication: A collaborative jio is a real distributed-systems project (causal ordering, convergence, operational transform vs CRDT) that Rust supports natively. `loom` in particular lets you model-check concurrent buffer code in CI on Linux — directly relevant to the owner's field and impossible to get in Go.

findings.claim: Windows path handling is a genuine, unavoidable Rust papercut: std::fs::canonicalize returns \\?\ verbatim UNC paths that much third-party software rejects, and verbatim paths disable / separators and . / .. normalization.
findings.evidence: rust-lang/rust issue #42869 (canonicalize returns UNC paths, still a known problem), issue #80884 (already-canonicalized paths can't be re-canonicalized with relative components), cargo issue #9770 (Windows device path / long-path meta issue). std::path::Prefix has VerbatimDisk/VerbatimUNC variants.
findings.implication: Budget for it explicitly: wrap canonicalize with a prefix-stripping helper, never store canonicalized paths in config or display them to users, and write CI tests on windows-2025 covering >260-char paths, UNC shares, and case-insensitive-but-case-preserving filename collisions.

findings.claim: Atomic save on Windows is a cross-cutting hazard no language solves for you: MoveFileEx can silently fall back to a non-atomic CopyFile, ReplaceFile requires the target to already exist, and antivirus file locking causes intermittent sharing violations that Chrome works around by retrying.
findings.evidence: Microsoft docs on ReplaceFile/MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING|MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH); antonymale.co.uk 'Atomic File Writes on Windows'; documented Chrome AV file-locking fix.
findings.implication: Design the save path once, with retry-with-backoff, and make it a first-class CI test on windows-2025. This is a top-3 source of 'editor ate my file' bugs and is completely invisible when developing on Linux.

surveys.recommendation:
**#1: Rust.** Not close, and for a reason I verified rather than assumed.

The deciding fact is the cross-compilation asymmetry with tree-sitter in the loop. From this exact headless container I built a 339-crate editor dependency set — tokio, tree-sitter 0.27.0 plus three C grammars, ratatui, ropey, arboard, nucleo — to musl, windows-gnu, macOS arm64, macOS x86_64, and a universal2 fat Mach-O. Tree-sitter's C runtime emitted real Mach-O arm64 objects. Go, doing the same thing, cannot: `go env CGO_ENABLED` returns 0 for every cross target, and Go+cgo to macOS fails even with `zig cc` because the Go runtime needs `-lresolv` and `-framework CoreFoundation` from an actual macOS SDK. Both maintained Go tree-sitter bindings are cgo. So in Go, macOS becomes a build target you can never reproduce locally — under a constraint that already says "no Mac anywhere," that is a compounding risk, not an inconvenience.

Secondary but real: ropey 1.6.1 gave 1.91 µs random inserts on a 125MB/1.77M-line buffer out of the box; Rust's Unicode tables are at 17.0.0 with Indic conjunct-break while Go's uniseg is frozen at 15.0.0 (and I demonstrated them disagreeing on Devanagari); and termina 0.4.0 — which Helix adopted precisely to delete its legacy Windows Console code — hands you uniform ConPTY/VT behavior across all three OSes, erasing the largest Windows terminal problem before you write a line.

Ranked verdict:
1. **Rust** — only language where every artifact builds here AND every editor component already exists.
2. **Go** — genuinely viable *if and only if* jio drops cgo tree-sitter. Fastest iteration by far (0.15s warm rebuild vs Rust's ~5s check), sub-millisecond GC, trivial pure-Go cross-compile to all six targets. Loses on tree-sitter, Unicode currency, and the absence of a mature rope.
3. **C/C++ with zig c++ as the toolchain** — portability is solved (I hit all 6 targets), but you hand-build the rope, the Unicode layer, the LSP client, and every buffer bug is a potential CVE.
4. **Zig** — 0.16.0's std.Io rewrite (2026-04-13) all but deleted std.posix and Ghostty still hasn't migrated. Use zig as jio's *linker*, not its language.
5. **TypeScript/Tauri** — Linux webkit2gtk is a system dependency, so no self-contained binary, and it is completely unverifiable on a headless box.
6. **Electron/Node SEA** — 124.8 MB for hello-world. Disqualified.

Concrete configuration: ship `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` (the gnu build needs GLIBC_2.34 and excludes pre-22.04 systems); build `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` natively on `windows-2025` (the mingw build links legacy msvcrt.dll); build macOS locally with `cargo-zigbuild --target universal2-apple-darwin` and *test* on `macos-26`. First setup command: `pip install ziglang && cargo install cargo-zigbuild && apt-get install mingw-w64 wine qemu-user-static`. Build jio as a TUI on termina/crossterm — it is the only UI shape you can actually test in this environment. Pin runner labels explicitly; never use `macos-latest`/`windows-latest`.

**Strongest argument AGAINST Rust:** the borrow checker is hostile to exactly the data model an editor wants — buffers, views, cursors, undo trees, and plugins all cross-referencing each other in cycles. This is not hypothetical: Helix works around it with one giant `Editor` struct and integer indices instead of references, and Zed had to invent GPUI's whole `Entity<T>`/Arc/RefCell system to make it tractable. A solo developer will lose real weeks to ownership refactors that Go's GC makes evaporate. And I *tested* the usual counterargument and it failed: Go's max STW pause was 0.182ms on a pointer-heavy 1.76M-object live heap, roughly 90x under a frame budget, so "GC ruins keystroke latency" is folklore at this scale. Add Go's 16x faster cold builds and 33x faster warm rebuilds — which matter enormously for a solo dev iterating in a 4-vCPU container — and the honest position is that Rust wins on tree-sitter cross-compilation, Unicode currency, and library availability, *not* on runtime performance.

**What would change my mind:** (a) jio ships without tree-sitter — regex or hand-written highlighting only — in which case Go's cgo problem vanishes and its iteration speed makes it the better solo-dev choice; or (b) a pure-Go tree-sitter runtime (the gotreesitter / wazero-wasm efforts) proves itself against the real grammar corpus, which would erase Rust's single decisive advantage.
risks: macOS is execution-only-in-CI, permanently. You can BUILD macOS binaries here (verified) but never RUN them — no darling, no macOS emulator exists. Every macOS runtime bug is discovered by a red CI job with no local reproduction and no debugger. Mitigate: keep OS-specific code in tiny, heavily-unit-tested modules behind traits; put the logic in platform-independent code that runs on Linux.

cargo-zigbuild's macOS output is linked by zig's LLD against libSystem stubs, not by Apple's real linker against a real SDK. It ran nothing on this box. Subtle differences (weak symbol resolution, TLS, dyld behavior, codesign compatibility) can produce binaries that link cleanly here and crash on a real Mac. Mitigate: also do a native cargo build on macos-26 in CI and diff behavior; treat zigbuild as a fast local check, not the release artifact.

macOS Gatekeeper: an unsigned, unnotarized binary downloaded from a browser is quarantined and refuses to launch with a scary dialog. This is orthogonal to linking and cannot be fixed from Linux — notarization needs an Apple Developer account ($99/yr) and `notarytool`. 'Just download and run' is FALSE on macOS without it. Users will need `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine`.

wine 9.0 gives false confidence. It ran the binaries with identical Unicode output, but wine does NOT faithfully model ConPTY, real console input events, NTFS case-insensitivity, mandatory file locking, antivirus interference, or long-path behavior. Bugs in exactly those areas are the ones that will actually bite, and wine will pass them.

Windows atomic save is a landmine invisible from Linux: MoveFileEx can silently degrade to a non-atomic CopyFile, ReplaceFile needs an existing target, and AV scanners cause intermittent sharing violations. Expect flaky, non-reproducible CI failures on windows-2025 that look like test bugs and are actually real data-loss bugs.

Rust's std::fs::canonicalize returns \\?\ verbatim UNC paths (rust-lang/rust#42869, open for years). Verbatim paths disable / separators and . / .. normalization, and re-canonicalizing them fails (#80884). Storing a canonicalized path in jio's session/config file will produce paths that break on the next run or that other tools reject.

Build-time creep. 339 crates is 71s clean today on 4 vCPU; a real editor with 15 tree-sitter grammars and a full LSP stack will be several minutes clean and 20-60s incremental. Without a workspace split and disciplined feature gating, the inner loop degrades badly in a container with no local cache warmth.

ropey 1.x is explicitly in maintenance mode (no new features; 2.0.0-beta.1 is published but not battle-tested). Adopting 2.0-beta means riding breaking API changes; staying on 1.6.1 means a frozen dependency. Neither is free.

tree-sitter grammar crate versions drift independently of the core (tree-sitter 0.27.0 vs tree-sitter-rust 0.24.2 vs tree-sitter-python 0.25.0 vs tree-sitter-json 0.24.8). ABI mismatches between the core and a grammar are a recurring, hard-to-diagnose failure class. Pin every grammar exactly and gate upgrades behind CI.
The 'free unmetered public-repo CI' assumption is load-bearing. If jio ever goes private, macOS minutes bill at a 10x multiplier and the whole validation strategy needs rethinking on a budget.

GitHub silently migrated macos-latest -> macos-26 in June 2026 and windows-latest -> VS2026. Using floating labels means your only macOS/Windows validation can change out from under you between two identical pushes, with failures that look like your code broke.
The universal2 fat binary doubles download size (837KB vs 411KB even for a stub; realistically ~8MB vs ~4MB). Consider shipping separate arm64/x86_64 artifacts and letting the installer choose.

cargo-xwin is unusable in this container (proxy blocks aka.ms). If you ever need MSVC-target artifacts locally — e.g. to debug an MSVC-only failure — you are stuck waiting on CI round-trips of several minutes per iteration.
open_questions: Is jio a TUI or a GUI editor? This is upstream of the language decision and I've assumed TUI, because a GUI cannot be exercised at all on this headless box. If a GUI is intended, the whole analysis needs redoing around GPUI/wgpu vs winit, and the CI story gets dramatically worse (software rasterizers, screenshot diffing, no real GPU on runners).
Will jio use tree-sitter? This is THE swing factor. Drop it and Go becomes a genuinely strong contender on iteration speed alone. I'd want that decided before the language is locked.

Is collaborative editing (CRDT) actually a goal, or just an appealing tie-in to the owner's distributed-computing background? If it's real, it strengthens Rust considerably (diamond-types 1.0.0, yrs 0.27.4, automerge 0.11.0, plus loom for model-checking). If it's aspirational, it shouldn't influence the choice.
Is there an Apple Developer account, or budget for one ($99/yr)? Without notarization, macOS 'download and run' does not work, regardless of language.

What is the minimum supported Windows version? Committing to Windows 10 1809+ (build 17763) lets you use termina/ConPTY and delete all legacy Console API handling. Supporting Windows 7/8 doubles the terminal code and I'd argue strongly against it.

Should the release Linux artifact be musl-static or a glibc build with an old-glibc container? musl's allocator is notably slower under heavy multithreaded allocation, which could matter for a rope-heavy editor. Worth benchmarking ropey specifically under musl before committing.
Has anyone benchmarked ropey 2.0.0-beta.1 against 1.6.1 for jio's access patterns? If 2.0 is meaningfully better it's worth starting there rather than migrating later.

How large is 'large'? My 125MB test was comfortable. If jio must open multi-GB files, the design changes to memory-mapped + lazy-loaded chunks (memmap2 0.9.11) and ropey's in-memory model stops being sufficient.

Does the owner already know Rust? If not, the borrow-checker learning curve on an editor's cyclic data model is the single biggest schedule risk in this recommendation, and Go's 33x faster feedback loop becomes a much stronger argument.

surveys.label: ui-paradigm
surveys.summary: I built and measured both candidate stacks on this box. A TUI editor shell (ratatui 0.30.2 + crossterm 0.29 + ropey 1.6.1) compiles to 653,976 bytes (509,152 stripped), pulls 91 crates, builds cold in 20s, uses 2.3 MB RSS and starts in 1.4–4.0 ms. The equivalent GUI shell (eframe/egui 0.35 + wgpu 29) compiles to 25,058,280 bytes (19,837,712 stripped) — 38x larger — pulls 345 crates (420 locked), takes 5 minutes cold, and cannot run at all on this box without apt-installing libxkbcommon-x11 and mesa, then Xvfb. eframe 0.36.1 already requires Rust 1.95 > the local 1.94.1, so the current release is unbuildable here today. That asymmetry alone nearly decides it under the no-computer constraint. The decisive CI finding is subtler: a bare PTY (script(1) or pty.fork) does NOT answer terminal capability queries — my crossterm probe emitted `ESC[?u ESC[c` and timed out — whereas the same binary inside a headless tmux pane correctly returned `Ok(false)`. So "spawn a PTY in CI" tests rendering but silently mis-tests capability negotiation. The second decisive finding is that character width is not a solved problem: across 12 test strings, unicode-width 0.2.2, tmux 3.4 and vt100 0.16.2 disagree on 7 of them (emoji 2 vs 1 vs 2 cells; ZWJ family 2 vs 5 vs 6; combining é 1 vs 2 vs 1). Any TUI editor's cursor arithmetic is therefore wrong on some real terminal, always. On Windows, crossterm historically enabled ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING on output but not ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT on input, so query/response escapes never got answers under ConPTY — which is exactly why Helix migrated to termina (merged 2025-08-31). Windows Terminal 1.25 (March 2026) did ship the kitty keyboard protocol, which removes the worst historic Windows key-input gap, but GitHub's windows-2025 runners host conhost, not Windows Terminal, so CI will never exercise the terminal your users actually run. My recommendation is (a) TUI as the only shipped frontend, but structured internally as (d): a pure headless core crate with zero terminal dependencies plus a thin frontend crate — an in-process trait seam, explicitly NOT the xi-editor RPC/process-boundary model that Raph Levien's own retrospective calls too complex to be worth it.

findings.claim: A realistic TUI shell (ratatui 0.30.2 + crossterm 0.29 + ropey 1.6.1 + unicode-width/segmentation) builds to 653,976 bytes (509,152 stripped), 91 crates in tree, 20.46s cold release build. Peak RSS while running in a tmux pane: VmRSS 2,356 kB / VmPeak 3,380 kB. Startup (exec to exit): min 1.40 ms, median 4.01 ms, p95 7.63 ms over 60 runs.
findings.evidence: Built at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/probe. `ls -l target/release/probe` -> 653976; `strip -s` -> 509152; `cargo tree --prefix none | sort -u | wc -l` -> 91; /proc/<pid>/status VmRSS 2356 kB; python perf_counter loop.
findings.implication: jio as a TUI ships a sub-1 MB single-file binary with a ~2 MB working set and instant startup. For comparison, /usr/bin/vim on this box is 4,126,400 bytes. This is a genuinely differentiating product property, not just an engineering convenience.

findings.claim: The equivalent GUI shell (eframe 0.35.0 / egui 0.35.0 / wgpu 29.0.4, one text_edit_multiline widget) builds to 25,058,280 bytes (19,837,712 stripped) — 38x the TUI binary — with 345 crates in tree (420 locked) and a 4m59s cold build. It cannot execute on this dev box out of the box: without DISPLAY it errors `neither WAYLAND_DISPLAY nor WAYLAND_SOCKET nor DISPLAY is set`, and under xvfb-run it panicked with `Library libxkbcommon-x11.so could not be loaded`.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/gui. Build log at /tmp/claude-0/.../tasks/b4dj2iu1i.output. Sizes from stat. Panic trace from xkbcommon-dl-0.4.2/src/x11.rs:59.
findings.implication: Choosing a native GUI means the owner cannot run his own editor until he has a computer again. Every GUI change would be blind-committed and validated only by a CI screenshot. That is a catastrophic feedback loop for a solo project in research phase.

findings.claim: The GUI path is locally runnable only after `apt-get install libxkbcommon-x11-0 mesa-vulkan-drivers libgl1-mesa-dri libegl1` + Xvfb, and then only via llvmpipe software rendering (`libEGL warning: DRI3 error: Could not get DRI3 device`). A screenshot was successfully captured: 800x600 PNG, 105 distinct gray levels, mean 2095.91, stddev 892.3 — i.e. the window did render content, not a blank frame.
findings.evidence: apt install succeeded; `timeout 40 xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1280x800x24" ./target/release/gui` survived to timeout (exit 143 = still alive); `import -window root` produced /tmp/egui_shot.png; `identify` + `convert -format '%[mean] %[standard-deviation] %k'`.
findings.implication: GUI screenshot testing IS mechanically possible on Linux CI. But it is Linux-only, software-rendered (so pixel output will differ from any real GPU), and gives you golden-image tests that break on every font/theme tweak. It validates 'a window appeared', not 'the editor works'.

findings.claim: A bare PTY does not answer terminal capability queries. Running the crossterm probe under `script -qec` and under python `pty.fork()` both produced `Err(Custom { kind: Other, error: "The keyboard enhancement status could not be read within a normal duration" })`, and the parent side saw the raw unanswered query bytes `\x1b[?u\x1b[c`. The identical binary inside a headless `tmux -f /dev/null new-session -d` pane returned `Ok(false)` promptly.
findings.evidence: Direct command output, three separate runs (script, python pty.fork with TIOCSWINSZ, tmux). Parent saw: b'\x1b[?u\x1b[c...The keyboard enhancement status could not be read within a normal duration'.
findings.implication: This is THE headless-CI trap. A PTY is a kernel object, not a terminal emulator — nobody is on the other end to reply to DA1/DECRQM. Any jio CI test that touches capability detection must run the binary inside a real VT emulator (tmux on Linux/macOS; an embedded VT engine everywhere). Otherwise you ship a 2-second startup stall for every user whose terminal is slow to reply, and CI will never see it.

findings.claim: Capability probing writes to stdout and reads stdin. Redirecting stdout to a file made the probe leak `\x1b[?u\x1b[c` into the file and time out, even inside tmux. Only when stdout stayed attached to the pane did detection return `Ok(false)`.
findings.evidence: Two tmux runs: `probe --probe > /tmp/tmuxout.txt` -> timeout + escape bytes in file; `probe --probe` with output read via `tmux capture-pane -p` -> `Ok(false)`.
findings.implication: jio must probe capabilities against /dev/tty (or the console handle on Windows), never stdout, and must degrade instantly when stdout is not a tty. Practically: gate all probing behind an is-terminal check and a hard ~100 ms timeout, and add a CI test that runs jio with stdout piped and asserts it does not stall.

findings.claim: unicode-width 0.2.2, tmux 3.4 and vt100 0.16.2 disagree on the display width of 7 of 12 test strings. Emoji U+1F600: uw=2, tmux=1, vt100=2. ZWJ family (man-ZWJ-woman-ZWJ-girl): uw=2, tmux=5, vt100=6. Combining e+U+0301: uw=1, tmux=2, vt100=1. VS16 heart: uw=2, tmux=3. Devanagari क्षि: uw=3, tmux=4, vt100 n/a. CJK 中文: uw=4, tmux=4 (agree). Flag DE, skin-tone thumbs-up, ambiguous ±/●: all agree at 2.
findings.evidence: Ran /tmp/.../probe/target/release/w (unicode-width 0.2.2 + unicode-segmentation 1.13.3) and measured tmux cell columns by printing a `|` sentinel and reading its column from `tmux capture-pane -p`; vt100 columns via `probe/src/bin/vtgrid.rs` cell-by-cell dump.
findings.implication: jio's cursor column arithmetic will be wrong on some real terminal for emoji, combining marks, and Indic text no matter which width table it picks. Design for this: keep the authoritative model in grapheme clusters, treat cell width as a per-terminal *rendering hint*, re-emit an absolute CUP (CSI row;col H) at the start of every line rather than relying on relative cursor motion, and never assume the terminal's cursor is where you computed.

findings.claim: ratatui 0.30.2 ships `backend::TestBackend`, a fully headless, deterministic, platform-independent render target with per-cell inspection, and it explicitly tracks width hazards — my render printed `Hidden by multi-width symbols: [(8, " "), (10, " "), (13, " ")]` and per-cell dump `[│][h][é][l][l][o][ ][中][ ][文][ ][ ]`.
findings.evidence: Built and ran /tmp/.../probe/src/bin/tb.rs against ratatui 0.30.2.
findings.implication: This is the single most valuable CI asset on the TUI path. 90%+ of jio's UI logic (layout, wrapping, selection painting, syntax colors, scrolling) can be snapshot-tested with zero terminal, zero PTY, identical bytes on ubuntu-latest, macos-26 and windows-2025. Combine with insta 1.48.0 for snapshot review.

findings.claim: A cross-platform PTY+VT integration harness works and I ran it: portable-pty 0.9.0 (which is `NativePtySystem = win::conpty::ConPtySystem` on Windows) driving a child, with vt100 0.16.2 parsing the byte stream into a grid. It produced `row0: "hi OK 中文"` and per-cell SGR assertions `cell(0,3) sym="O" fg=Idx(2) bold=true`.
findings.evidence: Built and ran /tmp/.../probe/src/bin/harness.rs. portable-pty source at /root/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-.../portable-pty-0.9.0/src/win/psuedocon.rs:34 declares `CreatePseudoConsole`, loaded from kernel32.dll with the message "this system does not support conpty. Windows 10 October 2018 or newer is required", and prefers a sideloaded conpty.dll (line 55). lib.rs:407 `pub type NativePtySystem = win::conpty::ConPtySystem`.
findings.implication: This is jio's tier-2 CI layer and it genuinely works on Windows runners: your test process becomes the terminal emulator, so conhost's limitations do not apply. Baseline requirement is Windows 10 build 17763 (1809). There is no winpty fallback in portable-pty 0.9.0, so Windows 8.1 and Win10 pre-1809 are out — state that as jio's floor.

findings.claim: crossterm 0.29.0 has no terminfo dependency at all and is TERM-agnostic. Its full dep tree contains bitflags, derive_more, libc, mio, parking_lot, rustix, signal-hook etc. — no terminfo, no termini, no ncurses. Empirically it returned `Ok(false)` and correct size with TERM='' , TERM=dumb and TERM=foobar-nonexistent inside tmux.
findings.evidence: `cargo tree -p crossterm --prefix none | sort -u`; four tmux runs with hostile TERM values.
findings.implication: This is precisely why crossterm works on Windows, where no terminfo database exists. It emits hardcoded ANSI. The cost is that it cannot adapt to a terminal that lacks a sequence — it just emits it. For jio that trade is correct: assume VT, feature-detect the few things that matter (truecolor, kitty keys, sync output, OSC 52), and hardcode the rest.

findings.claim: crossterm 0.29.0 default features are `bracketed-paste`, `derive-more`, `events`, `windows`. Notably `osc52` is OFF by default, as are `event-stream`, `serde`, `use-dev-tty`.
findings.evidence: `cargo add --dry-run crossterm` feature listing.
findings.implication: jio must explicitly opt into `osc52` for clipboard-over-SSH, and should also consider `use-dev-tty` so probing does not go through stdout (see the redirect trap above). Do not assume defaults give you clipboard.

findings.claim: Helix migrated its terminal backend from crossterm to termina, merged 2025-08-31. The cited reason: crossterm enabled ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING on the output handle but not ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT on the input handle, so under ConPTY it "lacked the ability to read VT inputs from ConPTY though, so we wouldn't ever get a response to request/response type escape codes". Termina instead tells Windows terminals to "speak VT" like a *NIX PTY, dropping the old Console API path.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/helix-editor/helix/pull/13307 (fetched); https://github.com/helix-editor/termina (fetched). termina requires 64-bit Windows 10.0.17763+, same floor as WezTerm, and offers a `windows-legacy` feature for the old console path.
findings.implication: crossterm does NOT fully paper over Windows. The specific hole is feature *detection* on Windows — you can write VT but not reliably read query responses. If jio wants kitty-keys or synchronized output on Windows, plan for the termina backend. ratatui 0.30.2 already shipped `ratatui-termina` for exactly this.

findings.claim: termina 0.4.0 has only 4 direct dependencies (bitflags 2.13.1, parking_lot 0.12.5, rustix 1.1.4, signal-hook 0.3.18) and no terminfo. termwiz 0.23.3 by contrast pulls 104 crates including terminfo 0.9.0 and nix 0.29.0. BUT: ratatui-termina 0.1.0 pins termina 0.3.3 while the current release is 0.4.0, so using both puts two copies of termina in the lockfile.
findings.evidence: `cargo tree` subtree dumps; Cargo.lock contains both `termina 0.3.3` (dependency of ratatui-termina) and `termina 0.4.0`.
findings.implication: termina is the leanest and most Windows-correct backend, but the ratatui integration is at 0.1.0 and already version-skewed. Start jio on ratatui-crossterm 0.1.2 (mature, ratatui's default), keep the backend behind jio's own trait, and switch to ratatui-termina once it tracks termina 0.4.x. Do not adopt bleeding-edge backends you cannot test on Windows by hand.

findings.claim: Windows Terminal 1.25 (Preview March 2026) shipped built-in kitty keyboard protocol support; microsoft/terminal issue #11509 ('Add keyboard protocol support (the kitty one)') is Closed with PR #19817 and milestone 'Terminal v1.25'. This finally lets Windows apps distinguish Esc from Ctrl+[ and receive Shift+Enter.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/issues/11509 (fetched: Closed, PR #19817, milestone Terminal v1.25); corroborated by 4sysops coverage of Preview 1.25 and by the Helix terminal-support wiki listing Windows Terminal 'Enhanced Keyboard' as supported.
findings.implication: The single worst historic Windows TUI limitation is now fixed in the terminal most Windows developers use. jio can plan on kitty keys as the good path on Windows — but must still degrade cleanly, because conhost, older WT, and every Windows CI runner will not have it.

findings.claim: Terminals cannot distinguish these without an escape hatch, because the byte on the wire is identical: Ctrl+I == Tab (0x09), Ctrl+M == Enter (0x0D), Ctrl+[ == Esc (0x1B), Ctrl+J == Ctrl+Enter/LF (0x0A), Shift+Enter == Enter, Ctrl+Shift+X == Ctrl+X (shift is dropped for control chars), and most Ctrl+digit / Ctrl+punctuation combos have no encoding at all. The escape hatches are xterm's modifyOtherKeys (XTMODKEYS), the fixterms/CSI-u encoding, and the kitty keyboard protocol (progressive-enhancement flags queried with CSI ? u).
findings.evidence: microsoft/terminal issue #13792 ('Send different key codes for Tab and Ctrl+I (READ: support modifyOtherKeys)'); invisible-island.net/xterm/modified-keys.html; leonerd.org.uk/hacks/fixterms/; kitty keyboard-protocol docs (sw.kovidgoyal.net is egress-blocked from this box, mirrored at github.com/kovidgoyal/kitty/blob/master/docs/keyboard-protocol.rst).
findings.implication: jio's default keymap must be designed for the LOWEST tier: no Ctrl+Shift, no Ctrl+digit, Tab and Ctrl+I identical, Enter and Ctrl+M identical. Treat kitty-protocol keys as a strict enhancement that unlocks *additional* bindings, never as the baseline. This is a product constraint, not an implementation detail — it is the main reason vim/helix use modal keys and leader chords instead of Ctrl+Shift combos.

findings.claim: Kitty keyboard protocol support as of 2026: supported by kitty, WezTerm (config), foot, Alacritty, iTerm2, Rio (config), Ghostty, and Windows Terminal 1.25+; xterm.js/VS Code added it in PR #5600 (Jan 2026, VS Code 1.109). NOT supported: VTE-based terminals (GNOME Terminal, Tilix, Terminator, Guake, Ptyxis) — patches were still under review as of Dec 2025. macOS Terminal.app does not support it.
findings.evidence: Aggregated from WebSearch results and the Helix Terminal-Support wiki matrix (fetched), which marks GNOME Terminal 'Enhanced Keyboard: ❌' and every modern terminal ✅. tmux 3.4 on this box defaults to `extended-keys off` (verified via `tmux show-options -g extended-keys`).
findings.implication: GNOME Terminal is the default on Ubuntu/Fedora — jio's likely Linux audience. So the no-kitty tier is not a rump case, it is the default Linux desktop. Also note tmux ships extended-keys off, so even a kitty-capable outer terminal loses the protocol inside tmux unless the user configures it.

findings.claim: OSC 52 clipboard is not universally usable. VTE-based terminals (GNOME Terminal, Ptyxis, XFCE, Terminator) do not implement it at all, citing security. xterm supports it but disabled by default (needs `XTerm*disallowedWindowOps: 20,21,SetXprop`). Windows Terminal has it behind an 'Allow OSC 52 to write to clipboard' setting. WezTerm, iTerm2, kitty, Alacritty accept it by default.
findings.evidence: miliucci.org/post/linux-terminals-osc-52-escape/ ('in 2026 Gnome has three "default" terminal emulators none of them support OSC 52, not even Ptyxis'); tmux Clipboard wiki; vim issue #19441; KDE bug 372116.
findings.implication: jio cannot rely on OSC 52 as its only clipboard. Needs a three-way strategy: native clipboard (arboard) when on a local session; OSC 52 when remote and the terminal accepts it; and an internal register/yank buffer that always works. OSC 52 is write-only and fire-and-forget — you cannot detect failure, so never report 'copied' based on having emitted it.

findings.claim: Windows console VT reality: ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING is off by default in conhost (registry HKCU\Console\VirtualTerminalLevel), but any app can enable it via SetConsoleMode, and it is set by default inside a ConPTY pseudo console (microsoft/terminal issue #9432). Microsoft deprecated legacy console mode in December 2023, making it an optional Feature on Demand from Windows 11 24H2; conhost itself is in maintenance mode with new work going to Windows Terminal.
findings.evidence: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/setconsolemode; microsoft/terminal issue #9432; deepwiki.com/microsoft/terminal/2.4-conpty-and-vt-io; search corroboration on the Dec-2023 legacy-console deprecation.
findings.implication: For jio the Windows story is 'call SetConsoleMode yourself and assume VT' — which crossterm and termina both do for output. The residual risk is input-side detection, which is what termina fixes. Windows 10 1809 (build 17763) is the honest minimum; declare it.

findings.claim: GitHub-hosted runner reality for GUI: macos-26 went GA for GitHub-hosted runners in Feb 2026 and macOS runners have an emulated display, so AppKit/NSWindow apps can create windows. windows-latest/windows-2025 migrated to Visual Studio 2026 by default the week of June 8–15, 2026. Linux runners need Xvfb (via coactions/setup-xvfb or GabrielBB/xvfb-action). Tauri's own docs state tauri-driver supports only Windows and Linux on desktop, because macOS has no WKWebView driver.
findings.evidence: github.blog/changelog/2026-02-26-macos-26-is-now-generally-available-for-github-hosted-runners/; github.blog/changelog/2026-05-14-github-actions-upcoming-image-migrations/; v2.tauri.app/develop/tests/webdriver/ci/ and .../webdriver/ ('only Windows and Linux are supported on desktop, as macOS has no WKWebView driver tool available').
findings.implication: GUI CI is technically possible on all three OSes but is three different fragile stacks (Xvfb+llvmpipe / emulated macOS display / Windows session), each producing golden images rather than semantic assertions. Tauri specifically has a hard macOS e2e hole. Compare with the TUI path where ONE harness (TestBackend + portable-pty + vt100) runs byte-identically on all three.

findings.claim: ratatui full-screen redraw cost (layout + diff, TestBackend, no I/O) measured here: 0.100 ms at 80x24, 0.519 ms at 200x50, 2.512 ms at 400x100 — i.e. a 398–10,000 fps ceiling before any terminal I/O.
findings.evidence: /tmp/.../probe/src/bin/bench.rs, 300 iterations after 5 warmups, styled two-span lines per row.
findings.implication: TUI input latency for jio will be dominated by the terminal emulator's parse+GPU present, not by jio. That is good (you inherit the terminal's latency work: kitty/Alacritty/Ghostty are all sub-frame) and bad (you cannot fix a slow terminal). It also means synchronized output (DECSET 2026) matters more than render optimization — emit it when detected to stop tearing.

findings.claim: The hybrid headless-core + RPC-frontends model has a documented failure precedent. Raph Levien's xi-editor retrospective states the project spent too many 'novelty points' — Rust core, rope, multiprocess front-end and plug-ins each with their own process, fully async, CRDT — and that the ambition of a standard protocol other editors would adopt 'absolutely failed to materialize' (Atom went to tree-sitter instead); he concluded the design would require significantly more work than necessary.
findings.evidence: https://raphlinus.github.io/xi/2020/06/27/xi-retrospective.html (via search summary; the page itself was reachable in results, direct fetch not attempted).
findings.implication: Do NOT put a process/RPC boundary in jio v1. The async, out-of-order, back-pressure and cursor-consistency problems of an RPC editor core are strictly harder than the editor itself, and they are exactly the problems that cannot be debugged without a machine. Take the *architectural* benefit of (d) — a core crate that knows nothing about terminals — with an in-process trait seam and zero serialization.

findings.claim: egui/eframe has meaningful API churn: eframe 0.35.0 changed `eframe::App` from `fn update(&mut self, ctx: &Context, frame: &mut Frame)` to `fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut Ui, frame: &mut Frame)` — my first attempt failed with `E0407: method 'update' is not a member of trait 'eframe::App'`. Separately, eframe 0.36.1 requires Rust 1.95 and would not resolve against the local rustc 1.94.1.
findings.evidence: cargo build error output E0407/E0046/E0308 against eframe 0.35.0; `cargo add eframe` reported 'Adding eframe v0.35.0 (available: v0.36.1, requires Rust 1.95)'.
findings.implication: A GUI-first jio means chasing a pre-1.0 toolkit's breaking changes while unable to run the result. ratatui 0.30 also had breaking changes (Alignment -> HorizontalAlignment, MSRV 1.86) but its API surface for an editor is far smaller and every break is caught by a headless test.

findings.claim: Terminal-native accessibility is essentially 'whatever the terminal exposes'. GUI toolkits have a real answer: AccessKit 0.25.0 provides cross-platform screen-reader support, is integrated in egui (native APIs on Windows and macOS, enabled by default in eframe — my build pulled accesskit_winit 0.32.2 and accesskit_unix 0.21.1), plus Slint, Freya and Xilem.
findings.evidence: accesskit.dev; emilk/egui PR #2294; my eframe build log shows accesskit_unix 0.21.1 and accesskit_winit 0.32.2 compiled as default deps.
findings.implication: This is the one dimension where GUI genuinely beats TUI and it cannot be papered over. If jio ever needs first-class screen-reader support, that is the trigger to add a GUI frontend — another reason to keep the core frontend-agnostic from day one. Note the flip side: TUI accessibility is not zero, since screen readers already handle terminals; it is just not under jio's control.

findings.claim: Ghostty has no Windows support and it is not planned for 1.3 (1.2.0 released 2025-09-15, patches through 1.2.3 on 2025-10-23); Windows remains long-term roadmap only. Community ports exist (noctty, formerly winghostty, renamed Aug 2026 after a trademark request). macOS Terminal.app gained 24-bit truecolor in macOS Tahoe (26) — previously it was the main truecolor holdout and Helix's wiki still lists it as unsupported for lacking truecolor.
findings.evidence: ghostty.org/docs/install/release-notes/1-2-0; ghostty-org/ghostty discussion #2563; termstandard/colors issue #69 'Terminal.app for macOS Tahoe supports truecolor'; helix-editor/helix wiki Terminal-Support (fetched) lists Terminal.app under unsupported for truecolor.
findings.implication: jio's truecolor floor just got better: with Tahoe, every current default terminal on all three OSes does truecolor. Detect via COLORTERM in {truecolor,24bit} first, then terminfo RGB/Tc, and keep a 256-color fallback palette — do not assume, because tmux and screen still downsample unless configured.

findings.claim: tmux works as a headless terminal emulator in CI and supports golden-screen assertions: `tmux -f /dev/null new-session -d -x W -y H <cmd>` then `tmux capture-pane -p` (text) or `-pe` (with SGR escapes, e.g. `hello ^[[31mRED^[[39m`). It is present on this box at version 3.4 and is preinstalled on GitHub's Linux and macOS runners.
findings.evidence: Direct runs on this box; `tmux capture-pane -pe | cat -v` output shown above.
findings.implication: tmux is jio's tier-3 CI layer for 'does it work through a real VT emulator' on Linux and macOS. It is NOT available on Windows runners — which is exactly the gap portable-pty+vt100 fills. Note tmux 3.4 defaults extended-keys off and disagrees with unicode-width on 7/12 strings, so treat it as an adversarial environment, which is useful.

findings.claim: microsoft/tui-test exists as a purpose-built cross-platform TUI test runner (Windows, Linux, macOS; shells bash/zsh/fish/pwsh/cmd/nushell; VT backends Alacritty, Ghostty, Rio, xterm.js) but is at 0.1.0-beta.3 and explicitly 'undergoing a major rewrite'.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/microsoft/tui-test (fetched).
findings.implication: Watch it, do not depend on it. A beta-stage rewriting test runner is the wrong foundation for a project whose only validation channel is CI. Build the harness from portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2, which I proved works today and whose combined dependency surface you control.

surveys.recommendation:
Build jio as a TUI editor — option (a) — with option (d)'s internal shape but none of its IPC.

Concretely:
1. Two crates from commit one. `jio-core`: rope (ropey 1.6.1), grapheme-cluster cursor model, undo, selections, syntax, LSP. It must not depend on crossterm/ratatui/termina, and CI must enforce that with a `cargo tree -p jio-core | grep -q crossterm && exit 1` check. `jio-tui`: ratatui 0.30.2 + ratatui-crossterm 0.1.2 (crossterm 0.29, with the `osc52` feature explicitly on). Put your own `Backend`/`Capabilities` trait between them so termina can be swapped in without touching core.
2. Three-tier CI, all of it headless, all of it on ubuntu-latest + macos-26 + windows-2025:
   - Tier 1 (the bulk, ~90%): ratatui `TestBackend` + insta 1.48.0 snapshots. Byte-identical on all three OSes, no terminal, milliseconds. This is where editor behaviour is actually tested.
   - Tier 2 (the cross-platform truth): portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2 — your test process *is* the terminal emulator, so it works on Windows via ConPTY exactly as on Unix. I built and ran this today; it gives you per-cell symbol + fg/bg + bold assertions.
   - Tier 3 (adversarial, Linux+macOS only): drive the real binary inside a headless tmux pane and assert with `capture-pane -pe`. tmux 3.4 disagrees with unicode-width on 7/12 strings and defaults `extended-keys off`, which makes it a useful hostile environment rather than a friendly one.
3. Design the default keymap for the *worst* terminal, not the best. No Ctrl+Shift, no Ctrl+digit; Tab==Ctrl+I and Enter==Ctrl+M are the same key. Kitty-protocol keys unlock extra bindings; they never carry a default binding. GNOME Terminal (VTE, no kitty protocol) is the default on Ubuntu and Fedora, so this tier is the majority Linux case, not an edge case.
4. Treat width as a rendering hint, not truth. Model in grapheme clusters (unicode-segmentation 1.13.3), compute cells with unicode-width 0.2.2, but re-emit an absolute `CSI row;col H` at the start of every painted line so a width disagreement corrupts one line's appearance instead of desynchronising the whole screen. Add a `jio --width-report` subcommand users can paste when their terminal disagrees.
5. Probe capabilities against /dev/tty (or the Windows console handle), never stdout, with a hard ~100 ms timeout, and add a regression test that pipes stdout and asserts no stall. This is the failure I reproduced three different ways today.
6. Clipboard: three-way — arboard when local, OSC 52 when remote and accepted, internal registers always. Never report "copied" on the strength of having emitted OSC 52; it is unacknowledged.

Why not the others, bluntly. (b) Native GUI is disqualified by the constraint, not by taste: eframe is 38x the binary, 345 crates, 5-minute builds, and literally would not execute on this box until I apt-installed X libraries and Mesa. The owner would be unable to run his own editor. (c) Web-tech shell inherits every GUI CI problem plus a WebView-version matrix, and Tauri's own docs admit tauri-driver has no macOS support. (d) as literally specified — separate processes with an RPC protocol — is the xi-editor trap; Levien's retrospective says the protocol ambition "absolutely failed to materialize" and the design needed far more work than necessary. Async cross-process cursor consistency is a harder problem than the editor, and it is the least debuggable class of bug without a machine.

What would change my mind: (i) if jio's actual goal is a *rendering* showcase — ligatures, proportional fonts, smooth scrolling, inline images — the terminal cell model is a hard ceiling and GUI wins outright; (ii) if first-class screen-reader accessibility is a launch requirement, AccessKit 0.25.0 in a GUI is the only real answer; (iii) if the owner gets a laptop, the GUI feedback-loop objection largely evaporates and the decision becomes a normal product call.
risks: A bare PTY answers no capability queries. I reproduced this three ways (script(1), python pty.fork, and stdout-redirected inside tmux): the probe emits ESC[?u ESC[c and times out. If jio's CI spawns a PTY and calls it a terminal test, capability negotiation is untested and every user gets a startup stall that CI never sees. Mitigation: hard timeout on every probe + an explicit no-response test case.

GitHub's windows-2025 runners host conhost, not Windows Terminal. The terminal your Windows users actually run (WT 1.25 with kitty protocol) will NEVER be exercised in CI. Everything Windows-terminal-specific — kitty keys, bracketed paste (the Helix wiki marks WT's as 'borked'), OSC 52 gated behind a WT setting — is validated only by the ConPTY-in-process harness, which by construction cannot reproduce WT's own bugs.

Width disagreement is unfixable, only containable. unicode-width 0.2.2, tmux 3.4 and vt100 0.16.2 disagree on 7 of 12 strings. Whichever table jio's TestBackend snapshots encode, they will be green in CI and wrong on some user's terminal for emoji, ZWJ sequences, combining marks and Indic text. CI cannot catch this class at all — you will only learn from bug reports you cannot reproduce.

macOS is validated only by CI and only through tmux + ConPTY-equivalent harnesses. Terminal.app and iTerm2 behaviours (Option-as-Meta, Terminal.app's fresh Tahoe truecolor implementation, Apple's IME interaction) are untestable. IME/CJK input in particular is a GUI-layer concern of the terminal emulator that no headless harness reaches — jio will be flying blind on Japanese/Chinese/Korean input on macOS.

IME composition is invisible to the application in a terminal. jio receives finished text, not preedit state, so it cannot render a composition underline or reposition a candidate window. This is a permanent product limitation of paradigm (a) and it is untestable in CI on any platform. If CJK users are a target audience, surface this early rather than discovering it post-launch.

Backend churn on a moving target. ratatui-termina is at 0.1.0 and already pins termina 0.3.3 while termina is at 0.4.0 (verified: both appear in my Cargo.lock). If jio adopts termina for Windows correctness, it is adopting a <1.0 crate whose ratatui glue is version-skewed, on the exact platform the owner cannot test by hand.

Rust/toolchain drift outpaces the dev box. eframe 0.36.1 already requires Rust 1.95 and cannot be resolved against the local rustc 1.94.1. CI runners will float ahead of the dev box, so 'builds here' and 'builds in CI' will diverge. Pin a rust-toolchain.toml from day one and make CI use it.

Snapshot tests rot into rubber stamps. TestBackend + insta will produce hundreds of golden buffers. Once a legitimate UI change invalidates 200 snapshots, the review reflex becomes `cargo insta accept`, and real regressions ride along. Keep a small hand-written assertion suite (cursor column after specific edits, selection boundaries) that no bulk-accept can silently change.

tmux and screen downsample truecolor and default extended-keys off. A jio that only ever validates through tmux in CI will encode tmux's behaviour as correct. Test at least one path with a direct ConPTY/PTY harness that is not tmux.

Legacy Windows floor. portable-pty 0.9.0 hard-fails with 'this system does not support conpty. Windows 10 October 2018 or newer is required' — no winpty fallback. Windows 8.1 and Win10 pre-1809 users get a crash, not a degradation, and no runner exists to catch it. Declare build 17763 as the minimum and detect it explicitly with a friendly error.

OSC 52 failures are silent and undetectable. It is write-only with no acknowledgement, and VTE terminals (GNOME Terminal, Ptyxis — the Ubuntu/Fedora defaults) ignore it entirely. jio can emit it, believe it worked, and tell the user 'copied' when nothing was copied. No CI test can distinguish success from silent drop.
open_questions: Is jio meant to be a *terminal* editor as a product identity, or is the terminal merely today's only testable target? If the long game is a Zed-class GUI editor, the core/frontend seam must be designed for pixels (subpixel positioning, variable line heights, inline widgets) from the start — retrofitting that onto a cell-grid-shaped core is where the real migration cost lives, not in the frontend code itself.

Does the owner expect to have a machine again within, say, 6 months? That single fact dominates the decision. If yes, the GUI objection is temporary and the architecture should hedge harder toward pixels; if no, commit fully to the TUI.

Should jio target modal editing? It is not a style question under this constraint — modal keymaps exist largely because terminals cannot express Ctrl+Shift+X. A non-modal jio will run out of expressible chords on GNOME Terminal specifically.

What is jio's minimum supported terminal? I would propose: VT + truecolor + bracketed paste required; kitty keyboard protocol, synchronized output (DECSET 2026), OSC 52 and grapheme clustering (DECSET 2027) all optional enhancements. This needs to be a written, tested contract, not an emergent property.

Should jio implement DECSET 2027 (grapheme clustering mode) negotiation? It is the only real fix for the ZWJ/combining-mark width problem, but support is thin and I could not verify which shipped terminals honour it as of 2026-09. Worth a dedicated probe.

How will the Windows kitty-protocol path be validated at all, given that GH runners have no Windows Terminal? Options: a self-hosted Windows runner with WT installed; asking a friend/colleague to run a `jio doctor` capability dump; or accepting the gap explicitly and shipping a user-facing diagnostic subcommand. Pick one deliberately.

Is there appetite for jio to embed its own VT parser (alacritty_terminal 0.26.0 is on crates.io) as a test oracle, so CI compares jio's own rendering intent against a production-grade emulator's interpretation? That would catch a real class of escape-sequence bugs that TestBackend cannot.

surveys.label: text-buffer-core
surveys.summary: I benchmarked ropey 1.6.1, crop 0.4.3, jumprope 1.1.2, plain String, Vec<String> and a hand-written naive piece table on this box (Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, rustc 1.94.1, --release) against 200 KiB / 64 MiB / 1 GiB corpora, and verified line-break, UTF-16, grapheme and encoding semantics with real test programs rather than trusting docs. Headline: all three rope crates are 60-180 ns per realistic (localized) edit; a plain String is 2.4 us/edit at 200 KiB and 1.51 ms/edit at 64 MiB, so the rope is non-negotiable above toy sizes. The published crate benchmarks are misleading — crop and jumprope advertise 3x wins over ropey using localized real-editing traces; under uniformly random edits ropey actually beats both. crop wins on the metrics that matter for an editor: lowest memory (1.054 bytes/byte vs ropey 1.153, jumprope 2.368, Vec<String> 1.834), fastest load (45 vs 71 ms) and fastest viewport iteration (19.9 vs 32.5 ms). The decisive non-performance argument is indexing: tree-sitter's InputEdit and Point are entirely byte-based, LSP's UTF-8 positionEncoding is byte-based, and ripgrep returns bytes — ropey 1.x forces char indices on insert/remove, creating an index-confusion bug class that only manifests on non-ASCII text, i.e. exactly what cannot be caught by manual testing you don't have. I also found a live correctness hazard: ropey's default unicode_lines feature counts U+2028/VT/NEL/FF as line breaks while crop, Rust's str::lines() and LSP do not — verified divergence. I caught and corrected one of my own measurement errors: an apparent 76x snapshot-sharing advantage for ropey was an allocator-reuse artifact; re-measured in fresh processes, a rope snapshot per keystroke costs 2.5-3.1 KB in both crates, which rules out snapshot-per-keystroke undo in favour of a Helix-style inverted ChangeSet log. 1 GiB is feasible (2.0 s load, 1.18 GB RSS) but should be a degraded read-only mode.

findings.claim: A plain String buffer is not viable above ~1 MiB, but is genuinely fine below it. Measured single-char insert cost: 2379 ns at 200 KiB, and 1.51 ms per insert at 64 MiB (15,148 ms for 10k inserts).
findings.evidence: Own benchmark, /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/bufbench: 'String: 10k random 1-char inserts (memmove) 15147.842 ms' on 64 MiB; 'String localized: 237.94 ms (2379 ns/edit)' on 200 KiB.
findings.implication: Do not build a String fast-path for small files. The rope is already 60-170 ns/edit at 200 KiB, i.e. 40x faster than String even at small sizes. One code path, always the rope.

findings.claim: The published crop/jumprope benchmarks measure LOCALIZED editing traces and do not generalize. Under uniformly random insert positions on 64 MiB, ropey is fastest (136 ms/100k) and crop (178 ms) and jumprope (345 ms) are slower — the reverse of their READMEs. Under localized edits the README ordering returns: crop 140 ns, jumprope 166 ns, ropey 168 ns.
findings.evidence: Own benchmarks. Random: ropey 136.061 ms, crop 178.085 ms, jumprope 345.446 ms per 100k inserts. Localized (cursor drifts, jumps every 500 edits): crop 14.05 ms, jumprope 16.62 ms, ropey 16.84 ms per 100k. crop README claims automerge-paper 12.39ms vs ropey 44.14ms.
findings.implication: Real typing is localized, so crop's and jumprope's advantage is real for the common case — but it is ~1.2x, not the ~3.5x advertised. Do not pick a crate on README benchmark numbers; the gap between crates is far smaller than the gap to any non-rope structure.

findings.claim: crop 0.4.3 has the lowest memory overhead of any candidate: 1.054 bytes of RSS per byte of text, vs ropey 1.153, Vec<String> 1.834 (85 bytes overhead per line), jumprope 2.368.
findings.evidence: Own benchmark on 64 MiB corpus, per-process RSS delta via /proc/self/statm: crop 'RSS delta over String: 67.5 MiB (bytes/byte 1.054)'; ropey 73.8 MiB (1.153); jumprope 151.5 MiB (2.368); Vec<String> 117.4 MiB (1.834).
findings.implication: On a 1 GiB file that is a ~100 MB RAM difference between crop and ropey. jumprope's 2.37x makes it unsuitable for large files regardless of its edit speed.

findings.claim: tree-sitter 0.27.0 is entirely byte-indexed: InputEdit carries start_byte/old_end_byte/new_end_byte plus Point{row, column} where column is BYTES from line start, and parse_with_options takes a callback FnMut(usize, Point) -> impl AsRef<[u8]>.
findings.evidence: Read directly from crate source at ~/.cargo/registry/src/*/tree-sitter-0.27.0/binding_rust/lib.rs lines 103-127 and 953: 'pub struct InputEdit { pub start_byte: usize, pub old_end_byte: usize, pub new_end_byte: usize, pub start_position: Point, ... }'.
findings.implication: A byte-indexed rope (crop, ropey 2.0) feeds tree-sitter directly. ropey 1.x's char-indexed insert/remove forces a byte_to_char conversion (measured 437-458 ns) plus byte->line and line_to_byte on every edit just to construct one InputEdit. This is the single strongest architectural argument for crop.

findings.claim: ropey 1.6.1's mutation API is char-indexed and cannot be opted out of: 'pub fn insert(&mut self, char_idx: usize, text: &str)' and 'pub fn insert_char(&mut self, char_idx: usize, ch: char)'.
findings.evidence: Read from ~/.cargo/registry/src/*/ropey-1.6.1/src/rope.rs lines 343 and 356.
findings.implication: Mixing a byte offset and a char index compiles fine (both usize) and behaves correctly on ASCII, failing only on non-ASCII input. With no macOS/Windows machine and CI-only validation, a silent bug class that only fires on CJK/emoji files is exactly the risk profile jio must avoid.

findings.claim: ropey's DEFAULT feature set (unicode_lines) counts U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR, U+000B VT, U+000C FF and U+0085 NEL as line breaks. crop, Rust's str::lines(), and LSP do not. Verified divergence on real strings.
findings.evidence: Own test program: for input 'let s = "a\u{2028}b";' ropey.len_lines()=2, crop.line_len()=1, str::lines()=1. Same 2-vs-1 split for VT, NEL, FF. ropey/src/lib.rs lines 125-147 documents unicode_lines as default and implying cr_lines.
findings.implication: A JS/Rust source file containing a literal U+2028 makes ropey report different line numbers than the LSP server, silently misplacing every diagnostic below that line. If ropey is used it MUST be built with default-features=false. crop has the correct semantics by construction.

findings.claim: Editing across a CRLF pair produces DIFFERENT line counts in ropey and crop, confirming CRLF is a real corruption hazard and not a theoretical one. Inserting 'X' between CR and LF in "win\r\nline\r\n": ropey goes 3 -> 4 lines, crop goes 3 -> 2 lines.
findings.evidence:
Own test program output: 'ropey -> "winX
line
" len_lines=4' vs 'crop -> "winX
line
" line_len=2'. VS Code blog: 'Dealing with CRLF or mixed line breaks sequences is a programmer's nightmare. For every modification, we need to check if it splits a Carriage Return/Line Feed (CRLF) sequence, or if it creates a new CRLF sequence.'
findings.implication: jio must normalize to LF in the buffer and re-emit the recorded line-ending style on save. This makes CRLF handling a two-point problem (load, save) that is fully testable in CI, instead of an invariant every edit operation must maintain.

findings.claim: crop 0.4.3 recognizes ONLY LF and CRLF as line terminators — which exactly matches LSP, but means a classic-Mac CR-only file loads as a single line.
findings.evidence: Own test: input 'a\rb\rc' gives ropey.len_lines()=3, crop.line_len()=1, str::lines()=1. crop/src/rope/iterators.rs:369 'terminators (`\n` or `\r\n`)'.
findings.implication: This is crop's one real functional gap. It is fixed by the same load-time normalization that solves CRLF: detect and convert CR-only to LF on load, record the style, restore on save. Not a blocker, but it must be handled at the I/O boundary or CR-only files render as one giant line.

findings.claim: ropey 1.6.1 and crop 0.4.3 both compute UTF-16 code-unit offsets correctly, verified against Rust's encode_utf16() ground truth including a ZWJ family emoji. crop's utf16-metric costs only +0.8% memory (1.0574 -> 1.0657 bytes/byte) and no measurable load time.
findings.evidence: Own test on 'aé漢👨‍👩‍👧‍👦b': bytes=32 chars=11, ropey.len_utf16_cu=15, crop.utf16_len=15, t.encode_utf16().count()=15. Separate feature-flag benchmark: crop baseline 1.0574 bytes/byte vs with utf16-metric 1.0657, load 51 ms vs 50 ms. ropey char_to_utf16_cu measured 605 ns over 100k calls.
findings.implication: Enable crop's utf16-metric unconditionally. LSP position mapping is essentially free and must not be bolted on later — negotiate positionEncoding with the server, prefer utf-8, but always be able to serve utf-16.

findings.claim: A rope snapshot per keystroke costs 2.5-3.1 KB in BOTH crates — persistent structural sharing does not make per-keystroke undo snapshots cheap. Measured in fresh processes: crop 2507 B/snapshot at 1454 ns, ropey 3137 B/snapshot at 2008 ns.
findings.evidence: Own benchmark src/bin/snap.rs, 20k localized edits on a 200 KiB base, separate process per crate to avoid allocator reuse. NOTE: an earlier run in a shared process reported 33 B/snapshot for ropey; that was an allocator-reuse artifact after dropping a prior 60 MiB history, and I discarded it.
findings.implication: Do NOT implement undo as a rope snapshot per keystroke — 20k undo steps would cost 50-60 MiB. Use a Helix-style inverted ChangeSet log (tens of bytes per edit) with typing-burst coalescing, and optionally keep a rope snapshot only at coalesced undo-step boundaries, where O(1) clone and ~1.1 us restore make it cheap.

findings.claim: A naive (non-tree) piece table degenerates catastrophically: after 200k random single-char edits on 64 MiB it held 399,399 pieces at 379 us per edit and 9.1 MiB of piece metadata.
findings.evidence: Own implementation and benchmark, src/bin/undo.rs 'piece' mode. This is ~280x slower per edit than ropey on the same workload. VS Code blog corroborates: a plain piece table has O(N) line lookup, 'we have to go through all nodes until we find the node containing that line'.
findings.implication: Piece table is only viable as a balanced piece TREE (VS Code's red-black tree storing left-subtree text length and line-break count). That is strictly more work to build than adopting a rope crate, with no measured advantage. Rejected for jio.

findings.claim: Array-of-lines (Vec<String>) is disqualified on memory and on structural edits, though it is unbeatable for viewport access. Measured 1.834 bytes/byte and 85 bytes overhead per line; inserting a line at the middle costs 1.3 ms (Vec memmove of 1.4M String headers); line->byte with no index is 256 us per lookup.
findings.evidence: Own benchmark: 'Vec<String> RSS delta: 117.4 MiB (bytes/byte 1.834) for 1433776 lines -> 85 B/line overhead'; '100 x insert new line at middle 132.429 ms'; viewport 50 lines was 0.000 ms (direct index). VS Code blog reports the equivalent JS structure at ~600 MB for a 35 MB file, 'roughly 20 times the initial file size'.
findings.implication: Rejected as the primary buffer. But its one strength is real: keep a cached, lazily-built viewport line index on top of the rope so redraw does not re-walk the tree per line — crop's viewport iteration is 19.9 ms/100k lines, which is fine, but a cache makes scrolling free.

findings.claim: jumprope 1.1.2 is disqualified for a text editor: it has no line tracking at all, and it has the worst memory profile of the candidates (2.368 bytes/byte).
findings.evidence: Own benchmark (jumprope exposes len_bytes/len_chars/insert/remove/substrings but no line API; there is no line_to_byte or line count in the crate). Memory measured at 151.5 MiB over a 64 MiB corpus. README confirms UTF-16 only via optional wchar_conversion feature.
findings.implication: Eliminated. An editor needs line/column on every keystroke for the gutter, LSP, and tree-sitter Points; rebuilding that on top of jumprope means writing the hard part yourself.

findings.claim: Ropey 2.0.0-beta.1 exists and is a byte-indexed redesign with pluggable metrics — it is the natural long-term successor, but it is still beta with an unstable API.
findings.evidence: cargo add --dry-run 'ropey@2.0.0-beta.1' succeeds; features are metric_lines_lf_cr + simd (default) with metric_chars, metric_lines_lf, metric_lines_unicode, metric_utf16 opt-in. CHANGELOG: 'Indexing is now byte based', 'All indexing metrics other than byte index are now behind feature flags... the char indexing metric is not enabled by default', 'all line-based APIs now take a LineType parameter'. Unreleased section still shows renames ('Renamed LineType::All to LineType::Unicode'); last tagged alpha 2025-06-01.
findings.implication: Confirms the ecosystem is converging on byte indexing + selectable line metrics, which is exactly crop's model. Designate ropey 2.0 as jio's migration target once it goes stable; do not build on a beta whose enum variants are still being renamed.

findings.claim: Helix's cursor model is the right one to copy: Range{anchor: usize, head: usize, old_visual_position}, Selection{ranges: SmallVec<[Range;1]>, primary_index}, with ranges mapped through a ChangeSet of Retain/Delete/Insert using Assoc::{BeforeSticky, AfterSticky}, then normalized (sorted + overlaps merged) and grapheme-aligned.
