findings.evidence: Read from helix-core source: selection.rs defines those structs, 'A selection can never be empty (always contains at least primary range)', from()/to() give min/max, map(changes: &ChangeSet), normalize()/merge(), grapheme_aligned(slice: RopeSlice). transaction.rs defines 'pub enum Operation { Retain(usize), Delete(usize), Insert(Tendril) }', ChangeSet{changes, len, len_after}, compose(), invert() ('returns a new changeset that reverts this one'), map_pos(pos, assoc).
findings.implication: This single model solves cursors, multi-cursor, undo (invert) and future OT/CRDT collaboration (compose) at once. Adopt it wholesale but in BYTE offsets rather than Helix's char offsets, since jio's rope will be byte-indexed. SmallVec<[Range;1]> means the single-cursor case costs no heap allocation.

findings.claim: Encoding must be handled entirely at the I/O boundary. encoding_rs 0.8.40 round-trips windows-1252, GBK, Shift-JIS and UTF-16LE+BOM losslessly for valid input, but invalid UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD, which is irreversibly lossy.
findings.evidence: Own test: latin1/GBK/Shift-JIS all decoded then re-encoded byte-identical (roundtrip identical: true, had_errors: false). UTF-16LE with BOM decoded correctly. But 'ok\xffbad\x80end' decoded to 'ok\u{FFFD}bad\u{FFFD}end' with had_errors=true — the original bytes are unrecoverable. Crates verified present: encoding_rs 0.8.40, chardetng 1.0.0, encoding_rs_io 0.1.8.
findings.implication: The rope must hold UTF-8 only. Decode on load with chardetng for detection + encoding_rs for conversion; store detected encoding, BOM presence and line-ending style on the Document; re-encode on save. Never let a non-UTF-8 byte reach the rope.

findings.claim: Lossless round-trip of invalid bytes IS achievable inside a normal Rust str/rope by escaping each invalid byte to a Plane-16 private-use codepoint (U+10FE00 + byte). I implemented and verified exact round-trip for lone 0xFF, latin-1 mojibake, truncated multi-byte sequences and arbitrary binary.
findings.evidence: Own implementation src/bin/lossless.rs: all five test cases report ROUNDTRIP_EXACT=true, including '\x00\x01\x7f\x80\xc0\xc1\xf5\xff'. Verified the escaped string is valid UTF-8 and stores/round-trips through ropey unchanged. Note surrogates U+DC80..DCFF (Python's PEP 383 surrogateescape) cannot be used because Rust str forbids them.
findings.implication: This gives jio the 'never corrupt a file you didn't fully understand' guarantee for free, at a cost of 4 buffer bytes per invalid input byte. Implement it in the loader; it is the difference between 'jio mangled my binary-ish config file' and not.

findings.claim: 1 GiB files are feasible but should trigger a degraded mode. ropey loads 1 GiB via from_reader in 2017 ms at 1181 MiB RSS (1.153x) with 22.9M lines; line_to_byte degrades to 1713 ns and random insert to 2882 ns (vs 667/1361 ns at 64 MiB).
findings.evidence: Own benchmark src/bin/undo.rs 'big' mode. Comparison: read_to_string of the same file is 2196 ms at 1.000x.
findings.implication: Set thresholds: <8 MiB load plainly; 8-256 MiB stream through a RopeBuilder in 64 KiB chunks (measured 91 ms for 64 MiB with crop's RopeBuilder, matching VS Code's 64 KiB chunking); >256 MiB open in large-file mode with tree-sitter and LSP disabled; refuse or warn above min(2 GiB, RAM/4).

findings.claim: mmap is excellent for read-only viewing and useless for an editable buffer: mapping 1 GiB takes 0.012 ms with zero RSS (lazy), touching all pages costs 672 ms, and UTF-8 validating the whole file costs 119 ms.
findings.evidence: Own benchmark, 'mmap' mode: 'mmap file 0.012 ms', 'RSS delta 0.0 MiB (lazy)', 'count newlines 671.902 ms', 'utf8 validate 118.759 ms'.
findings.implication: Use mmap only for the huge-file read-only/search path, never as the edit buffer. It also carries a cross-platform hazard you cannot test manually: on Unix, truncation of the underlying file by another process raises SIGBUS, and Windows file-locking semantics differ entirely — both are CI-detectable only if you write explicit tests for them.

findings.claim: The rope crates carry essentially zero cross-platform risk: no OS-specific code in ropey or crop, and str_indices' SIMD uses only baseline-guaranteed SSE2 on x86_64 and NEON on aarch64, with a scalar fallback for other targets.
findings.evidence: grep of crate sources: no target_os/windows/macos matches in ropey-1.6.1/src or crop-0.4.3/src. str_indices-0.4.4/src/byte_chunk.rs uses '#[cfg(all(feature="simd", target_arch="x86_64"))] pub(crate) type Chunk = x86_64::__m128i;' and the aarch64 uint8x16_t equivalent, plus a '#[cfg(not(any(target_arch="x86_64", target_arch="aarch64")))]' fallback. No runtime feature detection, no target-feature flags required. ropey has 29 unsafe sites, crop 23.
findings.implication: The buffer layer will behave identically on the Linux dev box and on macOS/Windows CI runners, including Apple Silicon. jio's genuine cross-platform risk lives entirely in the I/O boundary — line endings, encodings, path handling, file locking — which is precisely where the load/save normalization design must be tested.

findings.claim: crop 0.4.3 is actively maintained (released ~January 2026, Rust edition 2024) but is a single-maintainer crate with a far smaller user base than ropey (~320 stars vs ropey's ~341k downloads/month and 412 dependent crates, with Helix as its flagship user).
findings.evidence: crates.io version history via search: crop 0.4.3 published by Riccardo Mazzarini ~8 months before 2026-09-07. crop Cargo.toml declares edition = "2024". ropey download/dependent figures from crates.io/lib.rs search results. helix-core/Cargo.toml depends on ropey (workspace version) with unicode_lines as an optional feature, plus encoding_rs 0.8, unicode-segmentation, smartstring 1.0.1.
findings.implication: This is the real cost of choosing crop over ropey and the reason the rope must sit behind jio's own Buffer wrapper. Note Helix marks ropey's unicode_lines OPTIONAL, which suggests they hit the same line-break-semantics problem.

surveys.recommendation:
Start with crop 0.4.3, features = ["simd" (default), "graphemes", "utf16-metric"], wrapped behind jio's own `Buffer` newtype that exposes ONLY byte offsets.

Why crop over ropey 1.6.1 (the safe, boring alternative):
1. Byte-native indexing matches every other component in the stack — tree-sitter's InputEdit/Point (verified all-byte), LSP's utf-8 positionEncoding, ripgrep/memchr search results, and Rust's own `str`. ropey 1.x forces char indices on insert/remove, and a byte/char mixup compiles cleanly and works on ASCII, failing only on non-ASCII. With no macOS/Windows machine, silent bug classes that need exotic input to reproduce are the ones that will actually ship broken.
2. Correct line semantics by construction: LF + CRLF only, exactly matching LSP. ropey's default unicode_lines counts U+2028/VT/NEL/FF as line breaks (verified), which silently desyncs every diagnostic below such a character.
3. Lowest measured memory (1.054 bytes/byte vs 1.153), fastest load (45 vs 71 ms), fastest viewport iteration (19.9 vs 32.5 ms), fastest realistic localized edits (140 vs 168 ns), and cheaper snapshots (2507 vs 3137 B).
4. Built-in grapheme and UTF-16 APIs; ropey has no grapheme support at all (Helix had to write helix-core/src/graphemes.rs). crop's utf16-metric costs +0.8% memory.
5. crop panics loudly on a non-char-boundary offset rather than silently corrupting — I triggered this accidentally in my own benchmark, which is exactly the behaviour you want when you cannot debug on the target platform.

Architecture to build around it:
- `jio::Buffer` wraps `crop::Rope` and exposes byte offsets only. Every crop call site lives in one module so swapping to ropey 2.0 (or ropey 1.6.1) is a ~200-line change. Given CI-only validation this wrapper is not optional — it is what makes the decision reversible.
- Cursors: copy Helix's model exactly but in bytes. `Range { anchor: usize, head: usize }`, `Selection { ranges: SmallVec<[Range;1]>, primary_index: usize }`, half-open (inclusive left, exclusive right) regardless of anchor/head order, normalized by sort + merge-overlaps, grapheme-aligned before rendering or cursor movement. Multi-cursor is then free; vim's single cursor is just `ranges.len()==1`. Do NOT model cursors as a separate list that edits patch ad hoc (the VS Code approach) — you will get the ordering bugs wrong.
- Edits: one `ChangeSet { Retain(n) | Delete(n) | Insert(text) }` type. Every mutation goes through it. `apply` mutates the rope, `invert` gives undo, `compose` merges, `map_pos(pos, Assoc)` transforms cursors, marks, diagnostics and fold state through the same code path. This is the single highest-leverage design decision: it makes undo, multi-cursor and future collaborative editing one mechanism instead of three.
- Undo: an inverted-ChangeSet log with typing-burst coalescing, NOT a rope snapshot per keystroke (measured 2.5-3.1 KB each — 20k keystrokes would be 50-60 MiB). Optionally keep an O(1) rope clone at each coalesced undo-step boundary for instant restore (~1.1 us).
- Encoding: rope holds UTF-8 only. Decode at load with chardetng 1.0.0 + encoding_rs 0.8.40; store detected encoding, BOM and line-ending style on the Document; re-encode on save. Escape invalid bytes to U+10FE00+byte for exact lossless round-trip (verified working) — never U+FFFD.
- Line endings: normalize to LF inside the buffer, record the original style (and whether the file was mixed), re-emit on save. This makes CRLF a two-point problem (load/save) that CI can test byte-for-byte, instead of an invariant every edit must maintain. It is also the only way to guarantee a Windows file edited on Linux round-trips when you cannot open it on Windows yourself.
- Large files: <8 MiB load plainly; 8-256 MiB stream via RopeBuilder in 64 KiB chunks (91 ms for 64 MiB, same chunking VS Code chose); >256 MiB large-file mode with tree-sitter and LSP off; mmap only for read-only view/search; refuse above min(2 GiB, RAM/4).

CI test suite that substitutes for the machines you do not have (run on ubuntu/macos/windows runners): a proptest round-trip asserting load(save(x)) == x byte-for-byte over fixtures covering CRLF, LF, CR-only, mixed endings, UTF-16LE+BOM, GBK, Shift-JIS, latin-1, invalid UTF-8, and a 1 MiB no-trailing-newline file; a differential test asserting jio's line/column and UTF-16 offsets agree with an independent reference implementation; and a `.gitattributes` containing `* -text` plus `*.crlf binary` so git's autocrlf on the Windows runner does not silently rewrite your fixtures and make the tests pass for the wrong reason.

What would make me pick ropey 1.6.1 instead: if you want the maximum-boring choice and are willing to pay the char-index tax, ropey with `default-features = false, features = ["simd", "cr_lines"]` (never the default features) is defensible — Helix ships it on all three platforms, which is strong evidence it works. I would still not choose it, because the char/byte tax is paid on every tree-sitter edit forever.
risks: Git's autocrlf on the Windows CI runner will rewrite text fixtures on checkout, so a CRLF round-trip test can pass on Windows for the wrong reason (or fail spuriously) while passing honestly on Linux. Mitigate with an explicit .gitattributes ('* -text', fixtures marked 'binary') and assert on bytes read from disk, not on repo content. This is the single most likely way a line-ending bug reaches users undetected.

crop is effectively a single-maintainer crate with a small user base (~320 stars) compared to ropey (~341k downloads/month, 412 dependents, Helix as flagship). If it stalls or develops a correctness bug, jio is on its own. The Buffer wrapper bounds this to a ~200-line migration, but the risk is real and is the main reason to keep the wrapper disciplined from commit one.

crop treats a CR-only (classic Mac) file as a single line (verified). If load-time normalization is not implemented before the first release, such files render as one enormous line and every line-based feature misbehaves. This is easy to miss because CR-only files are rare and you will never produce one by accident on Linux.

Byte offsets can land mid-character. crop panics on a non-char-boundary offset — I triggered this in my own benchmark. Loud failure is the right behaviour, but a panic in the render path crashes the editor and loses unsaved work. Every externally-supplied offset (LSP responses, search results, restored session state) must be snapped to a char boundary at the trust boundary, and the editor needs a panic handler that persists the buffer before dying.

LSP positionEncoding is negotiated per server. If jio assumes utf-8 and a server only supports utf-16 (or vice versa), every position is silently wrong for non-ASCII lines only — invisible in ASCII test fixtures and undiagnosable without the actual server. Test both encodings explicitly against a real server in CI, with a fixture containing CJK and astral-plane emoji.

Grapheme clusters, not chars, are the cursor movement unit — verified that the ZWJ family emoji is 11 chars but 1 grapheme. Getting this wrong makes cursor movement visibly broken on emoji and Devanagari, and unicode-segmentation's tables change between Unicode versions, so a crate bump can silently shift cursor behaviour. Pin unicode-segmentation and treat a bump as a behaviour change (Helix pins unicode-width=0.1.12 for exactly this reason).

Snapshot-based undo looks cheap because clone() is O(1), but each divergent snapshot costs 2.5-3.1 KB. A naive 'snapshot every keystroke' undo stack silently consumes ~60 MiB per 20k keystrokes. This will not show up in any short test and will be reported as a memory leak much later.

Terminal rendering width (unicode-width) diverges between terminals and OSes far more than the buffer layer does. Wide CJK, emoji and combining marks will render misaligned on Windows Terminal vs iTerm vs Linux, and this is genuinely not verifiable in CI — no runner gives you a real terminal to look at. Budget for user bug reports here rather than expecting to catch it yourself.

The 1 GiB path allocates ~1.18 GB with ropey (~1.08 GB with crop). GitHub-hosted runners historically provide ~7-16 GB RAM but the editor plus test harness plus OS can still OOM on a large-file test, and an OOM-killed runner reports as a confusing generic failure. Gate large-file tests behind an explicit opt-in job rather than the default PR check.

mmap for the read-only huge-file path has genuinely divergent semantics across platforms: SIGBUS on Unix if the file is truncated underneath, and different sharing/locking rules on Windows that can block other processes from writing the file. Neither is reproducible on the Linux dev box, and both need deliberate CI tests or the feature should be deferred.
open_questions: Should jio normalize mixed-line-ending files to LF on load (simple, testable, but silently rewrites the file's mixed character on save) or preserve them exactly (faithful, but reintroduces the CRLF-splitting invariant into every edit)? My recommendation is normalize + record, but a user editing a deliberately-mixed fixture file would be surprised. Worth deciding explicitly and documenting.

Does crop's chunk/leaf structure expose a stable anchor abstraction, or must jio maintain its own mark/anchor table mapped through ChangeSets? Zed's SumTree tracks anchors natively; neither crop nor ropey does. This matters for diagnostics, folds, breakpoints and git gutter markers surviving edits, and I did not verify how expensive a separate anchor table becomes at thousands of marks.

Is ropey 2.0 likely to reach stable within jio's development window? Its last tagged alpha was 2025-06-01 and the beta's CHANGELOG still shows unreleased enum renames. If it stabilizes soon it is arguably a better long-term target than crop (same byte-native model, much larger community); if it stalls indefinitely the crop choice stands on its own.

If collaborative editing is ever wanted, is a ChangeSet/OT model (Helix, composable, what I recommend) sufficient, or does jio need a real CRDT (diamond-types, Loro, Automerge)? OT requires a central server to order operations; a CRDT does not but imposes per-character metadata and a different buffer integration. I did not benchmark any CRDT here. The ChangeSet design keeps the door open but does not make the migration free.

What is the actual latency budget? I measured operations in the 60-3000 ns range, which is far under a 16 ms frame for single edits, but I did not measure the full keystroke-to-pixel path with tree-sitter re-parse, LSP round-trip and terminal redraw included. The buffer is almost certainly not the bottleneck, but that should be confirmed before optimizing it further.

Should the viewport maintain a cached line index on top of the rope? crop's viewport iteration (19.9 ms per 100k lines) is fine, but I did not measure the realistic case of redrawing ~50 visible lines at 60 fps while tree-sitter highlighting queries run concurrently against the same rope.
sources: local crate sources: ~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-*/ropey-1.6.1/, ropey-2.0.0-beta.1/, crop-0.4.3/, str_indices-0.4.4/, tree-sitter-0.27.0/binding_rust/lib.rs

own benchmarks: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/bufbench/ (src/main.rs, src/bin/local.rs, src/bin/undo.rs, src/bin/snap.rs, src/bin/cropundo.rs), scratchpad/correct/ (src/main.rs, src/bin/lossless.rs), scratchpad/u16/, scratchpad/r2/

surveys.label: prior-art-postmortems
surveys.summary: I read the xi-editor retrospective in full (fetched as raw markdown from Raph Levien's blog repo, since his blog host is egress-blocked), and cloned and measured helix, zed, kakoune, micro, kibi and kilo on this box to get real numbers instead of vibes. The single clearest signal across all of them: nobody died from picking the wrong text data structure, and everybody who died or stalled did so from spending "novelty points" on architecture whose payoff was always one refactor away. Xi's own author's verdict is unambiguous — "I now firmly believe that the process separation between front-end and core was not a good idea", "async is a complexity multiplier", and "monolithic architectures, perhaps ironically, are better for community". The projects that won (Neovim, Vim, Emacs, VS Code) all kept the editing model in ONE process and put their process boundary at the presentation or extension edge, not at the model edge. The projects that shipped fast (Helix, Kakoune, Micro, Kibi) all deferred or refused a plugin system: Helix has 46.1k stars, 7,689 commits, and its Steel plugin PR has been open since 2023-10-31 (491 commits, 700+ comments, still draft in Aug 2026) — and it has not cut a release since 25.07.1 on 2025-07-18. Zed proves the cost of ambition quantitatively: I measured 1.61M lines of Rust across 244 crates, of which GPUI plus its per-platform backends is ~143k lines — more than all of Helix (107k) — and its actual text engine (rope + text + sum_tree) is only ~14.3k lines. Zed took from 2019 to 2026-04-29 to reach 1.0, with Windows arriving only in Oct 2025, with funding and a team. Meanwhile Kakoune (38.9k lines C++, 15 years old, widely respected) stores its buffer as a plain `Vector<StringDataPtr>` — an array of lines, not a rope — and explicitly refuses Windows. The most actionable prior art for jio's CI-only constraint is Helix's test harness: integration tests inject synthetic key events into `Application::event_loop_until_idle` and assert on rope text + selection, never touching a TTY, and the harness has a `LineFeedHandling::Native` mode that rewrites expectations to CRLF on Windows. That is exactly the pattern that makes macOS/Windows validation possible with zero macOS/Windows hardware.

findings.claim: Xi-editor's author names exactly five "novelty points" the project spent: Rust core, rope, multiprocess architecture (front-end and plug-ins each in their own process), fully embracing async, and CRDT for concurrent modification — and concludes the resulting system was "quite a complex system, and require[d] significantly more work than necessary".
findings.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raphlinus/raphlinus.github.io/main/_posts/2020-06-21-xi-retrospective.md — full text fetched; the bullet list and the sentence "I still believe it would be possible to build a high quality editor based on the original design. But I *also* believe that this would be quite a complex system, and require significantly more work than necessary."
findings.implication: jio gets a novelty budget of about ONE item. Rust itself is arguably already spent (it is now boring for editors — Helix/Zed/Lapce all ship on it), so spend the remaining budget on the editing model (e.g. selection-first), not on the process/concurrency architecture.

findings.claim: Raph Levien's flat verdict on the frontend/core process split: "As a conclusion, while the process split with plug-ins is supportable (similar to the Language Server protocol), I now firmly believe that the process separation between front-end and core was not a good idea."
findings.evidence: Verbatim from the retrospective's "Async is a complexity multiplier" section, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raphlinus/raphlinus.github.io/main/_posts/2020-06-21-xi-retrospective.md
findings.implication: Do not design jio as core-process + UI-process. One process; the UI reads the buffer as an in-process data structure. Keep out-of-process boundaries only where the industry already proved them: LSP/DAP subprocesses.

findings.claim: The specific failure modes of async-across-a-process-boundary that xi hit were mundane UI features, not exotic ones: live window resize with word wrap produced races and tearing between edits and rewrap, and scrolling (fetching text outside the frontend's cache) "took months to get it right" — "if we just had the text available as an in-process data structure for the UI to query, it would have been quite straightforward."
findings.evidence: Verbatim, retrospective section "Async is a complexity multiplier": "The reality was that adding async made everything more complicated, in some cases considerably so… all kinds of interesting things can go wrong, including races between editing actions and word wrap updates."
findings.implication: The features that break under async are precisely the ones jio must have on day one (scroll, resize, wrap). This is a direct argument for a synchronous core loop with async pushed to the leaves (LSP, file IO, syntax parsing) — the Helix `AsyncHook` model.

findings.claim: Levien's own conclusion on the CRDT: "I come to the conclusion that the CRDT is not pulling its (considerable) weight", and he sees "a much brighter future with a simpler, largely synchronous model" that still keeps revision tracking for async work.
findings.evidence: Quote sourced via WebSearch of xi-editor issue #1187 comment 491473599 (github.com/xi-editor/xi-editor/issues/1187#issuecomment-491473599); GitHub's HTML did not render the comment body to WebFetch and news.ycombinator.com is egress-blocked from this box, so this quote is search-derived. The retrospective itself points at that comment as "the CRDT part of this retrospective".
findings.implication: Collaborative editing / CRDT is a trap for jio. If multiplayer is ever wanted, it is a v3 concern built on an operation log, not a v1 data-structure decision. Zed does use a CRDT, but with a company behind it.

findings.claim: Modular architecture actively damaged xi's contributor community: "far too often things were blocking on some major architectural re-work (we have to redo the plug-in API before you can implement that feature)… So I think monolithic architectures, perhaps ironically, are *better* for community." Vi keybindings — the most-requested feature — were never merged.
findings.evidence: Verbatim, retrospective section "Community"; the vixi side-project (github.com/Peltoche/vixi) is cited as the workaround that never landed.
findings.implication: For a solo dev this is even sharper: the person you are blocking with "I need to finish the plugin API first" is yourself. Any architecture that makes a feature require an interface redesign first will kill jio's momentum.

findings.claim: Xi's GUI ambition metastasized: "If I had said that I would be building a GUI toolkit from scratch as part of this work when I set out, people would have rightly ridiculed the scope as far too ambitious. But that is how things are turning out." That toolkit (Druid) is now itself discontinued — "The Druid project has been discontinued" — superseded by Xilem, which is still self-described as "an experimental Rust architecture for reactive UI" in 2026 and requires Rust ≥1.96 (this box has 1.94.1).
findings.evidence: Retrospective section "There is no such thing as native GUI"; https://github.com/linebender/druid (archived, discontinuation notice); https://raw.githubusercontent.com/linebender/xilem/main/README.md (MSRV 1.96, "experimental"); local `rustc --version` = 1.94.1, `rustup check` reports stable 1.98.1 available.
findings.implication: A GUI jio is a decade-scale detour that even Raph Levien could not finish. Terminal UI is the only rational target for a solo dev with no GUI machine — and it is the only UI you can screenshot-test headlessly in CI.

findings.claim: Zed's cost of ambition, measured: 1,611,986 lines of Rust across 244 crates and 1,815 locked packages. GPUI is 88,619 lines, plus gpui_linux 15,391, gpui_windows 12,524, gpui_macos 10,510, gpui_apple 2,200, gpui_wgpu 4,944 — ~143k lines for the UI framework family alone, more than the entirety of Helix. By contrast Zed's whole text engine is small: rope 4,405 + text 6,592 (the CRDT) + sum_tree 3,327 ≈ 14.3k lines, while the `editor` crate is 171,571 lines.
findings.evidence: Direct measurement of a shallow clone on this box: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/zed-industries/zed` then per-crate `find … -name '*.rs' | xargs cat | wc -l`.
findings.implication: Two lessons for jio. (1) Writing the renderer/UI layer is ~10x the work of the text data structure — so never write your own rope, and never write your own UI framework. (2) Budget expectation: the editor surface (commands, UI, interactions) is where 10x the code goes, so make that layer cheap to add to.

findings.claim: Zed's timeline shows what cross-platform costs even when funded: started 2019, macOS-only public release 2023, Linux 2024, Windows only in October 2025, 1.0 on 2026-04-29 after a five-year preview cycle; stable is 1.15.0 as of 2026-08-12, and platform maturity still ranks macOS > Linux > Windows.
findings.evidence: WebSearch (zed.dev is egress-blocked): Phoronix "Rust-Written Zed 1.0 Code Editor Released", noqta.tn Zed-1.0 report, zed.dev/blog/zed-1-0 summary; README at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zed-industries/zed/main/README.md confirms macOS/Linux/Windows downloads today.
findings.implication: If a funded team needed 6 years to get a GPU-UI editor onto Windows, a solo dev with zero Windows hardware must choose a stack where Windows support is a dependency (crossterm), not a project.

findings.claim: Helix, the closest role model for jio, is 107,479 lines of Rust in 13 crates with 337 locked packages, plus 1,193 tree-sitter query files and a 5,657-line languages.toml — and it has 46.1k stars and 7,689 commits from a large contributor base, not one person.
findings.evidence: Direct measurement of `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/helix-editor/helix`: per-crate LOC (helix-term 31,759; helix-core 19,874; helix-view 15,657; helix-lsp-types 9,906; helix-tui 6,222; …), `grep -c '^\[\[package\]\]' Cargo.lock` = 337; repo page stats.
findings.implication: Calibrate: a competitive TUI editor is ~100k lines and a language-config corpus larger than the code. Solo jio should target the ~5–15k line band of Kibi/Ox/Amp and buy the rest (ropey, crossterm, tree-sitter, LSP) rather than build it.

findings.claim: Helix ships TWO terminal backends and picks by platform: `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies] crossterm = "0.28"`, with `termina` used everywhere else, and even its own test helpers do `#[cfg(windows)] use crossterm::event::{Event, KeyEvent}; #[cfg(not(windows))] use termina::event::…`. There are 73 platform-conditional sites across the codebase (only 6 are macOS-specific); the Windows-touching files are clipboard, path, uri, faccess, env, grammar loading, line_ending, application, and completion path handling.
findings.evidence: Local clone: helix-tui/Cargo.toml, helix-term/tests/test/helpers.rs lines 21–23, `grep -rn 'cfg(windows)|target_os = "windows"|cfg(unix)' --include=*.rs | wc -l` = 73.
findings.implication: This is jio's concrete Windows risk checklist. Note the asymmetry: macOS is nearly free for a TUI (6 sites), Windows is where the divergence lives. Choosing crossterm 0.29 as the single backend buys Windows at the cost of some Unix-side terminal features — the right trade for a CI-only project.

findings.claim: Helix's integration tests run the real editor headlessly: they build an `Application`, push synthetic `Event::Key` values from `parse_macro("ihello world<esc>")` into a tokio unbounded channel, call `app.event_loop_until_idle(&mut rx_stream)`, then assert on `doc.text()` + `doc.selection(view.id)`. No PTY, no TTY. The harness also has `LineFeedHandling::Native`, which rewrites every expected string to `helix_core::NATIVE_LINE_ENDING` (CRLF on Windows).
findings.evidence: Local clone: helix-term/tests/test/helpers.rs (test_key_sequences, LineFeedHandling), helix-term/tests/integration.rs (`#[cfg(feature = "integration")]`, `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread")]`), .cargo/config.toml alias `integration-test = "test --features integration --profile integration --workspace --test integration"`; helix-core/src/line_ending.rs (328 lines) defines `NATIVE_LINE_ENDING = Crlf` under `cfg(target_os = "windows")`.
findings.implication: This is the single most copyable artifact for jio. Design the editor so its event loop can be driven by an injected event stream from day one, and make line-ending handling a first-class type — then macOS/Windows correctness is testable on GitHub runners without ever seeing those machines.

findings.claim: Helix's CI matrix is `[ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm, windows-11-arm]`, running `cargo test --workspace` AND `cargo integration-test` on all five, with MSRV pinned at 1.90 in a separate check job, a nightly cron, and tree-sitter grammar caching. Some behaviours are simply not tested on Windows — e.g. several `#[cfg(unix)]`-gated file-permission tests in helix-term/tests/test/commands/write.rs.
findings.evidence: Local clone: .github/workflows/build.yml (verbatim matrix and steps); grep of cfg-gated tests.
findings.implication: Copy this matrix verbatim into jio from commit #1, including the ARM runners. Also copy the honesty: write down which behaviours are Unix-only-tested rather than pretending the matrix proves parity.

findings.claim: The plugin system is where Helix stalled. PR #8675 "Add Steel as an optional plugin system" was opened 2023-10-31 and is still an open draft as of Aug 2026 with 491+ commits and 700+ comments; maintainers abandoned WASM after "three separate attempts at integrating WASM that didn't lead anywhere", rejected Rhai ("too new and has a bus factor of one"), and rejected Lua partly on Neovim's experience. Meanwhile Helix's last tagged release is 25.07.1 (2025-07-18) — no release in ~14 months, despite active master commits through July 2026.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/helix-editor/helix/pull/8675 ; https://github.com/helix-editor/helix/discussions/3806 ; https://github.com/helix-editor/helix/tags and /releases (newest 25.07.1, 2025-07-18); local CHANGELOG.md heading scan shows an empty template above `# 25.07.1 (2025-07-18)`; /commits/master shows July 2026 activity.
findings.implication: The plugin system is the classic momentum killer, and it kills healthy projects too. jio must ship a useful editor with ZERO scripting, and treat extensibility as a v2 problem solved by an internal command registry + declarative keymap first.

findings.claim: Neovim succeeded because it put the process boundary at the *presentation* layer, not the model layer: the UI protocol is a grid-of-cells (grid_line/grid_resize/grid_scroll, ~40 events, ext_* opt-ins, "Clients must be prepared to ignore such extensions, for forward-compatibility"), while all editing logic stays in one process on a libuv event loop with a pushdown-automaton state machine. The built-in TUI itself only moved into a separate process in 0.9, with the explicit warning that this "might be the cause of subtle changes of behavior and bugs".
findings.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neovim/neovim/master/runtime/doc/dev_arch.txt (libuv Loop, MultiQueue, state_enter); .../api-ui-events.txt (grid model, ext_*); .../news-0.9.txt verbatim: "The |TUI| is changed to run in a separate process (previously, a separate thread was used)." plus "This is not supposed to be a visible change to the user, but might be the cause of subtle changes of behavior and bugs."; README goals "Enable advanced UIs without modifications to the core", "Maximize extensibility".
findings.implication: The lesson is NOT "copy Neovim's RPC". It is: the only durable remote boundary is a dumb rendering/notification protocol, and even that took Neovim ~9 years to make safe. jio should have an internal `Backend` trait (draw cells) and defer any RPC protocol indefinitely.

findings.claim: Kakoune — 38,888 lines of C++, still releasing (2026.05.21) after ~15 years — stores its buffer as `using BufferLines = Vector<StringDataPtr, MemoryDomain::BufferContent>`, i.e. an array of refcounted lines, NOT a rope; it uses a client/server split (client.cc, remote.cc) where each UI client is a separate process against one buffer-owning server; and it flatly refuses Windows: "Due to Kakoune relying heavily on being in a Unix-like environment, no native Windows version is planned."
findings.evidence: Local clone of github.com/mawww/kakoune: src/buffer.hh:122, `ls src | grep -E 'remote|client'`, LOC count; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mawww/kakoune/master/README.asciidoc ; doc/design.asciidoc ("Kakoune is a code editor. It is not an IDE…"; sorting lines "should be done using the Unix sort command"; explicit rejection of threading, binary plugins and an integrated scripting language).
findings.implication: Two things to steal: the selection-first orthogonal model, and the explicit written scope statement ("it is not an X"). One thing to avoid: Unix-only assumptions (shell-out-for-everything is what makes Kakoune un-portable). jio's "filter through a subprocess" feature must be optional, or Windows dies.

findings.claim: VS Code's two architectural wins were (a) replacing an array-of-lines buffer with a piece tree whose memory after load is close to the original file size, benchmarked on files like a 14MB/552k-line dictionary and a 54MB/3M-line heap snapshot, and (b) running extensions in a separate extension-host process with a responsiveness watchdog (~3s) so "a misbehaving extension cannot impact VS Code", with the UI surviving a disposable extension host.
findings.evidence: code.visualstudio.com is egress-blocked from this box; facts assembled from WebSearch of the 2018 "Text Buffer Reimplementation" post and from https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/41042 ("When the size of a file or the line breaks count increases, it takes more time to build the text buffer as we are splitting the content by line breaks, and holds more memory"), plus vscode-docs "Our Approach to Extensibility" summaries.
findings.implication: Confirms the correct place for process isolation: around untrusted third-party code, not around your own editing model. Also confirms that array-of-lines is a real scaling wall — which is why ropey (not a hand-rolled Vec<String>) is the right default for jio.

findings.claim: The minimal-core lineage proves a cross-platform editor can be tiny: antirez's kilo is 1,308 physical lines of C with no library at all ("Kilo does not depend on any library (not even curses)"), and Kibi is 2,652 lines of Rust total supporting Linux, macOS, Windows 10 1703+ and WASI — of which the ENTIRE Windows platform layer is 75 lines (enable ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT / ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING, query console screen buffer for size).
findings.evidence: Local clones: `wc -l kilo/kilo.c` = 1308; kibi src total 2652, `cat kibi/src/windows.rs` = 75 lines. Note the honest gap: kibi's `has_window_size_changed()` is `const fn … { false }` on Windows — no resize detection there, and window size falls back to the ESC[6n cursor-position probe.
findings.implication: jio's v0 is a weekend, not a quarter. And the Windows story for a TUI is genuinely ~100 lines of console-mode setup — provided you accept a VT-capable terminal (Windows 10 1703+) as a requirement and write it down.

findings.claim: Solo-developer editors stall on attention, not architecture: Ox (Rust, Lua-configurable, feature-rich) last committed 2025-03-13 with 0.7.7 (its 0.7.6 notes even mention "restored Windows binaries"); Zee (ropey + tree-sitter, Emacs-flavoured) last committed 2025-02-06; Amp is alive but slow (last commit 2026-06-10); Xray (GitHub's Rust+CRDT+WebGL editor) was archived 2019-07-23 with "GitHub has decided not to move forward with any aspect of this project."
findings.evidence: https://github.com/curlpipe/ox/releases and /commits/master; https://github.com/zee-editor/zee/commits/master; https://github.com/jmacdonald/amp/commits/main; https://github.com/atom-archive/xray (archive notice).
findings.implication: jio's real enemy is a 6-month gap in commits, not a suboptimal buffer. Sequencing should maximize the number of weeks where a visible, shippable improvement is possible — which argues for releasing binaries early and often.

findings.claim: Micro shows the approachability path: ~25,254 lines of Go, a plain LineArray buffer, gopher-lua plugins with a built-in plugin manager, one static binary, sane non-modal defaults, latest release 2.0.15 on 2025-12-31. But it now lives under a community org (module path `github.com/micro-editor/micro/v2`) and maintains its own forks of its terminal library (`github.com/micro-editor/tcell/v2 v2.0.13`) and json5.
findings.evidence: Local clone: LOC count, internal/buffer/line_array.go, go.mod contents.
findings.implication: Steal: sane defaults, ctrl-key bindings, single static binary, embedded scripting rather than a bespoke language, and shipping a plugin *manager* not just an API. Avoid: array-of-lines (bites on huge/long-line files) and the drift into maintaining forks of your dependencies.

findings.claim: Extensibility is the moat that outlives everything: Emacs 31.1 shipped 2026-08-24 (project ~50 years old) and Vim 9.2 shipped 2026-02-14 with patches to 9.2.0995 by 2026-08-22 — Vim continuing after Bram Moolenaar's death precisely because its value lives in scripts and community, not in its C. Neovim's whole thesis was that Vim's single-maintainer bottleneck over ~300k lines of C89 was the actual defect.
findings.evidence: WebSearch: gnu.org Emacs release history / Emacs 31.1 (2026-08-24) coverage; vim/vim releases (9.2.0995, 2026-08-22); Neovim fork rationale summaries and README goals "Simplify maintenance and encourage contributions", "Maximize extensibility".
findings.implication: jio does eventually need an extension story — but the winning form is a stable *command/action* vocabulary that scripts bind to, which you can define in v1 with zero runtime. Design the internal command registry first; choose the scripting language last.

findings.claim: Current, verified ground truth on this box for the crates prior art actually uses: ropey 1.6.1 (what Helix pins), crop 0.4.3, jumprope 1.1.2, crossterm 0.29.0 (crossterm's own README still says 0.27 — stale), termina 0.4.0, ratatui 0.30.2, tree-sitter 0.27.0, tree-house 0.4.0 (Helix's own tree-sitter wrapper, pinned at 0.4). A minimal ropey+crossterm binary builds and runs on rustc 1.94.1, and ropey treats "\r\n" as a single line break.
findings.evidence:
`cargo add --dry-run` for each crate on this machine; `cargo build` + `cargo run` of a probe crate printing `lines=3 chars=15 line1=["hello!!
"]` for input "hello
world
"; Helix master Cargo.toml (ropey 1.6.1, tree-house 0.4, MSRV 1.90, version 25.7.1).
findings.implication: The boring stack is available and compiles today. Note Helix's move to its own `tree-house` wrapper — a warning that raw tree-sitter Rust bindings have sharp edges (grammar loading is one of Helix's Windows-cfg sites).

surveys.recommendation:
Build jio as a single-process, synchronous-core terminal editor whose event loop is drivable by an injected event stream, and treat "can I test this on a GitHub runner without a TTY?" as the design constraint that outranks every aesthetic preference.

Concretely, the sequencing that avoids the common death:

Phase 0 — the harness before the editor (days, not weeks). Create `jio-core` (ropey Rope + Selection + Transaction/undo, pure functions, no IO) and `jio-app` with an `Application::event_loop_until_idle(stream)` that consumes an injected key-event stream. Write the Helix-style test helper `test(in_text_with_cursor_markers, "ihello<esc>", out_text)` in week one. Stand up the CI matrix [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest, ubuntu-24.04-arm, windows-11-arm] on commit #1 with fmt+clippy+test. If the harness comes second, it never comes.

Phase 1 — the boring core, one process. ropey 1.6.1 for text, crossterm 0.29 as the ONLY terminal backend (it is the only one that gets you Windows; Helix keeps crossterm specifically for Windows), a `Backend` trait with a headless test backend behind it. Explicit `LineEnding` type with a `NATIVE_LINE_ENDING` constant from the start — CRLF is the #1 way a Linux-developed editor fails in Windows CI, and Helix spends 328 lines on it. No tokio yet; a plain blocking read loop is fine and eliminates a whole class of untestable races.

Phase 2 — ship something a human can use, then keep shipping. Open/edit/save/undo/search/quit, plus tagged releases with prebuilt binaries for the three platforms from GitHub Actions. Kibi does the whole cross-platform job in 2,652 lines; kilo in 1,308. Getting to "usable and installable" fast is what keeps a solo project alive — Ox, Zee and Amp all stalled after the fun part, and xi stalled because features were blocked behind architecture.

Phase 3 — earn the editing model. This is where to spend the novelty budget: selection-first (Kakoune/Helix) multiple selections, because it is a model decision that costs code in `jio-core` and is fully unit-testable headlessly, not an architectural bet. Add tree-sitter for highlighting only after the editing model is stable, and be aware grammar loading is platform-divergent.

Phase 4 — extensibility LAST, and in the cheap form first. Route every user-visible action through an internal command registry + declarative keymap in TOML from Phase 1 onward (this costs almost nothing and is the real Neovim/Emacs lesson). Only if jio is alive and used a year in, embed Lua via mlua. Do not invent a language, do not wait for the WASM component model, do not build an RPC plugin protocol. Helix, a healthy 46k-star project with many contributors, has been unable to land a plugin system in nearly three years and has not cut a release in fourteen months while trying.

Permanent no-list, drawn from the corpus: no separate frontend process (xi's author's own verdict), no CRDT (his other verdict), no custom GUI toolkit (Druid died; GPUI+backends is ~143k lines), no custom rope (Zed's whole text engine is 14k lines but ropey is free), no custom terminal library (micro ended up forking tcell and maintaining it), no shell-out-for-everything (that is what makes Kakoune Windows-hostile).

What would change my mind: if jio's actual goal is a GUI/GPU editor or a research vehicle for collaborative editing, then the "ship a TUI" sequencing is wrong — but in that case the no-macOS/no-Windows-hardware constraint makes the project close to infeasible, and I would tell the owner to change the goal rather than the sequencing.
risks: CRLF is the highest-probability CI-only failure. Every test that hardcodes "\n" in expected output will pass on Linux/macOS and fail on windows-latest, and every save path that doesn't preserve the file's original line ending will silently corrupt diffs for Windows users. Mitigation: a LineEnding type and a Helix-style LineFeedHandling::Native mode in the test harness on day one; add a test that round-trips a CRLF fixture byte-for-byte.

No TTY on GitHub runners. Anything that calls into raw mode, queries terminal size, or waits on real stdin will hang or error in CI (Windows especially, where crossterm's event source touches console handles). Any test needing a real terminal is a test that will never run. Mitigation: the terminal must be behind a trait with an in-memory backend, and the editor loop must accept an injected event stream — exactly Helix's structure.

Windows terminal-mode assumptions. Kibi requires Windows 10 1703+ for ANSI VT and simply does not detect window resize on Windows (has_window_size_changed() returns false). Resize handling, bracketed paste, mouse, and the kitty keyboard protocol all differ or are absent on Windows and will not be caught by a passing `cargo test`. Mitigation: write down the minimum Windows terminal contract, and treat resize/mouse/paste as manually-unverifiable — keep them behind capability checks with graceful degradation.

Path, clipboard, file-permission and env divergence. Helix has 73 platform-conditional sites and they cluster in exactly these areas: clipboard, path/uri, faccess (permissions), env/PATH lookup, dynamic grammar loading. Atomic save (write temp + rename) behaves differently on Windows (no atomic replace over an open handle in all cases; ACL/readonly semantics differ). These are correctness bugs that unit tests on Linux cannot see. Mitigation: put every one of these behind a `sys` module with per-platform impls and test each in CI on all three OSes.

macOS in CI is a moving target: macos-latest migrated to macos-26 arm64 around June–July 2026, and there is no free x86_64 macOS default label anymore (macos-26-intel is a separate label). An arm64-only macOS matrix will not catch x86_64-specific issues, and Apple Silicon vs Intel differences in dependency builds are real. Mitigation: pin macos-26 explicitly rather than macos-latest, and decide consciously whether Intel macOS is supported.

tree-sitter grammar builds are the most fragile CI step: they need a C compiler on all three platforms, take minutes without caching, and grammar loading is one of Helix's Windows-cfg sites. Adding tree-sitter early risks converting a 3-minute CI into a 25-minute flaky CI. Mitigation: defer tree-sitter; when added, vendor a tiny grammar set and cache aggressively (Helix has a dedicated grammar-cache-version env knob).

Dependency churn in the TUI ecosystem: crossterm's own README advertises 0.27 while crates.io serves 0.29.0; ratatui is at 0.30.2; Helix has already migrated part-way from crossterm to its own `termina` and wraps tree-sitter in its own `tree-house`. Pre-1.0 crates will make breaking changes under jio. Mitigation: pin exact versions, keep the backend behind a trait so a swap is a 400–700 line file (that is the actual size of Helix's backends), and do not chase.

The plugin-system tarpit, empirically the biggest killer of momentum in this corpus. The temptation to design the extension API "properly" before shipping features is what stalled xi (features blocked on plug-in API rework) and is what has Helix at 14 months without a release. Mitigation: internal command registry + TOML keymap now; scripting runtime only after jio has users.

Solo-attention decay: Ox and Zee both went quiet after ~2 years of solid work. There is no architectural fix; the mitigations are release cadence, small always-shippable increments, and CI that stays green so returning after a gap is cheap (pin MSRV and dependency versions so a 3-month gap doesn't mean a day of build repair).

Research-environment risk for this very report: several primary sources are egress-blocked from this box (raphlinus.github.io, news.ycombinator.com, lobste.rs, zed.dev, code.visualstudio.com, en.wikipedia.org, viewsourcecode.org, lord.io, web.archive.org). I routed around that by fetching Levien's post as raw markdown from his blog's own GitHub repo and by cloning source, but the VS Code piece-tree numbers and a few Zed/Helix-community claims rest on search summaries rather than the primary page. Treat those specific items as medium confidence.
open_questions: Is jio meant to be modal/selection-first (Helix/Kakoune) or approachable/non-modal (Micro/nano)? This is the one place I'd spend the novelty budget, and it changes the core data model (multi-selection Transactions vs a single cursor), so it should be decided before Phase 1 rather than retrofitted.

Is a GUI ever a goal? If yes, the whole recommendation changes — and the no-hardware constraint likely makes it infeasible. If no, say so in the README the way Kakoune says no to Windows; a written scope statement is itself a survival tool.

How large must the largest supported file be? Kakoune (array of lines) and Micro (LineArray) are respected editors that never adopted a rope. ropey is still my default because it is free, but if the answer is "a few MB", the data-structure question is genuinely moot and shouldn't consume a day of thought.

Does jio need to open files it cannot decode as UTF-8 (latin-1 logs, UTF-16 Windows files, binary)? Encoding detection is a cross-platform correctness area that CI can test cheaply with fixtures, but it must be designed into the load/save path early rather than bolted on.

What is the acceptable Windows floor — Windows 10 1703+ VT-capable terminals only (Kibi's answer), or must legacy conhost work? This decides whether crossterm's Windows console-API fallback path matters, and it is exactly the kind of thing that cannot be checked without a Windows box, so it must become a documented requirement instead.

Should jio's LSP support come from an existing crate or hand-rolled? Helix carries helix-lsp (4,240 lines) plus helix-lsp-types (9,906 lines) — that is 13k lines of the 107k total, and it is where async genuinely is required. Worth an explicit decision about whether v1 has LSP at all.

Is there any appetite for a `--script` / headless mode? It costs almost nothing if the event loop is injectable from day one, and it doubles as the CI test driver, the benchmark harness, and the eventual macro facility. I'd argue yes, but it should be a deliberate choice.

surveys.label: crossplatform-pitfalls
surveys.summary: I verified most claims empirically on this box (rustc 1.94.1, ext4, LANG unset/POSIX locale) or against primary sources fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com (which, unlike vimhelp.org/learn.microsoft.com/docs.rs, is NOT blocked by the proxy — use `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/...` for primary sources). The single most dangerous finding is in encoding, not file saving: `encoding_rs::Encoding::encode()` silently emits UTF-8 when the encoding is UTF_16LE/UTF_16BE (`UTF_16LE.output_encoding() == UTF-8`), and replaces unmappable characters with literal HTML numeric character references (`🙂`) rather than failing. Both are documented WHATWG-web behaviours and both silently corrupt user files in an editor. Second: the naive "atomic save" (`tempfile::NamedTempFile` + `persist`) is a metadata shredder — I measured mode 0664 → 0600, xattrs dropped, hard link count 2 → 1 with the sibling link silently frozen at the old content, and a target symlink replaced by a regular file. Worse, as a non-root user a rename over a 0444 file *succeeds* and resets it to 0644, so atomic save silently defeats the read-only bit that in-place write correctly refuses. Vim's real default is `backupcopy=auto` (not "yes"; verified in `src/optiondefs.h`), and its heuristic is precisely readable in `src/bufwrite.c` — it also explains the infamous `4913` probe file that spams everyone else's watchers. VS Code's default is the opposite of what people assume: in-place `truncate + write + fdatasync`, with atomic-rename opt-in and explicitly refused for symlinks, plus a 60-second Windows rename retry loop for AV locks. On watching, I measured that an inotify watch on a *file* is permanently dead after an atomic replace (subsequent writes produce zero events) while notify on Windows always watches the parent directory — so the same code has different semantics per OS. Rust's `fs::rename` on Windows falls back to POSIX-semantics rename only for `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`, not `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`, which is the error real AV/indexer/OneDrive locks produce and which cannot be reproduced on a GitHub runner. Finally, GitHub's Windows image bakes `LongPathsEnabled=1` into the base image, so your Windows CI is strictly more permissive than your users' machines for long paths.

findings.claim: `encoding_rs::UTF_16LE.encode(s)` and `UTF_16BE.encode(s)` silently return UTF-8 bytes, not UTF-16, with had_errors=false. `UTF_16LE.output_encoding()` is literally `UTF-8`.
findings.evidence: Ran on this box with encoding_rs 0.8.40: `UTF-16LE .encode("hi") -> output_encoding=UTF-8 bytes=[104,105] err=false`; `UTF_16LE.output_encoding() = UTF-8`. This is WHATWG Encoding Standard behaviour (UTF-16 is decode-only for the web).
findings.implication: UTF-16LE files are everywhere on Windows (PowerShell `>` redirection, older Notepad, .reg exports, many .ini). If jio decodes with `UTF_16LE` and saves with `enc.encode()`, it will decode correctly and then write a UTF-8 file labelled UTF-16 — a total, silent format change with no error flag. jio MUST hand-roll UTF-16 output (`str::encode_utf16()` + `to_le_bytes()/to_be_bytes()` + BOM) and must never route save through `Encoding::encode`.

findings.claim: `encoding_rs::Encoding::encode()` replaces unmappable characters with HTML *decimal numeric character references* in the output bytes, not with an error or a replacement byte.
findings.evidence: Ran locally: `WINDOWS_1252.encode("café🙂\n")` -> `bytes=[99,97,102,233,10,38,35,49,50,56,53,55,56,59,10]` i.e. the literal ASCII `🙂`, with `had_errors=true`. encoding_rs 0.8.40 doc at src/lib.rs:3304 says "unmappable characters (that were replaced with HTML numeric character references)".
findings.implication: User opens a cp1252/GBK/Shift_JIS file, types one emoji, saves — the file now literally contains the text `🙂`. jio must use `Encoder::encode_from_utf8` with `..._without_replacement` variants, detect unmappable characters BEFORE writing, and block the save with a dialog offering "convert to UTF-8" / "drop character", exactly like VS Code's encoding prompt.

findings.claim: The naive atomic save (`tempfile::NamedTempFile::new_in(dir)` + `persist(target)`) silently downgrades permissions to 0600, drops all xattrs, and breaks hard links.
findings.evidence: Ran locally on ext4: BEFORE `mode=100664 nlink=2`; `tempfile default mode = 100600`; AFTER `mode=100600 nlink=1`, and the sibling hard link still reads the OLD content "hello". A separate Python probe: `after replace: mode=600 xattrs: []` vs `in-place: mode=664 xattrs: ['user.jio']`. tempfile 3.27.0 creates with 0600 by design (security).
findings.implication: `tempfile::NamedTempFile` is the wrong primitive for saving user files — it is designed for secrets, not for replacing existing files. If jio uses it, every saved file becomes owner-read-only. Use `atomic-write-file` 0.3.1 with `preserve_mode(true)`/`try_preserve_owner`, or fchmod/fchown the temp fd from the original's stat before the rename.

findings.claim: Renaming over a file the user cannot write succeeds and destroys the read-only bit; in-place write correctly fails.
findings.evidence: Ran as unprivileged user `nobody` via runuser: `in-place write on 0444: DENIED (Permission denied)` / `rename over 0444: SUCCEEDED, content='new\n' mode=644`. rename permission is governed by the *directory*, not the file.
findings.implication: Atomic save silently defeats read-only protection: `chmod 444 important.conf` no longer protects anything, and the protection bit is gone afterwards. jio must stat the target and refuse (or prompt "file is read-only, override?") before saving, independently of the write strategy. On Windows the asymmetry is reversed — MoveFileExW over a read-only file fails with ACCESS_DENIED, which is exactly why Rust std has the FileRenameInfoEx fallback.

findings.claim: Renaming a temp file onto a path that is a symlink replaces the symlink with a regular file and leaves the real target stale.
findings.evidence: Ran locally: `os.replace(tmp, symlink_path)` -> `islink=False`, and the real file still contains the old content. VS Code refuses atomic writes for symlinks for exactly this reason (src/vs/platform/files/node/diskFileSystemProvider.ts `canWriteFileAtomic`: "atomic writes are unsupported for symbolic links"). atomic-write-file's own docs say "If the path of an AtomicWriteFile is a symlink to another file, the symlink is replaced, and the target of the original symlink is left untouched."
findings.implication: This breaks every dotfile manager on earth (stow, chezmoi, yadm) — user edits ~/.config/nvim/init.lua which is a symlink into their dotfiles repo, saves, and the symlink is gone and the repo is unchanged. jio must `symlink_metadata()` the target and either canonicalize first or fall back to in-place write.

findings.claim: Vim's actual default is `backupcopy=auto` on every platform (not "yes" on Unix — that's the *Vi* default), and the "auto" heuristic chooses copy-in-place when: st_nlink > 1 (hard link), lstat fails or dev/ino differ from stat (symlink), a probe file cannot be created in the directory, or fchown/fchmod on the probe cannot reproduce the original uid/gid/mode. On Windows it checks `mch_is_linked()`.
findings.evidence: vim/vim src/optiondefs.h:445-451 — `#ifdef UNIX {"yes", "auto"} #else {"auto","auto"}` (first = Vi default, second = Vim default). Algorithm read verbatim from vim/vim src/bufwrite.c lines 1178-1300. Doc text from runtime/doc/options.txt lines 1165-1229.
findings.implication: This is the reference heuristic to copy. It is decidable entirely from `fs::symlink_metadata` + a probe write, so it is fully testable on a Linux CI runner. Note it costs one probe file create/chown/chmod/stat/unlink per save.

findings.claim: Vim's auto heuristic creates a probe file literally named `4913` (then 5036, 5159, … i += 123) in the target directory with O_CREAT|O_WRONLY|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW, then deletes it — and on MS-Windows retries the delete 10× at 50ms because a virus scanner may have opened it.
findings.evidence: vim/vim src/bufwrite.c lines 1213-1272, verbatim. I also measured that a create+delete of `4913` in a watched directory produces 4 inotify events (Create/Open/CloseWrite/Remove) with notify 8.2.0.
findings.implication: This is why vim triggers spurious rebuilds in webpack/cargo-watch/jest. If jio copies the heuristic, do the probe in a hidden name (`.jio-probe-<pid>-<rand>`) so watchers with sane ignore rules skip it, and cache the per-directory result for the session instead of probing on every save.

findings.claim: VS Code's DEFAULT text file write is in-place truncate + write + `fdatasync`, NOT atomic rename; atomic rename is opt-in per-call, is refused for symlinks, and disables fdatasync globally for the session if it ever fails.
findings.evidence: microsoft/vscode src/vs/base/node/pfs.ts `doWriteFileAndFlush` (open with flag 'w' + mode 0o666, writeFile, `fs.fdatasync`, on error `configureFlushOnWrite(false)` and a console warning). Atomic path in src/vs/platform/files/node/diskFileSystemProvider.ts `writeFile`/`canWriteFileAtomic`/`doWriteFileAtomic` — temp is a sibling `<basename><postfix>` in the same directory, with resource locks on both paths.
findings.implication: The two most-used editors in the world both default to preserving the inode. This is strong evidence that jio should default to in-place write and buy crash-safety from a separate journal, not from rename atomicity.

findings.claim: VS Code retries `rename` on Windows for EACCES/EPERM/EBUSY with incremental backoff for up to 60 seconds because AV software locks files, and falls back to copy+delete on EXDEV or when the source ends with a dot.
findings.evidence: microsoft/vscode src/vs/base/node/pfs.ts `rename()` / `renameWithRetry()`: `windowsRetryTimeout: number | false = 60000`; retry only for EACCES/EPERM/EBUSY; `Math.min(100, attempt * 10)` backoff; `if (... error.code === 'EXDEV' || source.endsWith('.')) { copy(); rimraf(); }`.
findings.implication: Any Windows rename in jio needs the same retry loop. A bare `fs::rename` will fail intermittently on real Windows machines in a way that GitHub runners (no third-party AV, no OneDrive, no Search indexer on the work dir) will essentially never reproduce. This is a design-by-construction item, not a CI item.

findings.claim: Rust 1.94.1's `std::fs::rename` on Windows is `MoveFileExW(MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING)` with a fallback to `SetFileInformationByHandle(FileRenameInfoEx, POSIX_SEMANTICS|REPLACE_IF_EXISTS)` ONLY when the error is `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`. It does not retry, and does not handle `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (32).
findings.evidence: Read the local toolchain source: /root/.rustup/toolchains/stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/std/src/sys/fs/windows.rs:1311-1394 (identical logic on rust master). Doc text in library/std/src/fs.rs:3010-3026.
findings.implication: ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION is what you get when another process holds the file open without FILE_SHARE_DELETE — Notepad, Office, Windows Search indexer, OneDrive, many AV engines. jio must map raw_os_error 32 and 5 to a retry loop and then to an in-place-write fallback, or Windows users will hit unexplainable save failures.

findings.claim: Rust's default `OpenOptions` on Windows opens with `FILE_SHARE_READ | FILE_SHARE_WRITE | FILE_SHARE_DELETE`, so jio holding its own file open does not block other processes from renaming over it.
findings.evidence: library/std/src/sys/fs/windows.rs:206 in the local 1.94.1 rust-src.
findings.implication: Good news: jio can keep a read handle open for the swap/identity check without becoming the process that breaks other editors. But it also means jio cannot rely on holding the file to prevent concurrent modification — use mtime+size+hash conflict detection on save (VS Code's `files.saveConflictResolution` setting exists for exactly this).

findings.claim: A temp file must live in the same directory as the target: cross-filesystem rename fails with `ErrorKind::CrossesDevices` (EXDEV, errno 18).
findings.evidence: Ran locally: rename /tmp -> /dev/shm gave `kind=CrossesDevices raw=Some(18)`.
findings.implication: Never put the save temp in std::env::temp_dir(). It also means the temp file is briefly visible in the user's directory (and to their file watcher and git status) — use a dotted name, and on Linux consider atomic-write-file's `unnamed-tmpfile` feature (O_TMPFILE + linkat) so nothing is ever visible.

findings.claim: An inotify watch on a FILE is permanently dead after an atomic replace; a watch on the DIRECTORY survives. notify on Windows always emulates single-file watching by watching the parent directory, so the semantics differ per OS for identical jio code.
findings.evidence: Ran with notify 8.2.0 on this box. Watching the file: in-place write -> 4 events; atomic replace -> `Modify(Metadata)`, `Remove(File)`; a further in-place write -> `NO EVENTS`. Watching the directory: full rename event sequence, still live. notify/src/windows.rs:308-341 — "emulate file watching by watching the parent directory" / "You attempted to watch a single file, but parent directory could not be opened."
findings.implication: jio must watch the parent directory and filter by filename, never `watcher.watch(file)`. Otherwise external-change detection silently stops working after any other editor saves atomically — on Linux only. This is testable on the Linux runner and IS one of the few cross-platform divergences you can catch cheaply.

findings.claim: notify 8.2.0's documented cross-platform caveats: network filesystems (NFS/SMB/WSL-to-Windows) may emit no events at all; macOS FSEvents cannot reliably observe files you don't own; on APFS `std::fs::copy` uses clonefile and fires metadata events on the SOURCE; Windows uses a fixed 16 KiB buffer and signals overflow via ERROR_NOTIFY_ENUM_DIR requiring a full rescan; Linux inotify counts every file AND folder against `max_user_watches`.
findings.evidence: notify/src/lib.rs doc header ("Known Problems") lines 34-100; notify/src/windows.rs:42 `const BUF_SIZE: u32 = 16384;` and completion_rescan_event() handling ERROR_NOTIFY_ENUM_DIR; measured limits on this box: `fs.inotify.max_user_watches=129912, max_user_instances=128, max_queued_events=16384`. notify stable is 8.2.0; 9.0.0-rc.5 exists but is not released (cargo add notify@9 -> "could not be found in registry index").
findings.implication: Watching a large project recursively will exhaust inotify watches on Linux and will silently drop events on Windows. jio should watch only the directories of open buffers (not the whole project), handle a rescan/`EventKind::Other` by re-stat'ing every open buffer, and fall back to `PollWatcher` when `recommended_watcher` errors with ENOSPC.

findings.claim: Paths must never round-trip through `String`. On Linux a filename with invalid UTF-8 gives `to_str() == None` and `Path::display()` produces a lossy string that CANNOT be reopened.
findings.evidence: Ran locally: created `bad\xffname.txt`; `path.to_str() = None`, `display = /tmp/xprobe_fn/bad\u{fffd}name.txt`, and `fs::read(displayed_string).is_ok() == false`. read_dir returns the exact bytes `[98,97,100,255,...]`.
findings.implication: Every path in jio must be `PathBuf`/`OsString` end to end — config files, session state, the file-picker, the status bar. Use `display()`/`to_string_lossy()` for rendering only and keep the `PathBuf` alongside. The Windows mirror is unpaired surrogates in UTF-16 filenames, which have the same property. Add a Linux CI test that opens, edits and saves a file whose name is invalid UTF-8 — this one IS catchable on Linux.

findings.claim: `encoding_rs::Encoding::decode()` performs BOM sniffing that OVERRIDES the encoding you asked for and silently strips the BOM; the boolean it returns is `had_errors`, not `had_bom`. Lossy decode is irreversible.
findings.evidence: Ran locally: `UTF_8.decode(utf16le_bom_bytes)` returned `enc=UTF-16LE`; `UTF_8.decode(utf8_bom_bytes)` returned text without the BOM so a naive decode→encode round-trip went from 10 bytes to 7. `UTF_8.decode(b"hello \xff\xfe world \xc3\xa9")` turned 17 bytes into 21 (each invalid byte became a 3-byte U+FFFD). encoding_rs 0.8.40 src/lib.rs:3060 documents the bool as "whether there were malformed sequences".
findings.implication: jio must record `(encoding, had_bom)` explicitly at open time and re-emit the BOM on save; and must use `decode_without_bom_handling_and_without_replacement` (which returns Option and is None on malformed input) to decide whether a file is losslessly representable. Files that are not losslessly decodable should open in a read-only/binary-ish mode rather than being silently U+FFFD-ified and then written back.

findings.claim: UTF-16LE without a BOM decodes as valid UTF-8 with no errors (NUL bytes are legal UTF-8), so BOM-less UTF-16 will silently open as mojibake full of NULs unless you add a NUL-density heuristic.
findings.evidence: Ran locally: `UTF_8.decode("hello".encode_utf16 as LE bytes)` -> `err=false text="h\0e\0l\0l\0o\0"`.
findings.implication: Detection order must be: (1) BOM, (2) NUL-byte heuristic over the first ~8 KiB (>~5% NULs at even/odd offsets ⇒ UTF-16LE/BE), (3) strict UTF-8 validation, (4) chardetng, (5) configured fallback. This exact ladder is trivially unit-testable with a byte-corpus and needs no OS-specific CI.

findings.claim: chardetng's current published version is 1.0.0 and its API is NOT the `new()` / `guess(None, true)` form widely documented online: it is `EncodingDetector::new(Iso2022JpDetection)` and `guess(tld: Option<&[u8]>, allow_utf8: Utf8Detection)`. It is also unreliable on short inputs.
findings.evidence: cargo add reported chardetng v1.0.0; compile error against the old API; enums read from src/lib.rs:2832 (`Utf8Detection::{Allow,Deny}`) and :2845 (`Iso2022JpDetection::{Allow,Deny}`). Measured: 8 bytes of GBK -> `GBK` (correct); 2 bytes of GBK -> `windows-1252` (wrong); latin-1 prose -> `windows-1252`.
findings.implication: A concrete example of stale memory being wrong. Also: never auto-detect on tiny files or on the first N bytes only — read at least 8-64 KiB, and always expose a 'Reopen with encoding…' command plus a per-workspace override, because detection WILL be wrong sometimes and the user needs an escape hatch that doesn't require re-saving.

findings.claim: `arboard` 3.6.1 fails on a headless box (this container, and any default `ubuntu-latest` runner) with an X11 connection error, and on Linux the clipboard contents vanish when jio exits unless a clipboard manager is running, because X11/Wayland make the copying process the data server.
findings.evidence: Ran locally with DISPLAY/WAYLAND_DISPLAY unset: `arboard::Clipboard::new() = ERR: Unknown error while interacting with the clipboard: X11 server connection timed out because it was unreachable`, taking ~1s. 1Password/arboard README "Clipboard Ownership" section documents the vanish-on-exit behaviour and the `SetExtLinux::wait` mitigation; the `wayland-data-control` feature is off by default and depends on ext-data-control-v1 / wlr-data-control-unstable-v1 which not all compositors implement.
findings.implication: Three consequences: (1) clipboard init must be lazy and non-fatal — never block startup on it (I measured a 1s stall); (2) jio needs its own internal registers as the primary clipboard so yank/put always works; (3) on exit after a yank, jio must either hold the Clipboard alive or call `wait`, or the user's copy silently disappears. Enable `wayland-data-control`. Clipboard cannot be meaningfully tested on `ubuntu-latest` without Xvfb, and real Wayland cannot be tested in CI at all.

findings.claim: crossterm 0.29.0 registers ONLY SIGWINCH; it has no SIGTSTP/SIGCONT handling, and `enable_raw_mode()` returns Ok(()) as a silent NO-OP if its global `TERMINAL_MODE_PRIOR_RAW_MODE` is already `Some`.
findings.evidence: crossterm-0.29.0/src/event/source/unix/mio.rs:48 registers `[signal_hook::consts::SIGWINCH]` only; grep for SIGTSTP/SIGCONT across src/ returns nothing. src/terminal/sys/unix.rs:108-123: `if original_mode.is_some() { return Ok(()); }`. It opens `/dev/tty` (src/terminal/sys/unix.rs:70) with a STDOUT_FILENO fallback. Windows resize comes from `InputRecord::WindowBufferSizeEvent` in src/event/source/windows.rs:66.
findings.implication: The Ctrl-Z bug trap: if jio catches SIGTSTP and re-enters raw mode on SIGCONT WITHOUT first calling `disable_raw_mode()`, the re-enable is a silent no-op and the user's terminal is left cooked after `fg`. The correct sequence (signal-hook's own lib.rs docs show it) is: on SIGTSTP → leave alt screen, disable_raw_mode, `low_level::emulate_default_handler(SIGTSTP)`; on SIGCONT → enable_raw_mode, enter alt screen, full redraw. Windows has no SIGWINCH and no SIGTSTP at all — resize arrives as WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT via ReadConsoleInput, which crossterm already normalizes to `Event::Resize`.

findings.claim: ratatui 0.30.2's `init`/`init_with_options`/`run` install a panic hook that restores the terminal, but it must be installed AFTER any hook of your own, and a panic hook does not run on SIGKILL, SIGSEGV, or `process::abort`.
findings.evidence: ratatui-0.30.2/src/init.rs:192-196, 335-342, 566-567 (`set_panic_hook` takes the current hook and wraps it). Verified from the vendored crate source.
findings.implication: jio needs three separate restoration paths: (1) normal exit, (2) panic hook, (3) a SIGTERM/SIGHUP handler that restores the terminal before dying. Nothing can save you from SIGKILL/power loss except the crash-recovery journal. A CI test can assert restoration for (1) and (2) by running jio under a pty and checking that the post-exit termios has ECHO/ICANON set and that the alt-screen exit sequence (ESC[?1049l) was emitted; that test runs fine on Linux and macOS but needs ConPTY on Windows.

findings.claim: `directories` 6.0.0 / `dirs` 7.0.0 map `config_dir` and `data_dir` on Windows to `{FOLDERID_RoamingAppData}` and on macOS to `~/Library/Application Support` — not to XDG.
findings.evidence: dirs-dev/directories-rs README ProjectDirs table (raw.githubusercontent.com/dirs-dev/directories-rs/main/README.md). `cargo add --dry-run` on this box: directories v6.0.0, dirs v7.0.0.
findings.implication: Roaming AppData is synced to the domain profile on managed Windows machines — putting undo history, session state, swap files or a plugin cache there will bloat every login. Use `data_local_dir`/`config_local_dir` (LocalAppData) for anything large or machine-specific and Roaming only for the small config file. On macOS, honour `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`~/.config` first if it exists and fall back to Application Support — that is what most CLI-adjacent tools do and what TUI users expect; document it.

findings.claim: GitHub's Windows runner images explicitly set `LongPathsEnabled=1` in the base image, so the Windows CI environment is strictly MORE permissive about long paths than a default user machine. Separately, Rust's std transparently prefixes `\\?\` for paths ≥248 UTF-16 units, which bypasses MAX_PATH for `std::fs` without any registry key or manifest — but not for `std::process::Command` or any Win32 API you call yourself.
findings.evidence: actions/runner-images `images/windows/scripts/build/Configure-BaseImage.ps1`: "Enable long path behavior" / `Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem' -Name 'LongPathsEnabled' -Value 1` (found via GitHub code search). Rust std sys/path/windows.rs:86-190 `maybe_verbatim`/`get_long_path` with `LEGACY_MAX_PATH = 248`. MS doc (MicrosoftDocs/win32 desktop-src/FileIO/maximum-file-path-limitation.md): both the registry value AND a `longPathAware` manifest element are required for Win32.
findings.implication: A long-path test that passes on `windows-latest` proves nothing about your users. If jio ever shells out (formatter, LSP, git) or calls Win32 directly, ship a `longPathAware` manifest via a build script + embed-resource, and add a CI step that flips LongPathsEnabled to 0 for one job so the un-enabled behaviour is actually exercised. Note the subtle asymmetry: for a short path Win32 normalization strips a trailing dot/space, but for a >248 path Rust hands Windows a verbatim path where normalization is disabled and the trailing dot survives — creating a file the user's Explorer cannot delete.

findings.claim: Windows filename rules that must be enforced by jio's Save-As, not discovered at write time: reserved device names CON/PRN/AUX/NUL/COM1-9/LPT1-9 *plus* the ISO-8859-1 superscripts COM¹/²/³ and LPT¹/²/³, reserved anywhere in any directory and even with an extension (NUL.txt == NUL); reserved characters `< > : " / \ | ? *`, NUL and 0x01-0x1F; and no trailing space or period.
findings.evidence: MicrosoftDocs/win32 desktop-src/FileIO/naming-a-file.md lines 30-60, fetched verbatim from raw.githubusercontent.com (learn.microsoft.com itself is proxy-blocked).
findings.implication: jio must validate filenames at Save-As time on ALL platforms if the file might ever land on a Windows/exFAT/SMB volume, and must surface a clear error rather than an opaque OS error. This is pure logic — write it as a table-driven unit test that runs on the Linux runner; it needs no Windows job.

findings.claim: macOS APFS is normalization-*preserving* but normalization-*insensitive* (hashes the normalized form), whereas HFS+ stored NFD on disk; and GitHub's `macos-latest` (now macOS 26 arm64) is case-INSENSITIVE APFS by default.
findings.evidence: Apple APFS FAQ / WWDC17 715 deck and eclecticlight.co explainer via WebSearch; actions/runner-images README shows `macos-latest` = macOS 26 Arm64, and actions/runner-images issue #865 confirms the default case-insensitive APFS image with no case-sensitive alternative. Verified locally that NFC and NFD forms of "café.txt" are different byte strings and compare unequal in Rust.
findings.implication: jio must never compare paths as strings to decide "is this the same file as an already-open buffer". Use OS-level identity (dev+ino on Unix, `GetFileInformationByHandle` volume serial + file index on Windows — the `same-file` 1.0.6 or notify's `file-id` crate). Two buffers on `README.md` and `readme.md` on macOS/Windows would otherwise silently overwrite each other. This IS testable on the macOS and Windows runners, and only there.

findings.claim: `atomic-write-file` 0.3.1 is the best-in-class Rust primitive for the rename path — `preserve_mode` (default on), `try_preserve_owner`, `openat`/`linkat`/`renameat` against a directory fd (immune to the directory being moved/remounted mid-save), fsync of both file and directory, and an optional `unnamed-tmpfile` (O_TMPFILE) feature — but it explicitly does NOT preserve timestamps, ACLs, xattrs or SELinux contexts, and has no permission/ownership preservation on non-Unix platforms.
findings.evidence: Vendored crate at atomic-write-file-0.3.1: src/lib.rs doc lines 98-140 (Notes and Limitations), src/unix.rs:51-74 (`preserve_mode`), src/imp/unix/linux.rs:29 (O_TMPFILE), src/imp/unix/mod.rs `rename_temporary_file` does `renameat` then `fsync(dir)`. README notes crash tests that simulate kernel panics.
findings.implication: Use it if you offer a 'replace' save strategy, but understand it does not solve the xattr/ACL/Finder-tag problem. On macOS the metadata-preserving primitive is `-[NSFileManager replaceItemAtURL:...]` / `renamex_np(RENAME_SWAP)`; on Windows it is `ReplaceFileW` (which explicitly preserves the original's creation time, ACLs and encryption attribute — MoveFileExW does not). If jio ships atomic save on those platforms it should call those, not plain rename.

findings.claim: This dev box has LANG/LC_ALL unset (POSIX/C locale) and cannot simulate foreign filesystem semantics: vfat and ext4-casefold loopback mounts both fail because the microVM kernel lacks the modules.
findings.evidence: `locale` output: `LANG=` and `LC_CTYPE="POSIX"`. `/proc/filesystems` lists only ext2/ext3/ext4 as block filesystems. `mount -o loop /tmp/fat.img` -> "unknown filesystem type 'vfat'"; ext4 `-O casefold` image -> "wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock".
findings.implication: Two things. (1) jio must not depend on locale for correctness — Rust strings are UTF-8 regardless, but do NOT use libc `wcwidth`/`setlocale`; use the `unicode-width` crate, and use a TZ-safe time API (the `time` crate returns `IndeterminateOffset` for local offset in multi-threaded programs on Linux; prefer `jiff` or `chrono` which parses tzdata directly). (2) Case-insensitivity / no-xattr / no-hardlink / no-symlink filesystem behaviour CANNOT be simulated on this dev box, so those tests must run on the real macOS and Windows runners — or on `ubuntu-latest`, where a vfat/exfat loopback image is likely available (unverified, worth a one-off probe job).
