surveys.recommendation: Default jio's save to IN-PLACE REWRITE (open existing fd, truncate, write, `fdatasync`), not temp+rename — this is what both VS Code (verified in pfs.ts) and vim-with-backupcopy=auto-falling-back-to-copy actually do, and it is the only strategy that preserves hard links, symlink identity, xattrs/Finder tags/resource forks, ACLs/SELinux labels, ownership, the read-only bit, and the inode (so `tail -f`, `crontab -e`, Docker single-file bind mounts, and other people's file watchers keep working). Buy crash-safety separately with a vim-style journal: a `<state_dir>/swap/<hash>.jio` write-ahead log fsync'd every ~200 keystrokes or 4s idle (vim's `updatecount`/`updatetime` model), containing the original file's identity (dev+ino / volume-serial+file-index), mtime, size, and the redo log — that survives SIGKILL and power loss, which rename atomicity does not. Offer `save.strategy = "rewrite" | "replace" | "auto"` with `auto` implementing vim's exact bufwrite.c heuristic (refuse rename when nlink>1, when symlink_metadata says symlink, when a hidden probe file can't be created in the directory, or when fchown/fchmod on the probe can't reproduce uid/gid/mode), and implement `replace` with `atomic-write-file` 0.3.1 + `preserve_mode(true)` + `try_preserve_owner` — never `tempfile::NamedTempFile`, whose 0600 default I measured silently destroying 0664 permissions. On Windows, wrap every rename in a retry loop on raw_os_error 5/32/33 with backoff (VS Code allows 60s) and fall back to in-place; and reach for `ReplaceFileW` rather than `MoveFileExW` because only the former preserves ACLs and creation time. For encoding, adopt a strict bytes-in/bytes-out model: keep the original bytes, record `(encoding, had_bom, had_lossy_bytes)`, decode with `decode_without_bom_handling_and_without_replacement`, NEVER call `Encoding::encode` (it emits UTF-8 for UTF_16LE/BE and `&#NNN;` for unmappable characters — both verified), hand-roll UTF-16 output, and refuse to save when the encode round-trip is not byte-identical outside edited regions. Everywhere else: `PathBuf`/`OsStr` only (a lossy `display()` string is not reopenable — verified); watch the parent directory, never the file (a file watch is permanently dead after any other editor's atomic save — verified); own the panic hook *and* SIGTERM/SIGHUP *and* SIGTSTP/SIGCONT, remembering that `crossterm::enable_raw_mode()` is a silent no-op if you didn't disable first; make clipboard init lazy, non-fatal, and backed by internal registers, with `wayland-data-control` enabled and OSC 52 as the SSH path. Set up the CI matrix (ubuntu-24.04, macos-latest arm64/APFS-case-insensitive, windows-latest Server 2025, windows-11-arm) in the FIRST week — not because it will catch the AV/OneDrive/SMB failures (it cannot), but because the case-insensitivity, Unicode-normalization, path-validity and terminal-restoration tests are only meaningful there, and retrofitting a green matrix onto an existing codebase is much more expensive than growing one. What would change my mind on the in-place default: if jio targets huge files where a truncate-window crash is more likely than a metadata-sensitive user, or if telemetry showed users overwhelmingly editing plain files with no links/xattrs — but the safe default is the one that cannot silently destroy something the user cannot see.
risks: Windows `ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION` (32) from AV engines, the Windows Search indexer, OneDrive, Office, and Notepad holding files open without FILE_SHARE_DELETE is the #1 real-world Windows save failure, and GitHub's clean runners have none of those processes. It is unreproducible in CI and must be handled design-first (retry loop + in-place fallback + a clear error naming the locking process via RestartManager if you want to be fancy).

GitHub's Windows image bakes `LongPathsEnabled=1` into the base image (verified in Configure-BaseImage.ps1), so long-path tests pass in CI and fail for users. Add a dedicated job that sets the registry value to 0 before running, or the whole long-path story is untested.

`macos-latest` is now macOS 26 on arm64 with case-INSENSITIVE APFS. Any test that relies on creating both `A.txt` and `a.txt` will behave differently than on the Linux runner, and a test that passes on Linux because paths are case-sensitive proves nothing about the identity logic users will hit.

This dev box cannot mount vfat, exfat, ntfs3 or ext4-casefold (kernel lacks the modules — verified), so foreign filesystem semantics cannot be rehearsed locally at all. Every case-insensitivity, no-xattr, no-hardlink and no-symlink behaviour is first exercised on a CI runner you cannot attach a debugger to.

Dropbox/OneDrive/iCloud/Google Drive and SMB/NFS shares cannot be tested anywhere in this setup. Atomic saves are known to generate conflicted-copy storms with sync clients (they see delete+create rather than modify), and notify documents that network filesystems may emit no events at all. Whatever jio does here ships unvalidated.

Power-loss and SIGKILL durability cannot be tested without a VM harness (`dm-flakey`, `qemu` forced reset, or the crash-test approach atomic-write-file uses in its own CI). Without it, the journal's fsync ordering (data fsync before rename, then directory fsync) is asserted by code review only.

Clipboard is effectively untestable: `ubuntu-latest` has no display server (arboard fails with an X11 timeout — verified), real Wayland compositors and data-control protocol support cannot be exercised, OSC 52 through tmux/ssh has no CI representation, and I could not confirm whether the Windows or macOS runners have a usable window station / pasteboard for a headless test process. Expect clipboard bugs to be found only by users.

Terminal lifecycle (SIGWINCH resize redraw, Ctrl-Z suspend/restore, panic restoration) needs a pty harness. That is straightforward on Linux/macOS but requires ConPTY on Windows, where crossterm's resize path is a completely different code path (WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT, not a signal) — so the Windows resize path is the least-tested code in a typical TUI.

The `4913`-style probe file that vim's auto heuristic requires will fire other developers' file watchers (I measured 4 inotify events for one create+delete). If jio does this on every save it will be blamed for spurious webpack/cargo-watch rebuilds.

inotify watch exhaustion: this box allows 129912 watches / 128 instances, but a recursive watch of a node_modules-sized tree will blow through it and `recommended_watcher` will fail with ENOSPC at some arbitrary point during a session, not at startup — so the failure surfaces as 'external change detection randomly stopped working'.

The vim swap-file model has a well-known UX cost: stale `.swp` files after a crash produce the dreaded E325 ATTENTION prompt, and on network/shared homes vim's own docs warn about bogus warnings. If jio copies the model it inherits the annoyance; put the journal in the XDG state dir keyed by a hash of the canonical path rather than next to the file.

Roaming AppData: `directories`/`dirs` map `config_dir` and `data_dir` to FOLDERID_RoamingAppData on Windows. Storing undo history or a plugin cache there will make login slow on domain-managed machines, and nobody will report it as a jio bug.
open_questions: Do the GitHub `macos-latest` (macOS 26 arm64) and `windows-latest` (Server 2025) runners have a usable clipboard for a headless test process — i.e. does NSPasteboard work outside an Aqua session, and does OpenClipboard succeed in the runner's window station? I could not verify this; it determines whether any clipboard test is possible at all outside of Xvfb on Linux.

Does macOS `renamex_np(RENAME_SWAP)` / `-[NSFileManager replaceItemAtURL:]` actually preserve `com.apple.metadata:_kMDItemUserTags` (Finder tags) and `com.apple.quarantine` across a save? Search results were inconclusive; this needs an empirical `xattr -l` test on a macOS runner.

Does Windows `ReplaceFileW` preserve NTFS alternate data streams and the compression/encryption attribute in practice, and does it work on OneDrive Files-On-Demand placeholder files (reparse points)? Needs a Windows runner test with `dir /r` and `fsutil`.

Are vfat/exfat/ntfs3 loopback mounts available on `ubuntu-latest`? If yes, a cheap Linux job could cover case-insensitivity, missing xattrs, missing hard links, missing symlinks and missing permission bits, dramatically reducing dependence on the macOS/Windows jobs. Worth one throwaway workflow run to find out.
Is `notify` 9.0.0 going to ship before jio needs to pin a watcher? Only 9.0.0-rc.5 is referenced in the repo docs; stable is 8.2.0 (verified). Committing to 8.x means an upgrade later.

What exactly does Windows 11 do today with DOS device names that have an extension (`con.txt`)? One secondary source claims path normalization no longer special-cases them except for NUL, but I could not confirm this against a Microsoft primary source, and the naming-a-file doc still lists the old rule. Until confirmed, assume the conservative rule.

Should jio honour `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` on macOS and Windows (what most TUI users expect) or the platform convention (`~/Library/Application Support`, `%APPDATA%`)? This is a product decision, not a technical one, but it must be made before the first release because migrating a config location afterwards is user-hostile.

For files that are not losslessly decodable in any encoding (genuinely binary, or mixed-encoding), should jio refuse to open, open read-only, or open in a byte-oriented mode? Vim's approach (open it, mangle it, hope) is not acceptable in 2026; VS Code's (detect binary, refuse) loses the ability to fix a single stray byte.

surveys.label: rust-ecosystem
surveys.summary: All versions below were verified today (2026-09-07) on this box via the crates.io sparse index and real `cargo add`/`cargo build`/`cargo tree` runs on rustc 1.94.1. Two discoveries reframe the whole CI-only constraint. First, `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target aarch64-apple-darwin` work locally for pure-Rust code — an 803-crate editor stack type-checks for Windows in 10s on this Linux box — but any C dependency (tree-sitter, git2, syntect's default onig) kills it with `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "lib.exe"`. Second, mingw-w64 AND wine 9.0 are installed here: I cross-built a full Windows .exe with statically linked tree-sitter C grammars and ran it under wine, correctly. Windows is therefore NOT CI-only for anything except real console/ConPTY behaviour. Third, the terminal layer is the one thing that genuinely cannot be tested without a PTY: with no TTY, crossterm 0.29's `size()` silently returns a bogus `Ok((80,24))` while `enable_raw_mode()` returns ENXIO — and under a PTY, `supports_keyboard_enhancement()` blocks a hard-coded 2000ms before erroring. On the ecosystem itself: Helix has left crossterm and the official tree-sitter bindings, moving to `termina 0.4.0` (its own crate, MIT OR MPL-2.0) and `tree-house 0.4.0`; ratatui 0.30.2 (19 Jun 2026) split into ratatui-core/widgets/backends and now ships a `ratatui-termina` backend; `lsp-types 0.97.0` has been frozen since 2024-06-04 and rust-analyzer merged a switch to `gen-lsp-types` on 2026-06-24. On rope performance nothing is a bottleneck: 100k random inserts into an 18.8MB/400k-line rope take 98ms (ropey 1.6.1), 144ms (crop 0.4.3), 231ms (jumprope 1.1.2). The single largest engineering cost in the whole plan is grammar distribution: 12 mainstream tree-sitter grammars statically linked produce an 11.4 MB binary.

findings.claim: Cross-`cargo check` to x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin works on this headless Linux box for pure-Rust code. `rustup target list --installed` already shows aarch64-apple-darwin, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, x86_64-apple-darwin, x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, x86_64-unknown-linux-{gnu,musl}. My full 803-crate candidate stack (ratatui+crossterm+ropey+gen-lsp-types+gix+tokio+ripgrep libs) checked clean for windows-msvc in 10.18s.
findings.evidence: `cd /tmp/claude-0/jio-stack && cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` -> "Finished `dev` profile ... in 10.18s" (after removing tree-sitter). Also /tmp/claude-0/jio-research: both windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin "Finished".
findings.implication: Type-level and cfg-level portability is a LOCAL, sub-15-second gate, not a CI round-trip. Make `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --target aarch64-apple-darwin` a pre-commit step. This removes most of the fear behind the CI-only constraint.

findings.claim: Any C dependency breaks that local cross-check. tree-sitter 0.27.0 compiles lib.c in its build script, so `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` fails with `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "lib.exe"`, and macOS fails because clang has no Darwin SDK. git2 0.21.0 fails identically; gix 0.87.1 (pure Rust, 574 crates) cross-checks fine.
findings.evidence: `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` in /tmp/claude-0/tsvendor -> `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "lib.exe": No such file or directory`. Same for /tmp/claude-0/x-git2. /tmp/claude-0/x-gix -> "Finished ... in 22.51s".
findings.implication: Put every C-touching subsystem (tree-sitter, and syntect-with-onig if used) behind a cargo feature, e.g. `--no-default-features --features core`, so the pure-Rust core keeps its fast local portability gate. This is a real architectural constraint, not hygiene.

findings.claim: mingw-w64 (`/usr/bin/x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc`) and wine 9.0 (`/usr/bin/wine`) are installed on this box. I cross-built a real Windows PE32+ .exe containing three statically-linked tree-sitter C grammars and RAN it under wine with correct output; I also ran the 18MB rope benchmark as a Windows binary with results within 10% of native Linux.
findings.evidence: `cargo build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` -> `tsvendor.exe: PE32+ executable (console) x86-64 ... for MS Windows`. `wine tsvendor.exe` -> `toml: abi=13 ok -> (document (table ...))` / `runtime supports ABI 13..=15`. `wine ropebench.exe` -> `insert100k ropey=106.606ms crop=140.8792ms jumprope=243.727ms`.
findings.implication: Windows is only CI-only for console/ConPTY input and MSVC-specific linking. Everything else — path handling, CRLF, UTF-16 filenames, file locking semantics, parsing, rendering-to-buffer — can be smoke-tested here today via windows-gnu + wine. Add a `just check-windows` that builds windows-gnu and runs the test binaries under wine.

findings.claim: With no controlling TTY (exactly a GitHub Actions step), crossterm 0.29.0 `terminal::size()` returns a SILENTLY WRONG `Ok((80, 24))`, while `enable_raw_mode()` returns `Err(ENXIO)` and `event::poll()` returns `Err("Failed to initialize input reader")`. Under a real PTY, raw mode works but `supports_keyboard_enhancement()` blocks for a hard-coded `Duration::from_millis(2000)` and then errors, because nothing answers the `ESC[?u ESC[c` query.
findings.evidence: Ran /tmp/claude-0/jio-research/src/main.rs headless and again under python `pty.fork()`. Headless: `size(): Ok((80, 24))`, `enable_raw_mode(): Err(Os { code: 6 ... })`. Under PTY: `enable_raw_mode(): Ok("ok")`, `supports_keyboard_enhancement(): Err("The keyboard enhancement status could not be read within a normal duration")`. Timeout constant at crossterm-0.29.0/src/terminal/sys/unix.rs:~246.
findings.implication: Two concrete bugs you would otherwise ship: (a) never trust `size()` without also checking `IsTerminal`, or jio silently renders at 80x24 in pipes; (b) call `supports_keyboard_enhancement()` off the startup path or with your own timeout, or jio hangs 2s on every start in tmux/CI/dumb terminals. Every terminal test MUST run under a PTY.

findings.claim: crossterm 0.29.0's Windows event source uses the Win32 Console API (`crossterm_winapi::Console::read_single_input_event` / `InputRecord`), not VT parsing, and `supports_keyboard_enhancement()` on Windows is literally `Ok(false)`. So the Kitty keyboard protocol is structurally unavailable on Windows through crossterm, even on Windows Terminal, which has supported it since Preview v1.25.622.0.
findings.evidence: crossterm-0.29.0/src/event/source/windows.rs uses `crossterm_winapi::{Console, InputRecord}`. crossterm-0.29.0/src/terminal/sys/windows.rs:75-77 -> `pub fn supports_keyboard_enhancement() -> std::io::Result<bool> { Ok(false) }`. Kitty flags in event.rs also note "Alternate keys and Unicode codepoints are not yet supported by crossterm" and REPORT_ASSOCIATED_TEXT is commented out.
findings.implication: If jio wants Ctrl+Shift+K, key-release events, or unambiguous Esc on Windows, crossterm cannot deliver it. This is the single strongest argument for termina.

findings.claim: termina 0.4.0 (github.com/helix-editor/termina, Michael Davis, MIT OR MPL-2.0, MSRV 1.71) is Helix's replacement for crossterm. It speaks VT on Windows via ConPTY (requires 64-bit Windows 10.0.17763+), so the Kitty protocol and bracketed paste DO work on Windows Terminal, with a `windows-legacy` feature for the old console path. It opens `/dev/tty` explicitly rather than hijacking stdin/stdout, and its event model is filter-based: `Terminal::poll<F: Fn(&Event)->bool>(filter, timeout)` and `read(filter)`, plus an `event-stream` feature. Without a TTY it fails fast and honestly at `PlatformTerminal::new()`.
findings.evidence: termina-0.4.0/README.md feature table (VTE Mode vs Legacy Console Mode: Kitty ✓/✕, bracketed paste ✓/✕, AltGr ✓/✕). src/terminal.rs:95-129 trait Terminal { poll, read }. src/terminal/unix.rs:93 `.open("/dev/tty")`. My probe headless: `PlatformTerminal::new() FAILED: No such device or address (os error 6)`.
findings.implication: The filter-based read is the right primitive for an editor: you can synchronously await a DA1/DECRQM response without swallowing the user's keystrokes — exactly what crossterm's `supports_keyboard_enhancement` hack fights. Opening /dev/tty also means `jio < file` and `cmd | jio` work.

findings.claim: ratatui 0.30.2 (released 19 Jun 2026) split into ratatui-core 0.1.2, ratatui-widgets 0.3.2, ratatui-macros 0.7.2, and per-backend crates ratatui-crossterm/termwiz/termion 0.1.2 plus the new ratatui-termina 0.1.0. MSRV 1.88. TestBackend lives in the core and works fully headless, including correct wide-character handling. But ratatui-termina 0.1.0 pins termina 0.3.3 while termina is at 0.4.0, giving you two copies and a type error if you also depend on termina directly.
findings.evidence: `cargo tree` shows ratatui v0.30.2 -> {ratatui-core 0.1.2, ratatui-crossterm 0.1.2, ratatui-widgets 0.3.2, ratatui-macros 0.7.2}. `cargo tree -i termina` -> "There are multiple `termina` packages in your project ... termina@0.3.3, termina@0.4.0". TestBackend dump: `"│héllo 世界 x      │" Hidden by multi-width symbols: [(8, " "), (10, " ")]`.
findings.implication: ratatui + termina is available today but you must pin `termina = "0.3"` to match ratatui-termina, or write your own ~200-line Backend impl over termina 0.4. Backend-version skew is a recurring tax in this ecosystem; budget for it.

findings.claim: Helix does NOT use ratatui. It vendors a fork of tui-rs as `helix-tui` (package name `tui`), and the reason is visible in the types: Helix's Style has `underline_style: Option<UnderlineStyle>` with `{Reset, Line, Curl, Dotted, Dashed, DoubleLine}`, which ratatui-core 0.1.2 does not have — ratatui's Modifier has only UNDERLINED, and underline_color is behind a feature flag. Helix master's helix-term now depends on `termina` with `crossterm 0.28` retained for Windows only, plus `termini 1`.
findings.evidence: helix-view/src/graphics.rs UnderlineStyle enum (fetched). ratatui-core-0.1.2/src/style.rs:104-114 Modifier bitflags (no curl/dotted/dashed), :246-249 underline_color behind `#[cfg(feature = "underline-color")]`. helix-term/Cargo.toml: `tui` (helix-tui) features ["termina","crossterm"], `termina` workspace, `crossterm 0.28` (Windows only).
findings.implication: This is the concrete cost of ratatui for an editor: you cannot render LSP diagnostics as undercurl. Everything else (immediate-mode double-buffered `Buffer::diff_iter` damage tracking, viewport, insert_before) is exactly what you'd hand-roll anyway. Start on ratatui; if undercurl becomes a must, fork ratatui-core (it's small and MIT) rather than the whole renderer.

findings.claim: Static-linking tree-sitter grammars is expensive and I measured it: 3 grammars -> 1.27 MB release binary; 12 mainstream grammars (rust, python, js, ts, tsx, go, c, cpp, json, markdown, html, bash) all actually referenced -> 11.4 MB (11.26 MB stripped). cpp alone is a 3.5 MB .a, typescript 2.9 MB.
findings.evidence: `ls -la /tmp/claude-0/tsprobe/target/release/tsprobe` -> 11427072 bytes; `strip -o /tmp/stripped` -> 11264888 bytes. Per-grammar .a sizes measured with `find target/release/build -name '*.a'`: tree-sitter-cpp 3486388, tree-sitter-typescript 2946026, tree-sitter-bash 1417546, tree-sitter-rust 1154522.
findings.implication: 50 grammars statically linked is realistically a 30-60 MB binary. That is shippable (rust-analyzer is bigger) but it is a decision, not an accident. The alternative Helix chose is runtime dynamic loading of .so/.dll/.dylib built by `hx --grammar build`, which requires a C compiler on the user's machine — worse for a CI-only project because you cannot test the build-on-user-machine path.

findings.claim: The tree-sitter grammar problem is NOT ABI, it is Rust crate version pinning. tree-sitter 0.27.0 accepts grammars with ABI 13, 14 and 15 simultaneously (`MIN_COMPATIBLE_LANGUAGE_VERSION=13`, `LANGUAGE_VERSION=15`). But `tree-sitter-toml 0.20.0` drags in a second runtime, `tree-sitter v0.20.10`, and its `language()` returns a `tree_sitter_0_20::Language` which is a hard type error against 0.27's `Parser::set_language`. Vendoring the grammar's `parser.c`/`scanner.c` and compiling it with `cc`, then wrapping the raw symbol in `tree_sitter_language::LanguageFn::from_raw`, works perfectly for all three ABIs.
findings.evidence: `cargo add tree-sitter-toml` -> "Adding tree-sitter v0.20.10". Build error: `mismatched types` at `p2.set_language(&lang)`. My /tmp/claude-0/tsvendor build.rs + `LanguageFn::from_raw` output: `toml: abi=13 ok`, `json: abi=14 ok`, `c: abi=15 ok`, `runtime supports ABI 13..=15`.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: never depend on `tree-sitter-*` wrapper crates. Vendor grammar C sources as git submodules or a fetch script, compile them all in one build.rs with `cc`, and declare `unsafe extern "C" { fn tree_sitter_x() -> *const (); }`. This decouples you from 50 independently-versioned crates and is the only approach that scales to 50 grammars. Watch for grammars whose external scanner is `scanner.cc` (C++) — those drag in libstdc++/libc++ and are the ones most likely to break on Windows MSVC in CI.

findings.claim: Helix has replaced the official tree-sitter Rust bindings with its own `tree-house 0.4.0` (+ tree-house-bindings 0.3.2), citing correctness fixes, newer tree-sitter C sources, and a 5-10% speedup. Meanwhile tree-sitter 0.27.0 does give you exactly the viewport APIs you need: `QueryCursor::set_byte_range` / `set_point_range` / `set_containing_byte_range`, `Tree::edit`, `Tree::changed_ranges`, `Parser::set_included_ranges` (injections), and `parse_with_options` with a `ParseProgressCallback` for cancellation.
findings.evidence: helix Cargo.toml workspace deps: `tree-house = { version = "0.4", default-features = false }`. tree-sitter-0.27.0/binding_rust/lib.rs:3355 set_byte_range, :3369 set_point_range, :3388 set_containing_byte_range, :1537 Tree::edit, :1558 changed_ranges, :1438 set_included_ranges, :953 parse_with_options.
findings.implication: "Highlight only what's on screen" is a solved, first-class API: parse the whole file (fast, incremental via Tree::edit) but run the highlight Query only over the visible byte range. Do NOT try to parse partially. Start with the official 0.27 bindings; tree-house is an optimisation to consider once you have a working highlighter, and it is MPL-ish territory worth checking.

findings.claim: syntect 5.3.0's DEFAULT feature set is `default-onig`, which pulls in the C Oniguruma library (onig + onig_sys). Switching to `default-features = false, features = ["default-fancy"]` makes it 100% pure Rust with identical behaviour: 75 built-in syntaxes, 7 built-in themes, and it then cross-checks to x86_64-pc-windows-msvc from Linux.
findings.evidence: Default build `cargo tree | grep -i onig` -> `onig v6.5.3`, `onig_sys v69.9.3`. After switching: onig count 0, same output `builtin syntaxes: 75`, `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` -> "Finished ... in 11.17s".
findings.implication: If you use syntect at all, the fancy-regex build is mandatory for this project — it is the difference between local cross-checking and CI-only. But syntect's model is fundamentally sequential (stateful `ParseState` per line), so "highlight only the viewport" means caching ParseState snapshots every N lines. tree-sitter gives you random access. Use syntect only as a fallback for languages with no grammar.

findings.claim: `lsp-types 0.97.0` was released 2024-06-04 and gluon-lang/lsp-types is effectively unmaintained; it still depends on `bitflags 1.3.2`. rust-analyzer MERGED a switch to `gen-lsp-types` on 2026-06-24 (PR rust-lang/rust-analyzer#22115), citing LSP 3.18 SnippetTextEdit support, missing Eq/Hash derives, poor Uri interop introduced in 0.96, and type names not matching the spec. gen-lsp-types 0.11.0 is generated from the official LSP metamodel and compiles and round-trips fine here. Separately, `async-lsp 0.2.4` pins `lsp-types 0.95.1`, so depending on both async-lsp and lsp-types gives you two incompatible copies.
findings.evidence: WebSearch + WebFetch of PR #22115 ("Merged (merged on June 24, 2026 via commit 3f41d0b)"). `cargo tree` in /tmp/claude-0/lspprobe shows `async-lsp v0.2.4 -> lsp-types v0.95.1` alongside top-level `lsp-types v0.97.0`. gen-lsp-types 0.11.0 probe printed `Position { line: 3, character: 7 }` / `{"line":3,"character":7}` / `UTF8`.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: `gen-lsp-types 0.11.0` for the types, and write your own ~400-line JSON-RPC transport over `tokio::process` rather than adopting async-lsp (whose lsp-types pin you cannot escape). tower-lsp 0.20.0 is server-side and stale; its successor is `tower-lsp-server 0.23.0`. rust-analyzer's `lsp-server 0.10.0` is a clean sync transport worth reading.

findings.claim: UTF-16 position conversion is a solved rope operation, and it is cheap. ropey 1.6.1 ships `char_to_utf16_cu`/`utf16_cu_to_char`/`len_utf16_cu` unconditionally; crop 0.4.3 has an opt-in `utf16-metric` feature (`utf16_code_unit_of_byte`, `byte_of_utf16_code_unit`, `utf16_slice`). 200k random conversions on an 18.8 MB rope: ropey 129ms, crop 156ms — ~0.65us each. proptest confirmed ropey's round-trip is exact over 200 random cases including astral-plane text.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/ropebench output `utf16 x200k ropey=128.968347ms` / `crop=155.890572ms`. /tmp/claude-0/ropebench/tests/rope_props.rs `utf16_conversion_is_monotonic ... ok` asserting `r.utf16_cu_to_char(r.char_to_utf16_cu(c)) == c`. crop panics if you hand `utf16_code_unit_of_byte` a non-char-boundary — a sharp edge I hit.
findings.implication: Do not hand-roll UTF-16 offsets, and do not do it per-line by scanning. Also: negotiate `positionEncoding: utf-8` in your LSP initialize (PositionEncodingKind::UTF8 exists in both lsp-types and gen-lsp-types) — most modern servers accept it, and then the whole problem disappears for those servers. Keep the rope path as the fallback.

findings.claim: Rope choice is not performance-critical. On an 18.8 MB / 400k-line file: construction ropey 18.9ms / crop 13.7ms / jumprope 23.0ms; 100k random single-char inserts ropey 97.6ms / crop 144.3ms / jumprope 230.8ms (~1us per insert); 200k random `line()` lookups ropey 190ms / crop 193ms; chunk iteration ropey 2.3ms over 37264 chunks (avg 506 B) vs crop 0.8ms over 36570 chunks (avg 516 B). ropey 1.6.1 is MIT-only and char-indexed; ropey 2.0.0-beta.1 (MIT OR Apache-2.0) is a full rewrite to byte indexing with a `LineType` enum {LF, LF_CR, Unicode} behind feature flags. xi-rope 0.3.0 has 4 total versions and is dead.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/ropebench full output, both natively and under wine (within 10%). ropey CHANGELOG.md: 2.0.0 alpha 1 2024-10-20, alpha 3 2025-06-01; index shows 2.0.0-beta.1 as latest, 1.6.1 as latest stable. ropey 1.6.1 has no grapheme API (docs say so explicitly); crop has `graphemes()` behind a `graphemes` feature.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: ropey 1.6.1 with `features=["simd"]` — what Helix ships, fastest at editing, best-documented, and its ~500-byte chunks feed tree-sitter's `Parser::parse_with` callback directly. Do NOT adopt ropey 2.0-beta for a project you want to ship; do keep your rope behind a thin `TextBuffer` trait so you can move to 2.0 (or crop) later, since byte indexing is where everything else in the stack already lives.

findings.claim: unicode-width 0.2.2 is at Unicode 17.0.0 and does string-level, ligature-aware width. Summing per-char widths is WRONG: a family ZWJ emoji has `str.width() == 2` but sum-of-char-widths == 8. Ambiguous-width characters are handled by the `cjk` feature: `"○".width() == 1` but `.width_cjk() == 2`. Control characters lie — `"\t".width() == 1`, `"\0".width() == 1`, `"\n".width() == 1` — the crate explicitly warns not to rely on that.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/uniprobe output table: `Family ZWJ  width=2 cjk=2 sum_ch=8 n_graph=1`; `Ambiguous ○  width=1 cjk=2`; `Tab width=1 sum_ch=0`. `unicode_width::UNICODE_VERSION == (17, 0, 0)`. Devanagari `क्ष` -> width 2, n_graph 1.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: `unicode-segmentation 1.13.3` for grapheme clusters + `unicode-width 0.2.2` called PER GRAPHEME, never per char, with a user config toggling `width()` vs `width_cjk()` for CJK terminals. Handle tab/control chars yourself before calling either. icu_segmenter 2.3.0 (84 crates, 7.3s build) is more correct for line/word/sentence breaking but has no width API at all and no terminal story — do not use it for cell widths.

findings.claim: The complete headless end-to-end test harness works today and is pure Rust: `portable-pty 0.9.0` (wezterm, MIT, has a ConPTY backend for Windows) spawns the editor in a real PTY, and `vt100 0.16.2` parses the output into a virtual screen with per-cell contents, fg colour and attributes. Both cross-check to x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin from this Linux box. Separately, ratatui's TestBackend + `insta 1.48.0` gives a fast inner-loop snapshot test of a frame buffer.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/ptytest ran `sh -c "printf '\\033[2J...'"` in a PTY and asserted `cell(0,0) contents="j" fgcolor=Idx(1) bold=true`, `cursor = (2, 13)`. `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` -> Finished. portable-pty-0.9.0/src/win/{conpty.rs,psuedocon.rs}. /tmp/claude-0/probe-rat/tests/snapshots/snap__editor_frame_snapshot.snap contains the box-drawn frame including the wide-char annotation.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: portable-pty + vt100 for e2e (NOT expectrl 0.9.0 or rexpect 0.7.1 — those are expect-style line matchers, wrong shape for a full-screen TUI, and rexpect is Unix-only). This is the harness that makes the CI-only constraint survivable: identical test code runs on all three GitHub runners, and locally under wine for windows-gnu.

findings.claim: Logging from a TUI without corrupting the screen is a solved 6-line problem: `tracing 0.1.44` + `tracing-subscriber 0.3.23` + `tracing-appender 0.2.5`'s `non_blocking` writer to a rolling file, with `.with_ansi(false)`. `#[instrument]` gives you free span context. stdout stays completely clean.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/logtest produced zero stdout during logging; jio.log contains `INFO ThreadId(01) edit{buffer="main.rs"}: logtest: applying edit rope_len=4096` and `ERROR ... error=cannot open main.rs: nope`.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: tracing over log — the span context (which buffer, which LSP request id) is what you actually need when debugging an editor from a log file, and it is the only way to debug something you cannot attach a debugger to on macOS/Windows CI. Pair with thiserror 2.0.20 for library-internal errors and anyhow 1.0.104 only at the top-level command boundary.

findings.claim: You need tokio, and it is cheaper than the alternatives. With the Helix feature set (rt-multi-thread, io-util, io-std, process, time, macros, sync, fs) tokio 1.53.1 is only 20 crates and 12.1s to build; smol 2.0.2 is 78 crates and 12.3s; crossbeam-channel 0.5.17 is 3 crates and 1.5s. Helix uses tokio specifically for `process` (async child-process stdio for LSP/DAP), `time` (debounce/idle timers), io-std and fs.
findings.evidence: `cargo tree -e normal | wc -l` in /tmp/claude-0/async-{tok,sml,cbm}: 20 / 78 / 3. Build times measured with date +%s%N. helix-term/Cargo.toml tokio features list.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: tokio, but only in the LSP/DAP/process layer — keep the editor core, rope, and renderer synchronous and single-threaded, talking to the async world over `tokio::sync::mpsc`. Async child-process stdio that works identically on Windows (named pipes/IOCP) and Unix is the one thing threads+crossbeam genuinely cannot give you cheaply, and getting it wrong is exactly the class of bug you cannot debug on a CI-only Windows box.

findings.claim: Search: the `regex 1.13.1` crate rejects lookaround and backreferences by design; `fancy-regex 0.19.1` accepts them (it is a backtracking layer over regex). For multi-file search, `grep-searcher 0.1.17` + `grep-regex 0.1.14` + `ignore 0.4.33` (all Unlicense OR MIT, BurntSushi) work as libraries out of the box with binary detection, line numbers and gitignore-aware parallel walking.
findings.evidence: /tmp/claude-0/misc output: `regex ERR foo(?=bar)`, `regex ERR (a)\1`, `regex ERR (?<!x)y`; `fancy OK` for all three. grep-searcher+ignore found 10 hits across 5 files with `f3.rs:3: // TODO fix 3`.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: regex 1.13.1 for the common path (linear-time, no catastrophic backtracking — critical since users type patterns into your search box), with fancy-regex 0.19.1 behind an explicit opt-in flag and a timeout. Use grep-searcher/ignore for project-wide search; do NOT shell out to ripgrep, since that adds an external binary you cannot guarantee on Windows CI.

findings.claim: Config: `toml 1.1.5+spec-1.1.0` has reached 1.0 and `toml_edit 0.25.13+spec-1.1.0` (both MIT OR Apache-2.0, MSRV 1.85) round-trips comments and formatting perfectly. I edited a value and added a key; the leading `# jio config` and the inline `# how many spaces` comment survived exactly. Helix uses `toml 1.1`.
findings.evidence:
/tmp/claude-0/misc toml_edit round-trip printed `# jio config
[editor]
# how many spaces
indent = 2
line-numbers = true
theme = "gruvbox"`. helix workspace Cargo.toml: `toml = "1.1"`.
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: `toml 1.1` (serde deserialize into your Config struct) for reading, `toml_edit 0.25` only where jio writes config back (`:set` commands), so user comments survive. For hot-reload use `notify 8` + `notify-debouncer-full 0.6`; note that macOS FSEvents and Windows ReadDirectoryChangesW have materially different coalescing behaviour, so debouncing is mandatory and this is one of the few things you truly must verify in CI.

findings.claim: Plugin-runtime costs differ by two orders of magnitude in dependency count: mlua 0.12.1 (lua54+vendored) is 17 crates / 9.5s; rhai 1.26.0 is 34 crates; steel-core 0.8.3 is 256 crates; wasmtime is 351 crates / 3m19s cold; extism 1.30.0 is 658 crates. wasmtime's MSRV advances one Rust release per version: 47.0.4 needs 1.94, 48.0.1 needs 1.95, 49.0.0-rc.1 needs 1.96 — on rustc 1.94.1 cargo silently downgraded me to 47.0.4.
findings.evidence: `cargo tree -e normal | wc -l` per project. `cargo add wasmtime` -> "Adding wasmtime v47.0.4 (available: v48.0.1, requires Rust 1.95.0)". Index rust_version fields: 47.0.4->1.94.0, 48.0.1->1.95.0, 49.0.0-rc.1->1.96.0. wasmtime is Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception.
findings.implication: Defer this entirely — it is the single easiest thing to over-engineer early. When you do it: DEFAULT PICK mlua 0.12.1 with vendored Lua 5.4 for a scripting layer (tiny, boring, ubiquitous), or wasmtime if you want sandboxing — but understand wasmtime puts your project on a permanent MSRV treadmill and a 3-minute CI build, which is a real tax when your only macOS/Windows feedback loop is CI minutes.

findings.claim: Git and fuzzy-find: `gix 0.87.1` is pure Rust (574 crates, ~55s build) and cross-checks to Windows; `git2 0.21.0` is 9 crates but wraps libgit2 C and does NOT cross-check. gix's feature matrix is fragile — `default-features = false, features = ["max-performance-safe"]` fails to compile with 16 errors in gix-hash (E0004, non-exhaustive match). For fuzzy finding, `nucleo 0.5.0` (helix-editor, MPL-2.0) / `nucleo-matcher 0.3.1` works well with path-aware config; `fuzzy-matcher 0.3.7` is stale.
findings.evidence: gix windows-msvc check "Finished ... in 22.51s"; git2 -> `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "lib.exe"`. `error: could not compile gix-hash (lib) due to 16 previous errors` with max-performance-safe. nucleo-matcher probe with `Config::DEFAULT.match_paths()` ranked `src/editor/rope.rs` 122 above `tests/rope_props.rs` 113 for query "srope".
findings.implication: DEFAULT PICK: gix 0.87.1 with DEFAULT features (do not hand-tune the feature set), for the local cross-check alone. DEFAULT PICK: nucleo 0.5.0 — but note the MPL-2.0 licence. MPL is file-level copyleft, fine to link from an MIT/Apache binary, but if you modify nucleo's files you must publish those files. Same caveat applies to termina's MPL-2.0 option (it is dual MIT OR MPL-2.0, so take MIT) and to Helix's tree-house.

surveys.recommendation:
Go Rust. The concrete stack, all verified to compile together today on rustc 1.94.1 (803 crates, ~40s dev build):

TERMINAL: `termina 0.4.0` over crossterm. crossterm 0.29.0 hard-codes `supports_keyboard_enhancement() -> Ok(false)` on Windows and reads events through the Win32 Console API, so Kitty protocol on Windows is structurally impossible there; termina speaks VT via ConPTY and gets Kitty + bracketed paste + AltGr on Windows Terminal. Its filter-based `poll(filter, timeout)`/`read(filter)` is the right primitive for query/response terminal negotiation, and it opens /dev/tty so piping works. crossterm 0.29 has also had no release in over a year. Termion is disqualified outright — I proved it does not compile for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc. If you want to de-risk: start on crossterm 0.29 behind a 150-line `TerminalBackend` trait and switch, since Helix shipped exactly that migration.

RENDERING: `ratatui 0.30.2` via `ratatui-termina 0.1.0` (pin `termina = "0.3"` to match). Do not hand-roll. Ratatui already gives you exactly the damage tracking you'd write (`Buffer::diff_iter` over a double buffer), and TestBackend + insta is the fastest verification loop you will have on a headless box. The one thing it costs you is undercurl (no `underline_style`), which is why Helix forked tui-rs. Accept that and fork ratatui-core later if diagnostics rendering demands it.

TEXT: `ropey 1.6.1` with `features = ["simd"]`, behind your own `TextBuffer` trait. Fastest at the operation that matters (98ms for 100k random inserts into 18MB), what Helix ships, and it has built-in UTF-16 CU conversion for LSP. Do not adopt ropey 2.0-beta or crop for v1.

UNICODE: `unicode-segmentation 1.13.3` + `unicode-width 0.2.2`, width computed per grapheme cluster, never per char (family emoji: 2 vs 8), with a cjk/ambiguous-width config toggle. Not icu4x.

SYNTAX: `tree-sitter 0.27.0`, but VENDOR the grammar C sources and compile them yourself in one build.rs with `cc 1.4.5`, wrapping raw symbols in `tree_sitter_language::LanguageFn::from_raw`. Never depend on `tree-sitter-*` wrapper crates — I proved they pull conflicting runtime versions. Budget ~1 MB per mainstream grammar. Use `QueryCursor::set_byte_range` to highlight only the viewport. syntect only as a pure-Rust (`default-fancy`) fallback.

LSP: `gen-lsp-types 0.11.0` (rust-analyzer merged the switch away from lsp-types on 2026-06-24), your own JSON-RPC transport over `tokio::process` — not async-lsp, whose lsp-types 0.95.1 pin you cannot escape. Negotiate `positionEncoding: utf-8` first, fall back to rope-based UTF-16 conversion.

REST: regex 1.13.1 (fancy-regex 0.19.1 opt-in) + grep-searcher/grep-regex/ignore; toml 1.1 read + toml_edit 0.25 write; tokio 1.53.1 confined to the process/LSP layer with a sync core; tracing + tracing-appender non-blocking to file; thiserror 2 internally, anyhow 1 at the boundary; gix 0.87.1 default features; nucleo 0.5.0 (MPL-2.0, note it).

THE THING THAT SHOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE YOUR PLAN: this box can already do far more Windows validation than "CI-only" implies. mingw-w64 and wine 9.0 are installed — I cross-built a Windows .exe containing statically linked tree-sitter C grammars and ran it under wine correctly, and ran the full rope benchmark as a Windows binary. Combined with `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target aarch64-apple-darwin` (which work for pure Rust in ~10s), the only genuinely CI-only surfaces are: real ConPTY console input, macOS anything, and MSVC-specific linking. Structure the repo to exploit that: (1) feature-gate every C dependency so `cargo check --target ... --no-default-features` stays green locally; (2) make every terminal test run under portable-pty + vt100 so the same test file runs on all three runners; (3) add a local `windows-gnu + wine` smoke job. What would change my mind on the terminal pick: if termina 0.4 has no release in 6 months or the ratatui-termina version skew persists past ratatui 0.31, fall back to crossterm and accept no Kitty protocol on Windows.
risks: Terminal size and raw mode fail differently on every platform and I measured it: headless Linux gives a SILENTLY WRONG `size() == Ok((80,24))` with `enable_raw_mode()` returning ENXIO, while Windows-under-wine gives `size() == Err(Invalid handle)`. If jio trusts size() it will render at 80x24 in any pipe or CI step and you will not notice until a user reports it. Gate on IsTerminal and treat a missing TTY as a hard, explicit startup error.

crossterm's `supports_keyboard_enhancement()` has a hard-coded 2000ms timeout and returned an error under my PTY because nothing answered the CSI query. Any terminal-capability probe on the startup path is a 2-second hang in tmux, screen, CI, and dumb terminals. This class of bug (synchronous query with no responder) is invisible on a developer's real terminal and only shows up where you cannot look.

Statically linking 50 tree-sitter grammars means a 30-60 MB binary (measured: 11.4 MB for 12). Worse, the C compile is the exact thing that breaks local cross-checking, so grammar build failures on Windows MSVC and macOS will surface ONLY in CI, and grammars with C++ external scanners (scanner.cc) are the most likely to break there. Add grammars a few at a time and make each addition a separate CI-verified commit, not a batch.

`ignore 0.4.33` walking + case-insensitive filesystems: macOS APFS is case-insensitive-preserving by default and Windows NTFS is case-insensitive, so gitignore matching, buffer deduplication by path, and 'is this file already open' checks will behave differently there than on ext4. This is pure logic — test it under wine and with a case-insensitive loopback image locally rather than discovering it in CI.

Line endings. ropey 1.6.1's default `unicode_lines` feature counts VT/FF/NEL/LS/PS as line breaks, not just LF/CRLF. Combined with Windows checkouts (git autocrlf) and tree-sitter byte offsets, an off-by-one in CRLF handling will produce corrupt edits that only reproduce on Windows. Write proptests over CRLF/mixed/lone-CR content NOW, and run them under wine.

Duplicate-crate version skew is endemic here and cargo will not stop you: async-lsp 0.2.4 pins lsp-types 0.95.1 against a 0.97.0 top-level dep; ratatui-termina 0.1.0 pins termina 0.3.3 against 0.4.0; tree-sitter-toml 0.20.0 pins tree-sitter 0.20.10 against 0.27.0. Each produces a confusing 'mismatched types' error at a distance. Add `cargo deny` with a duplicate-versions check to CI early.

macOS is the one platform with NO local escape hatch — no SDK, and clang cannot cross-compile C for Darwin here. Anything touching C, plus all Cocoa-adjacent behaviour (FSEvents coalescing in notify, `/dev/tty` semantics, SIGWINCH timing), is genuinely blind until CI runs. Budget for slow macOS iteration and keep macOS-specific cfg blocks as small and as data-driven as possible.

gix 0.87.1's non-default feature combinations do not compile (16 errors in gix-hash with `max-performance-safe`). Its 574-crate tree also means a supply-chain audit surface and slow clean CI builds. Do not tune its features; if git integration becomes a build-time problem, shelling out to the `git` binary is a legitimate v1 answer.

MPL-2.0 appears in nucleo 0.5.0 and in Helix's tree-house. It is file-level copyleft, so linking is fine from an MIT/Apache binary, but any modification to those files must be published. If you vendor-and-patch nucleo (tempting for a picker), you inherit that obligation. termina is dual MIT OR MPL-2.0 — take MIT explicitly in your NOTICE.

wasmtime advances MSRV one Rust release per version (47->1.94, 48->1.95, 49->1.96) and takes 3m19s to build cold with 351 crates. Adopting it for plugins locks jio's MSRV to roughly current-stable forever and materially slows every CI run on three platforms. Do not take this on before the editor works.
open_questions: Does termina 0.4.0's Windows ConPTY VT path actually work on a real GitHub Actions windows-latest runner? Wine cannot emulate ConPTY faithfully and I could not test it. This needs a throwaway CI job spawning a termina app under portable-pty on windows-latest BEFORE committing to termina — it is the single highest-value experiment available right now.

Will ratatui-termina track termina 0.4+? Right now it pins 0.3.3. If it lags, you either pin termina 0.3 (losing 0.4 fixes) or write your own ~200-line Backend. Worth asking in the ratatui repo before building on it.

What is the real cost of writing a Backend over termina directly and skipping ratatui? Helix's helix-tui is roughly 3k lines. For an editor whose only widgets are a text viewport, a statusline, a completion popup and a picker, the ratatui widget ecosystem may buy almost nothing while costing undercurl. I lean ratatui for speed-to-first-pixel, but this deserves a spike.

Which is better for jio: the official tree-sitter 0.27 bindings or Helix's tree-house 0.4.0? tree-house claims correctness fixes and 5-10% speedup and handles injections/locals properly, but it is a single-consumer crate with a Helix-shaped API and likely MPL licensing. I did not compile or benchmark it.

Can macOS C compilation be unblocked locally with osxcross or a vendored SDK? If yes, the entire CI-only constraint essentially evaporates. Not attempted — no SDK is present and the licensing of redistributing the macOS SDK is genuinely restrictive.

Is ropey 2.0.0-beta.1 close to stable? The changelog shows alpha1 Oct 2024, alpha3 Jun 2025, beta1 sometime after. Byte indexing would align the whole stack (tree-sitter, LSP utf-8, regex all speak bytes) and eliminate char<->byte conversions. If the author is close to 1.0-ing it, waiting or using crop 0.4.3 changes the calculus.
How many grammars does jio actually need at v1? If the answer is 10-15 rather than 50, static linking is a non-issue (11 MB) and the whole dynamic-loading vs WASM debate can be deferred by a year.

Does `positionEncoding: utf-8` negotiation actually succeed with the servers you care about (rust-analyzer, gopls, tsserver, pyright, clangd)? If most say yes, the UTF-16 rope conversion becomes cold-path code and you can simplify significantly. This is a one-afternoon experiment with real servers on this box.
sources: https://index.crates.io/ (sparse index, queried directly for every version and MSRV reported)
https://proxy.golang.org/ (queried via `go list -m -versions` for all Go appendix versions)

surveys.label: ci-build-release
surveys.summary: The "no local machine" constraint is not a blocker for jio — but it forces two decisions early. First: keep the repo PUBLIC. GitHub-hosted standard runners are free and unlimited for public repos, including Linux arm64 (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`), Windows arm64 (`windows-11-arm`), macOS arm64 (`macos-latest` = macOS 26, 3 vCPU/7 GB) AND — critically — free Intel macOS (`macos-15-intel` / `macos-26-intel`, 4 vCPU/14 GB, verified in github/docs `supported-github-runners.md`). In a private repo the same matrix drains free minutes at 10x for macOS and 2x for Windows, and macOS goes from free to the dominant line item. Second: I verified on this box that 8 of 10 interesting targets cross-compile from Linux with tooling already present — including macOS universal2 fat Mach-O with a valid ad-hoc LC_CODE_SIGNATURE (needed for arm64 to exec at all) — and that cross-built Windows and aarch64 binaries actually RUN here under `wine` and `qemu-aarch64-static`. So you get a fast local inner loop and CI is the outer loop, not the only loop. The one hard cliff: the moment a dependency links a macOS framework (I proved this with `arboard`, which pulls AppKit/libobjc), cargo-zigbuild dies with "unable to find dynamic system library 'objc'". That makes clipboard-crate choice an architecture decision, not a detail — use OSC 52 escape sequences and macOS stays cross-compilable. On distribution: for a CLI/TUI editor you do NOT need the $99 Apple Developer account or a Windows code-signing certificate to ship credibly, because Homebrew *formulae* (unlike casks, which as of Sept 1 2026 are being purged if they fail Gatekeeper) require no notarization and ad-hoc sign at install time, and curl/wget never set `com.apple.quarantine` so a curl-pipe-sh installer bypasses Gatekeeper's first-run check entirely. Windows is the weaker story: an unsigned .exe extracted from a browser-downloaded ZIP carries Mark-of-the-Web and gets the full "Windows protected your PC" SmartScreen block, which Scoop/WinGet avoid because they don't set MOTW. cargo-dist 0.32.0 is alive (commits Sept 4, 2026) but effectively single-maintainer, and I verified its default runner map still targets the DEPRECATED `macos-14` image and builds Linux on `ubuntu-22.04` (glibc 2.35) — so don't take its defaults. PR CI under 5 minutes is comfortable: a realistic 97-crate editor dep set (ropey+crossterm+ratatui+serde+toml+notify) cold-builds in 27s debug / 58s release and clippies in 15s on a 4-vCPU box identical in spec to a public-repo runner.

findings.claim: Free-for-public-repo standard runners in Sept 2026 cover every OS/arch jio needs, INCLUDING Intel macOS. The public-repo table lists: ubuntu-latest/24.04/22.04/26.04 (x64, 4 vCPU/16 GB), ubuntu-24.04-arm/22.04-arm/26.04-arm (arm64, 4 vCPU/16 GB), windows-latest/2025/2022 (x64, 4/16), windows-11-arm + windows-11-vs2026-arm (arm64, 4/16), macos-15-intel + macos-26-intel (Intel, 4 vCPU/14 GB), macos-latest/14/15/26 + xcode-27 (arm64, 3 vCPU M1/7 GB). Private repos get half the vCPUs on Linux/Windows and burn minutes at Linux 1x / Windows 2x / macOS 10x.
findings.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/docs/main/data/reusables/actions/supported-github-runners.md — two tables, "Standard runners for public repositories" (free & unlimited) vs "private and internal"; located via mcp__github__search_code for "macos-15-intel" repo:github/docs
findings.implication: Make github.com/zhangyuxuan1999/jio PUBLIC and keep it public. That single choice turns the entire 8-target release matrix from a metered cost into $0. If jio ever goes private, drop macOS from PR CI immediately — at 10x multiplier it will eat the 2000-minute free tier alone.

findings.claim: `macos-15-intel` and `macos-26-intel` are STANDARD runners (free for public repos), not billed "large" runners — but Intel macOS on Actions dies in August 2027. GitHub: "The new label will run on macOS 15 and will be available from now until August 2027... This will be the last available x86_64 image from Actions, and after that date the x86_64 architecture will not be supported on GitHub Actions." Separately `macos-*-large` / `-xlarge` ARE billed even on public repos.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/actions/runner-images/issues/13045 (quoted); free-tier status confirmed by the public-repo table in github/docs supported-github-runners.md which lists macos-15-intel/macos-26-intel at 4 vCPU/14 GB
findings.implication: Ship x86_64-apple-darwin natively on `macos-15-intel` today at zero cost. But put a note in the repo: by mid-2027 you must either drop Intel macOS, or produce it by cross-compiling on an arm64 macOS runner (Xcode carries both SDKs, so `cargo build --target x86_64-apple-darwin` on macos-latest works) — which is what my release.yml sketch already does. Do NOT design a pipeline that depends on an Intel macOS runner existing.

findings.claim: macos-14 (both `macos-14` arm64 and `macos-14-large`) is DEPRECATED: "will begin deprecation on July 6th and will be fully unsupported by November 2nd" (2026). macos-latest now resolves to macOS 26 arm64; windows-latest = Windows Server 2025 with VS2026.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/actions/runner-images/issues/13518 (title, open, updated 2026-08-20); label table at https://github.com/actions/runner-images and raw README
findings.implication: Any workflow (yours or a generated one) that pins macos-14 breaks by Nov 2 2026. This is the specific reason not to accept cargo-dist's defaults — see next finding.

findings.claim: cargo-dist 0.32.0's DEFAULT runner map is already stale. I installed it and ran `dist plan` on a real crate: aarch64-apple-darwin -> macos-14 (deprecated!), x86_64-apple-darwin -> macos-15-intel, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -> windows-2022, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -> ubuntu-22.04, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu -> ubuntu-22.04-arm. Its supported `targets` list has no aarch64-pc-windows-msvc at all, and its docs mention no cross-compilation, no macOS notarization.
findings.evidence: Local: `cargo install cargo-dist --locked --version 0.32.0`; `dist init --yes --hosting=github`; `dist plan --output-format=json` -> ci.github.artifacts_matrix.include. Config docs: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/main/book/src/reference/config.md
findings.implication: If you adopt cargo-dist you MUST override `github-custom-runners` for the darwin targets on day one, and you still can't ship Windows-on-ARM. Building x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu on ubuntu-22.04 also hard-links glibc 2.35, which excludes Debian 11, Ubuntu 20.04, RHEL 8/9. That's a worse Linux artifact than you get for free with zigbuild.

findings.claim: cargo-dist is NOT archived and IS actively maintained — commits on 2026-09-04 (three days ago), latest release v0.32.0 (2026-05-21) — but it is effectively a one-person project: essentially every recent merge is authored/co-authored by mistydemeo, and the axo hosted docs domains (opensource.axo.dev, blog.axo.dev) no longer resolve in DNS while the GitHub Pages book does.
findings.evidence: crates.io via `cargo info cargo-dist` -> 0.32.0; https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/commits/main (Sep 4 2026 commits incl. "Add Azure signing support"); https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/releases; local `getent hosts opensource.axo.dev` -> NO DNS, `axo.dev` -> 104.154.78.154
findings.implication: Don't reject cargo-dist as dead — that rumor is wrong. But bus factor 1 plus a company whose doc subdomains have gone dark is a real risk for something that owns your entire release path. My call: hand-roll release.yml first (~170 lines, all of which you understand), and adopt cargo-dist later only if you specifically want its shell/powershell/homebrew/msi installer generation.

findings.claim: VERIFIED cross-compile matrix from this exact Linux container, using a realistic 97-crate editor dep set (ropey 1 + crossterm 0.29 + ratatui 0.29 + serde + toml + notify 8 + anyhow): x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu OK (native); x86_64-unknown-linux-musl OK (plain cargo, produces static-pie); aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu OK via cargo-zigbuild in 36s (plain cargo FAILS: rust-lld "incompatible with elf64-x86-64", no linker); aarch64-unknown-linux-musl OK via zigbuild in 68s (statically linked); x86_64-apple-darwin 36s and aarch64-apple-darwin 34s via zigbuild; universal2-apple-darwin OK (real fat Mach-O, 928K); x86_64-pc-windows-gnu OK with plain cargo in 20s (mingw preinstalled).
findings.evidence: Local builds in /tmp/.../scratchpad/edbench; `file` output: "Mach-O universal binary with 2 architectures: [x86_64...] [arm64...]", "ELF 64-bit LSB executable, ARM aarch64, statically linked, stripped", "PE32+ executable (console) x86-64"
findings.implication: You can build 8 of 10 shippable artifacts locally in ~3 minutes total, without touching CI. That collapses the feedback loop for build/packaging bugs from a 10-minute CI round trip to seconds. Use this for iterating on the release script; use CI for the authoritative artifacts.

findings.claim: You can actually RUN the cross-built artifacts on this box: `wine` and `qemu-aarch64-static` (QEMU 8.2.2) are installed. The x86_64-pc-windows-gnu build of the 97-crate binary ran under wine and printed correct output; the aarch64-unknown-linux-musl build ran under qemu-aarch64-static and printed correct output.
findings.evidence: Local: `WINEDEBUG=-all wine target/x86_64-pc-windows-gnu/release/edbench.exe` -> "5"; `qemu-aarch64-static target/aarch64-unknown-linux-musl/release/edbench` -> "5"
findings.implication: The "no Windows machine" problem is partially solvable locally. wine will catch path-separator bugs, CRLF bugs, and missing-symbol link errors before CI. It will NOT faithfully emulate the Windows console/VT input layer, so terminal-input behavior still needs a real windows-latest runner. Add a `wine` smoke step to a local pre-push script, not to CI (CI has real Windows for free).

findings.claim: cargo-zigbuild pins glibc precisely and it works. `cargo zigbuild --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.28` produced a binary whose maximum required symbol version is GLIBC_2.28 (objdump -T shows 2.3.4/2.14/2.16/2.18/2.28 and nothing higher). zig 0.16.0 is already available on this box via the Python `ziglang` package (`/usr/local/lib/python3.11/dist-packages/ziglang/zig`), and cargo-zigbuild 0.23.4 is already installed.
findings.evidence: Local: `objdump -T target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/xtest | grep -oE 'GLIBC_[0-9.]+' | sort -uV | tail -5`; `python3 -m ziglang version` -> 0.16.0
findings.implication: This is the answer to the glibc problem, and it beats the alternatives. ubuntu-22.04 (the oldest free runner) is glibc 2.35 — too new; it excludes Debian 11 (2.31), Ubuntu 20.04 (2.31), RHEL 8 (2.28), Amazon Linux 2. Pinning 2.28 covers essentially everything still in service. `pip install ziglang` in CI is one line and needs no container, no `cross`, no Docker-in-Actions.

findings.claim: HARD LIMIT, and it's an architecture decision: cross-compiling macOS from Linux works ONLY while nothing links a macOS framework. Adding `arboard` (clipboard) makes `cargo zigbuild --target aarch64-apple-darwin` fail with: `error: unable to find dynamic system library 'objc' using strategy 'paths_first'` after the link line requests `-framework AppKit -framework Foundation -framework CoreGraphics -lobjc`.
findings.evidence: Local: fresh crate + `cargo add arboard` + `cargo zigbuild --release --target aarch64-apple-darwin`; full linker invocation captured in error output
findings.implication: Choose the clipboard strategy NOW, before writing code. OSC 52 terminal escape sequences (pure Rust, zero system deps, works over SSH — which is a feature for an editor) keep macOS cross-buildable from Linux forever. `arboard`/`copypasta` force every macOS artifact through a macOS runner and kill your local macOS inner loop. Same logic applies to any future crate touching AppKit, Security.framework, or Metal. Legally sourcing the macOS SDK on Linux is not an option: Apple's SDK license restricts use to Apple-branded hardware.

findings.claim: Cross-compiled aarch64-apple-darwin binaries from zig DO carry a valid ad-hoc LC_CODE_SIGNATURE, so they will exec on Apple Silicon. I parsed the Mach-O load commands: arm64 build has LC_CODE_SIGNATURE present:True; x86_64 build has it absent (Intel doesn't require it). Both carry LC_BUILD_VERSION platform=1 minos=13.0 sdk=26.4.
findings.evidence: Local Python Mach-O load-command parser over target/{aarch64,x86_64}-apple-darwin/release/xtest
findings.implication: This kills the most common objection to cross-building macOS from Linux ("arm64 macOS refuses unsigned binaries"). It's handled. But note the minos=13.0 zig picked — that silently drops macOS 11/12 users. If you care, set MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET explicitly and verify the LC_BUILD_VERSION in CI; also re-`codesign -s -` after any `lipo`, because lipo invalidates the signature.

findings.claim: Windows MSVC targets cannot be built on THIS box — but for an environment reason, not a tool reason. `cargo-xwin` 0.23.1 installs fine but dies at `HTTP GET https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/channel failed: CONNECT proxy failed: proxy server responded 403/403`. Plain `cargo build --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` fails with "link.exe was not found".
findings.evidence: Local: `XWIN_ACCEPT_LICENSE=1 cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (full backtrace via xwin::manifest::get_manifest)
findings.implication: Do not build a pipeline around cargo-xwin. Both windows-msvc targets go on `windows-latest` (free), where aarch64-pc-windows-msvc cross-compiles from the x64 runner with just `rustup target add` — no `windows-11-arm` runner needed for building, only for smoke-testing. For local iteration use `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`, which works today and runs under wine.

findings.claim: Homebrew is the single best macOS channel and it costs $0, because formulae are exempt from the notarization crackdown. Homebrew maintainers: "For formulae (which are usually CLI executables), notarisation does not apply" and "The only requirement for regular executables is the code signing on Apple Silicon, and that can be done ad-hoc (which we do)." Meanwhile CASKS are being purged: `--no-quarantine`/`--quarantine` were deprecated in Homebrew 5.0 (Nov 2025) and "We are ending support for all casks that fail Gatekeeper checks on September 1st, 2026" — i.e. six days ago.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/orgs/Homebrew/discussions/4582 (quoted); https://github.com/Homebrew/brew/issues/20755 (quoted)
findings.implication: Ship jio as a Homebrew FORMULA in your own tap (github.com/zhangyuxuan1999/homebrew-jio). Zero Apple money, zero notarization, `brew install zhangyuxuan1999/jio/jio` works on both architectures. Never package a CLI editor as a cask. homebrew-core is not available to you yet: it requires >=30 forks OR >=30 watchers OR >=75 stars plus use by someone other than the author (https://docs.brew.sh/Acceptable-Formulae), and jio has none.

findings.claim: A curl-pipe-sh installer genuinely bypasses Gatekeeper, and this is documented behavior, not a hack. Quarantine is applied only by apps with LSFileQuarantineEnabled=true in Info.plist (Safari, Chrome). "/usr/bin/curl and /usr/bin/wget do not append the quarantine extended attribute to downloaded files", and "Gatekeeper only works when the com.apple.quarantine is set". Conversely, a .tar.gz downloaded in a browser IS quarantined and — since macOS 15 Sequoia removed the Control-click bypass — the user must go to System Settings > Privacy & Security > "Open Anyway" per binary.
findings.evidence: https://eclecticlight.co/2020/10/29/quarantine-and-the-quarantine-flag/ ; https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/information-property-list/lsfilequarantineenabled ; https://appleinsider.com/articles/24/08/06/apple-removes-control-click-option-for-skipping-gatekeeper-in-macos-sequoia
findings.implication: Your README's primary macOS install line must be `curl -fsSL https://.../install.sh | sh`, NOT "download the .tar.gz from Releases". Same script serves Linux. The GitHub Releases tarball is the fallback for people who read scripts before running them — for them, document `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./jio` in one line right next to the download link. This is worth ~$99/yr and a notarization pipeline you cannot debug without a Mac.

findings.claim: Windows is the weaker story and there is no free equivalent of the Gatekeeper workaround. Windows 11 File Explorer PRESERVES Mark-of-the-Web through ZIP extraction, so an unsigned jio.exe pulled out of a browser-downloaded zip triggers full SmartScreen. A cert doesn't fully fix it either: "Every new app — regardless of how well it's signed — will trigger a SmartScreen warning on first download until it accumulates enough download history"; unsigned apps get the more severe block. Azure Trusted Signing (renamed Azure Artifact Signing) is ~$9.99/mo Basic (5,000 signatures), issues ~72-hour certs from a Microsoft-trusted CA, and is limited to verified US/Canada/EU/UK businesses and self-employed individuals; some users report the role assignment wanting an Entra ID P2 license.
findings.evidence: MOTW/zip: https://windows.dfirhandbook.com/windows-artifacts/file-download/zone.identifier and 7-Zip MOTW-bypass reporting; signing: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/artifact-signing ; https://github.com/microsoft/winget-cli/discussions/4327 ; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5595324/
findings.implication: Do NOT buy a certificate for v0.1. A German student can plausibly qualify for Azure Artifact Signing as an EU self-employed individual at ~120 EUR/yr, which is far cheaper than a traditional EV cert — revisit it only when Windows download volume justifies it. Until then, route Windows users through Scoop (`scoop install jio`), which fetches over plain HTTP and does not set MOTW, so no SmartScreen prompt appears at all.

findings.claim: PR CI under 5 minutes is comfortable, with real numbers. On this 4-vCPU/15 GB box — the same shape as a public-repo standard runner — the 97-crate editor dep set cold-builds in 27s (debug), 58s (release), clippy --all-targets in 15s, no-op rebuild 0s. The target/ dir is 521 MB, which matters because GitHub caps caches at 10 GB per repository with 7-day eviction on unaccessed entries.
findings.evidence: Local timings in /tmp/.../scratchpad/edbench; cache limit quoted from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/docs/main/content/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching.md: "the limit is 10 GB per repository"
findings.implication: Use Swatinem/rust-cache@v2 (latest v2.9.2, major tag still v2) and skip sccache entirely — sccache's win is remote/shared CAS across a team, which you don't have. Critically, set `save-if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` on PR jobs: without it, every PR writes a ~300-500 MB cache entry, and 3 OSes x N open PRs will blow past 10 GB and cause cache thrashing that makes CI slower than no cache at all.

findings.claim: The Free plan allows 20 total concurrent jobs but only 5 concurrent macOS jobs; a matrix can generate at most 256 jobs; a job may run 6 hours.
findings.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/docs/main/content/actions/reference/limits.md — concurrency table (Free 20 / Pro 40 / Team 60 / Enterprise 500; macOS column 5)
findings.implication: My 8-entry release matrix has at most 2 macOS jobs, so it never queues. But note that PR CI (3 jobs incl. 1 macOS) plus a release run (8 jobs incl. 2 macOS) plus a second PR will start serializing macOS. Add `concurrency: cancel-in-progress: true` on the CI workflow — it is the single highest-leverage line for keeping PR feedback fast.

findings.claim: Rust release builds are already bit-reproducible across build directories, WITHOUT any flags — I built the same crate twice in two different absolute paths and got identical SHA-256 (81e90feb...). Separately, cargo's `trim-paths` profile option is STILL unstable in Cargo 1.94.1: "The package requires the Cargo feature called `trim-paths`, but that feature is not stabilized in this version of Cargo (1.94.1)".
findings.evidence: Local: two clean `cargo build --release` runs in /scratchpad/edbench and /scratchpad/edbench2, sha256sum identical; trim-paths error text from cargo directly
findings.implication: You get reproducibility essentially for free in the release profile (no debuginfo => no embedded paths). Do NOT put `trim-paths = "all"` in Cargo.toml — it will hard-fail the build on stable, and plenty of blog posts wrongly claim it's stable. If you want path scrubbing on stable use RUSTFLAGS="--remap-path-prefix=$PWD=/jio". Publish SHA-256 sums plus GitHub artifact attestations and you have a credible supply-chain story with zero extra cost.

findings.claim: The runner's Rust is NEWER than your dev box: ubuntu-24.04 image (version 20260831.293.1) ships Rust/Cargo 1.98.0, while this container has 1.94.1 (2026-03-25).
findings.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/actions/runner-images/main/images/ubuntu/Ubuntu2404-Readme.md (image version 20260831.293.1, Rust 1.98.0); local `rustc --version` -> 1.94.1
findings.implication: Without pinning, CI compiles with a different rustc than you ever run locally — new clippy lints will fail PRs you can't reproduce, and `RUSTFLAGS: -D warnings` turns that into a red X on every push. Commit a `rust-toolchain.toml` with an explicit `channel` and let dtolnay/rust-toolchain honor it, or accept the drift deliberately and run a separate nightly/beta job that is allowed to fail.

findings.claim: Current action versions verified against their release pages (2026-09-07): actions/checkout v7.0.1 (v6 and v5 lines still maintained), actions/upload-artifact v7.0.1, actions/download-artifact v8.0.1, Swatinem/rust-cache v2.9.2 (major tag v2), softprops/action-gh-release v3.0.3, taiki-e/upload-rust-binary-action v1.30.2, actions/attest-build-provenance v4.2.2 — the latter now documented as "simply a wrapper on top of actions/attest... new implementations should use actions/attest instead". cargo-dist 0.32.0's own generated workflow pins checkout@v6, upload-artifact@v7, download-artifact@v8.
findings.evidence: Release pages for each repo on github.com; cargo-dist pins read directly from the .github/workflows/release.yml it generated locally
findings.implication: Anything you remember about `actions/checkout@v4` is two to three majors stale. Pin these by tag now and let Dependabot (`.github/dependabot.yml` with `package-ecosystem: github-actions`, weekly) carry them forward; for a security-sensitive release workflow, pin by commit SHA instead.

findings.claim: Supply-chain tooling is all current and cheap to wire in: cargo-deny 0.20.2, cargo-audit 0.22.2, cargo-auditable 0.7.5, cargo-about 0.9.2, cargo-binstall 1.23.0, release-plz 0.3.162, cargo-release 1.1.5, cross 0.2.5, sccache 0.17.0 — all confirmed live on crates.io today. release-plz maintains a rolling release PR from conventional commits (changelog via git-cliff, breaking-change detection via cargo-semver-checks), tags, publishes to crates.io and cuts the GitHub release — but it does NOT build or upload binaries.
findings.evidence: Local `cargo info <crate>` against the live crates.io index for each; https://github.com/release-plz/release-plz
findings.implication: Correct split of responsibilities: release-plz owns version+changelog+tag (triggered on push to main), your release.yml owns binaries (triggered on the `v*` tag release-plz creates). Don't use cargo-release as well — it overlaps release-plz and you'd be maintaining two version bumpers. Run cargo-deny in PR CI (EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v2) rather than cargo-audit; deny is a superset (advisories + licenses + bans + sources) and one job.

findings.claim: WinGet's community repo does not require code signing, but "as the feature is still experimental, the community repository does not accept portable applications" — and a bare Rust CLI zip is exactly a 'portable' package. Scoop by contrast is designed for it: a bucket is a git repo of JSON manifests with `checkver`/`autoupdate` that the Excavator bot refreshes from GitHub Releases automatically.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/microsoft/winget-cli/discussions/4327 ; winget-create portable discussions; https://github.com/ScoopInstaller/Scoop/wiki/App-Manifest-Autoupdate
findings.implication: Scoop before WinGet, decisively. Your own Scoop bucket is one JSON file and a `scoop bucket add` line in the README — an afternoon. WinGet means a PR into microsoft/winget-pkgs, a moderation queue, possible portable-package rejection, and re-submission on every release. Chocolatey is worse still (heavier moderation, nuspec/PowerShell packaging) for near-zero incremental audience over Scoop+WinGet.

findings.claim: windows-11-arm needed the Rust toolchain added to the image after the fact, and aarch64-pc-windows-msvc still has known toolchain gaps — coverage instrumentation produces malformed profiles on that target, which currently blocks coverage collection on windows-11-arm runners.
findings.evidence: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/150123 ; https://github.com/actions/partner-runner-images/issues/77 (referenced; the repo itself now 404s on direct fetch, suggesting the image moved to GitHub-managed pipelines)
findings.implication: Treat aarch64-pc-windows-msvc as a build-and-smoke-test target, not a first-class tested platform. Build it on windows-latest (x64 cross), run only `jio --version` on windows-11-arm, and don't try to run llvm-cov there. Don't gate releases on it in v0.1.

surveys.recommendation:
MY CALL: this is feasible, and the pipeline below is what I'd ship. Six decisions, in priority order.

**1. Make the repo public — today, before anything else.** Every runner you need (Linux x64/arm64, Windows x64/arm64, macOS arm64 AND Intel) is free and unlimited on a public repo. Private turns the same matrix into metered spend with a 10x macOS multiplier. This is the highest-leverage single decision in the whole document.

**2. Ban macOS-framework-linking crates from the dependency graph.** Use OSC 52 for clipboard, not `arboard`. I proved arboard breaks Linux->macOS cross-compilation (`unable to find dynamic system library 'objc'`). Keeping macOS cross-buildable from Linux means you can debug packaging locally in 35 seconds instead of a 10-minute CI round trip, and it's an SSH-friendly clipboard anyway. Write this into CONTRIBUTING.md as a hard rule.

**3. Ship these 8 targets, with this build strategy** (cross-compile where it's strictly better, native where it isn't):

| target | where | how | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu | ubuntu-latest | `cargo zigbuild --target ...gnu.2.28` | glibc 2.28 floor beats ubuntu-22.04's 2.35 |
| aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu | ubuntu-latest | `cargo zigbuild --target ...gnu.2.28` | same, no arm runner needed |
| x86_64-unknown-linux-musl | ubuntu-latest | plain cargo | fully static, works everywhere |
| aarch64-unknown-linux-musl | ubuntu-24.04-arm | plain cargo | free arm runner, native |
| aarch64-apple-darwin | macos-latest | plain cargo | native, correct SDK |
| x86_64-apple-darwin | macos-latest | plain cargo (cross) | Xcode has both SDKs; survives Intel-runner EOL in Aug 2027 |
| x86_64-pc-windows-msvc | windows-latest | plain cargo | MSVC ABI is what Windows users expect |
| aarch64-pc-windows-msvc | windows-latest | plain cargo (cross) | no arm runner needed to build |

Plus a `universal2` lipo job on macos-latest, re-`codesign -s -` after lipo (lipo invalidates the ad-hoc signature).

**4. Do NOT buy an Apple Developer account or a Windows cert for v0.1.** Ship these three channels first, in this order:
- **(a) `curl | sh` installer.** Serves Linux + macOS from one script. curl never sets `com.apple.quarantine`, so Gatekeeper is bypassed by construction. Highest reach for lowest effort.
- **(b) Homebrew tap** (`zhangyuxuan1999/homebrew-jio`), as a FORMULA not a cask. Formulae are exempt from notarization and Homebrew ad-hoc signs at install. homebrew-core is closed to you until >=75 stars / >=30 forks / >=30 watchers.
- **(c) Scoop bucket** (`zhangyuxuan1999/scoop-jio`). One JSON manifest with `checkver`+`autoupdate`; Scoop's download path sets no Mark-of-the-Web, so no SmartScreen prompt. This is the *only* way to give Windows users a clean install without a certificate.

Everything else — WinGet, Chocolatey, AUR, Nix, .deb/.rpm, Snap, Flatpak — is later, community-driven, or both. `cargo install jio` comes free with publishing to crates.io (do it, it costs nothing and gives Rust users a path), but it's slow and needs a toolchain, so it's not a real distribution channel.

**5. Version/changelog: release-plz on main -> tag -> your release.yml on the tag.** release-plz 0.3.162 maintains a rolling release PR from conventional commits, generates the changelog with git-cliff, detects breaking changes with cargo-semver-checks, tags, and publishes to crates.io — but it does not build binaries, which is exactly the split you want. Skip cargo-release (overlaps). Adopt conventional commits from commit #1; retrofitting them is miserable.

**6. cargo-dist: not yet.** It's alive (commits three days ago) but effectively single-maintainer, its defaults pin the deprecated `macos-14`, it can't target aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, and it links glibc 2.35. Hand-roll first. Revisit only when you specifically want its shell/powershell/homebrew/MSI installer *generation*, and if you do, override `github-custom-runners` on day one.
