## CI workflow (target: <5 min on PRs). Validated YAML at `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/yaml/ci.yml`

```yaml
name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  CARGO_INCREMENTAL: 0
  RUSTFLAGS: "-D warnings"
  RUST_BACKTRACE: 1
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          key: lint
      - run: cargo fmt --all --check
      - run: cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features --locked
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { os: ubuntu-latest,  name: linux-x64 }
          - { os: macos-latest,   name: macos-arm64 }
          - { os: windows-latest, name: windows-x64 }
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          key: ${{ matrix.name }}
          save-if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}   # <- keeps you under the 10 GB cache cap
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@nextest
      - run: cargo nextest run --locked --all-features --no-fail-fast
      - run: cargo test --locked --doc
  msrv:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.85.0
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with: { key: msrv }
      - run: cargo check --locked --all-features
  deny:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v2
        with:
          command: check bans licenses sources advisories
```

Measured basis for the <5 min claim: on a 4-vCPU box identical in spec to a public-repo runner, a 97-crate editor dep set cold-builds in 27s debug and clippies in 15s. With a warm rust-cache the test job is dominated by checkout + toolchain + cache restore, ~90-150s. macos-latest is the slow leg (3 vCPU / 7 GB) — budget ~2x Linux there.

## Release workflow. Validated YAML at `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/yaml/release.yml`

```yaml
name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
  id-token: write
  attestations: write
env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO: "thin"
  CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP: "symbols"
jobs:
  build:
    name: ${{ matrix.target }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 45
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu,   os: ubuntu-latest,    mode: zigbuild, glibc: "2.28" }
          - { target: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu,  os: ubuntu-latest,    mode: zigbuild, glibc: "2.28" }
          - { target: x86_64-unknown-linux-musl,  os: ubuntu-latest,    mode: cargo }
          - { target: aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, os: ubuntu-24.04-arm, mode: cargo }
          - { target: aarch64-apple-darwin,       os: macos-latest,     mode: cargo }
          - { target: x86_64-apple-darwin,        os: macos-latest,     mode: cargo }
          - { target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc,     os: windows-latest,   mode: cargo }
          - { target: aarch64-pc-windows-msvc,    os: windows-latest,   mode: cargo }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with: { key: rel-${{ matrix.target }} }
      - name: Install zig + cargo-zigbuild
        if: matrix.mode == 'zigbuild'
        run: |
          pip install ziglang==0.16.0
          cargo install cargo-zigbuild --locked --version 0.23.4
      - name: Build (zigbuild, glibc-pinned)
        if: matrix.mode == 'zigbuild'
        run: cargo zigbuild --release --locked --target ${{ matrix.target }}.${{ matrix.glibc }}
      - name: Build (native)
        if: matrix.mode == 'cargo'
        run: cargo build --release --locked --target ${{ matrix.target }}
      - name: Package (unix)
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        shell: bash
        run: |
          V="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"; D="jio-${V}-${{ matrix.target }}"
          mkdir -p "dist/$D"
          cp "target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/jio" "dist/$D/"
          cp README.md LICENSE* "dist/$D/" 2>/dev/null || true
          tar -C dist -czf "dist/$D.tar.gz" "$D"
          (cd dist && shasum -a 256 "$D.tar.gz" > "$D.tar.gz.sha256")
      - name: Package (windows)
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $V = "${env:GITHUB_REF_NAME}".TrimStart("v"); $D = "jio-$V-${{ matrix.target }}"
          New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "dist/$D" | Out-Null
          Copy-Item "target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/jio.exe" "dist/$D/"
          Compress-Archive -Path "dist/$D" -DestinationPath "dist/$D.zip"
          (Get-FileHash "dist/$D.zip" -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLower() | Out-File "dist/$D.zip.sha256"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with: { name: artifacts-${{ matrix.target }}, path: "dist/*.tar.gz*", if-no-files-found: ignore }
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with: { name: artifacts-win-${{ matrix.target }}, path: "dist/*.zip*", if-no-files-found: ignore }

  # THE MOST IMPORTANT JOB IN THE FILE: run every artifact on the OS it targets.
  # This is your only substitute for owning a Mac and a Windows box.
  smoke:
    needs: build
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { os: macos-latest,     target: aarch64-apple-darwin }
          - { os: macos-15-intel,   target: x86_64-apple-darwin }
          - { os: windows-latest,   target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc }
          - { os: windows-11-arm,   target: aarch64-pc-windows-msvc }
          - { os: ubuntu-24.04-arm, target: aarch64-unknown-linux-musl }
          - { os: ubuntu-22.04,     target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu }
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with: { pattern: "artifacts-*${{ matrix.target }}", merge-multiple: true, path: dl }
      - name: Unpack and run --version
        shell: bash
        run: |
          cd dl
          if ls *.tar.gz >/dev/null 2>&1; then tar xzf *.tar.gz; ./jio-*/jio --version; fi
          if ls *.zip  >/dev/null 2>&1; then unzip -q *.zip;  ./jio-*/jio.exe --version; fi

  universal:
    needs: build
    runs-on: macos-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with: { pattern: "artifacts-*apple-darwin", merge-multiple: true, path: dl }
      - name: lipo into universal2
        run: |
          cd dl && for f in *.tar.gz; do tar xzf "$f"; done
          V="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          mkdir -p "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin"
          lipo -create -output "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin/jio" \
            jio-*-x86_64-apple-darwin/jio jio-*-aarch64-apple-darwin/jio
          codesign -s - -f "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin/jio"   # lipo invalidates the ad-hoc sig
          tar -czf "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz" "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin"
          shasum -a 256 "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz" > "jio-${V}-universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz.sha256"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with: { name: artifacts-universal, path: "dl/*universal*.tar.gz*" }

  publish:
    needs: [build, smoke, universal]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with: { pattern: "artifacts-*", merge-multiple: true, path: dist }
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v4      # or actions/attest directly
        with: { subject-path: "dist/*.tar.gz,dist/*.zip" }
      - uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v3
        with:
          files: |
            dist/*.tar.gz
            dist/*.zip
            dist/*.sha256
          generate_release_notes: true
          fail_on_unmatched_files: true
```

The `smoke` job is the part most people skip and it is the part your constraint makes non-negotiable: it downloads each built artifact and executes it on the actual OS/arch it claims to support, on free runners, before the release is published. Without it, "cross-compiled from Linux" means "shipped untested."

## Sequencing for a solo dev
Week 1: public repo + `ci.yml` + `rust-toolchain.toml` + `deny.toml` + `.github/dependabot.yml` (cargo + github-actions, weekly). Week 2: `release.yml` including the smoke job, exercised with a `v0.0.1` throwaway tag. Week 3: install.sh + Homebrew tap + Scoop bucket, all three auto-updated from the release job. Later: release-plz, crates.io publish, WinGet, AUR/Nix (let contributors bring those).

**What would change my mind:** if jio turns out to need a GUI (a real `.app`), everything above inverts — you'd be in cask territory, notarization becomes mandatory, the $99 Apple account becomes unavoidable, and macOS cross-compilation from Linux is dead on arrival. Decide TUI-vs-GUI before writing the release pipeline. Likewise, if the repo must be private, delete macOS from PR CI immediately and keep it only in the release matrix.
risks: THE BIG ONE: cross-compiled artifacts that are never executed. Linux->macOS zigbuild produces a plausible-looking Mach-O even when the result would crash on a real Mac (missing framework symbols only surface at link or dlopen time, and zig's libc stubs are not the real libSystem). Mitigation is non-optional: the `smoke` job must run every artifact on its target OS before publishing. Treat a missing smoke job as a shipping-broken-binaries guarantee.

macOS deployment target drift you cannot see. zig stamped LC_BUILD_VERSION minos=13.0 on my cross-built binary while rustc's own default for aarch64-apple-darwin is 11.0. Neither is visible in any build log. Users on macOS 11/12 get a cryptic launch failure and you have no Mac to reproduce it. Add an explicit MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET and assert the LC_BUILD_VERSION in CI with `otool -l | grep -A3 LC_BUILD_VERSION`.

Terminal behavior is the one thing CI cannot test. A text editor lives in raw-mode TTY input, bracketed paste, VT sequences, resize events, and the Windows console API. GitHub runners have no interactive TTY. wine will not faithfully emulate Windows console input. You will ship keyboard-handling bugs on macOS Terminal.app, iTerm2, Windows Terminal and conhost that no green check catches. Budget for early external testers on each platform and design the input layer to be unit-testable from recorded byte streams.

Cache thrash silently degrading CI. target/ is 521 MB for a modest dep set. Three OSes plus a release matrix, all saving caches on every PR, will exceed the 10 GB per-repo cap and trigger eviction churn that makes cached CI slower than uncached. The `save-if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` guard is the fix and it is easy to forget when adding matrix entries.

Runner image labels moving under you. macos-latest already moved to macOS 26; windows-latest moved to VS2026 in June 2026; macos-14 is fully unsupported by Nov 2, 2026; Intel macOS runners disappear entirely in Aug 2027. A release workflow that is only exercised at tag time can be broken for months before you notice. Run the release workflow on a schedule (weekly `workflow_dispatch` or cron) against main so image migrations surface as a red build, not as a failed release.

Toolchain skew between this container (rustc 1.94.1) and the runners (1.98.0 on ubuntu-24.04). Without a committed rust-toolchain.toml, `RUSTFLAGS: -D warnings` plus newer clippy means PRs fail with lints you cannot reproduce or fix locally, and you cannot install the newer toolchain reliably if the container's rustup is pinned.

aarch64-pc-windows-msvc is the least-trodden path in the matrix: coverage instrumentation is known broken there (rust-lang/rust#150123), the windows-11-arm image only recently got a Rust toolchain, and you have zero users to report problems. Cross-building it from windows-latest is easy; validating it is not. Do not block a release on it.

Signing/notarization is a one-way door. If you later buy the $99 Apple account and start signing with a Developer ID, you must keep signing forever — users who installed a signed build and then get an unsigned update hit Gatekeeper hard. Same for Windows: once SmartScreen reputation is attached to a certificate, switching or letting it lapse resets reputation to zero. Deciding 'no signing for now' is cheap; deciding 'signing' is a recurring commitment.

cargo-dist bus factor. If you do adopt it and mistydemeo stops, your release path is a large generated YAML file you did not write, pinned to a specific dist version, with defaults that already reference a deprecated runner image. Hand-rolled YAML is more lines but zero dependency risk.

GitHub Actions is a single point of failure for a project with no other machines. An extended Actions outage, a policy change to public-repo free minutes, or an account issue means you cannot build ANY artifact for ANY platform. Keep the release process expressible as plain shell commands (a `xtask` or Makefile the workflow merely calls) so it can be re-hosted, and keep the Linux-side cross-build path working as a partial escape hatch.
open_questions: TUI or GUI? This flips the entire macOS distribution answer. A TUI/CLI ships as a Homebrew formula with no notarization and no Apple account; a GUI .app is a cask, and as of Sept 1 2026 Homebrew removes casks that fail Gatekeeper — meaning $99/yr plus a notarization pipeline you cannot debug without a Mac. Answer this before writing release.yml.

Clipboard strategy: OSC 52 (keeps Linux->macOS cross-compilation alive, works over SSH) vs arboard/copypasta (proven to break zigbuild with a libobjc link error, forces every macOS artifact through a macOS runner)? Same question for any future syntax-highlighting choice — tree-sitter pulls C grammars, which adds a C cross-toolchain dimension to every target I benchmarked with pure Rust.
Is the repo going public, and when? Nearly every cost claim here is conditional on it. If it stays private for a while, I would cut the release matrix to 4 targets and drop macOS from PR CI entirely.

What is the actual glibc floor you want to support? I picked 2.28 (RHEL 8 / Debian 10). If you only care about currently-supported distros, 2.31 or even 2.35 is fine and you can drop cargo-zigbuild from the pipeline entirely, simplifying two matrix rows to plain cargo.

Does jio need any dynamic system library at all on Linux (e.g. wayland/X11 for clipboard, or openssl)? If yes, the fully-static musl artifacts become misleading and cargo-zigbuild's glibc pinning gets much more delicate. I benchmarked a pure-Rust dep set; a single -sys crate changes the picture.

Is a German student self-employed status enough to qualify for Azure Artifact Signing (~$9.99/mo, verified US/CA/EU/UK businesses and self-employed individuals)? I could not confirm the individual-verification requirements for a student without a registered business, and one user report suggests role assignment may require an Entra ID P2 license. Worth checking before assuming cheap Windows signing is available.

Do you want to publish to crates.io from day one? It's free and gives `cargo install jio`, but it burns the name permanently and forces you into semver discipline (release-plz + cargo-semver-checks) earlier than a v0.x editor may want.

I could not verify whether GitHub Actions has any newer policy on free-tier abuse for public repos in 2026 (docs.github.com is blocked from this container; I read the docs source from github/docs instead). If GitHub tightens public-repo minutes, the whole cost model needs revisiting.

surveys.label: headless-testing
surveys.summary: I built a working 388-line proof-of-concept editor + full test harness on this box and ran every tier of the proposed pyramid for real. Verified working today on Linux: ratatui 0.30.2 `TestBackend` + insta 1.48.0 snapshots; portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2 driving the REAL binary through a PTY (typing, Ctrl-S save-to-disk, Ctrl-Q exit, resize down to 1x1) in 60 ms; proptest 1.11.0 differential test (ropey 1.6.1 vs naive `Vec<char>`, 500 cases, 0.73 s); OSC 52 clipboard captured and base64-decoded through `vt100::Callbacks`. Whole 8-test suite incl. 3 PTY E2E tests: 2.5 s wall. Two findings change the plan materially. First, `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target aarch64-apple-darwin` both work on this headless Linux box (16 s / 8 s) and I proved they catch `#[cfg(windows)]` type errors that native check misses entirely — this is the cheapest high-value technique available and it needs zero CI. Second, mingw-w64 + Wine 9.0 are installed here, I cross-built a real `winsmoke.exe` in 10.7 s and drove it through a Linux PTY: it ran, took keystrokes, saved the file, exited cleanly — and when I removed the `KeyEventKind::Press` filter it produced `"hhii"` instead of `"hi"`, faithfully reproducing the #1 Windows-only text-editor bug locally. Wine's *rendering* is garbage (raw SGR escapes leak into the grid), so Wine is a logic/input canary, not a render oracle. On the key question: portable-pty on Windows hardcodes `PSUEDOCONSOLE_INHERIT_CURSOR`, which makes ConPTY emit `ESC[6n` and block (3 s timeout) unless your harness replies — winpty-rs documents exactly this hang, and vt100 has no DSR callback so you must sniff the raw byte stream. ConPTY also rewrites and reorders SGR sequences, so screen *snapshots* are not portable across OSes. Verdict: PTY E2E is a Linux-primary tier, macOS-secondary, Windows-smoke-only; the real Windows/macOS coverage comes from a pure `Key -> Cmd -> Effect` core plus a `#[cfg]`-free platform tier that runs as ordinary `cargo test` on all three runners.

findings.claim: Cross-target `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target aarch64-apple-darwin` work on this headless Linux box with no extra setup — rust-std for both is already installed — and they catch cfg-gated compile errors that a native check cannot see.
findings.evidence: `rustup component list --installed` shows rust-std-{aarch64,x86_64}-apple-darwin, rust-std-{aarch64,x86_64}-pc-windows-msvc, rust-std-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu. Timings: win-msvc check 15.94 s, mac-arm64 check 8.18 s (cold), both `Finished dev profile`. Proof of value: I added `#[cfg(windows)] pub fn win_only() -> u32 { let x: String = 5; x.len() as u32 }` — native `cargo check` reported 0 errors; `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` reported `error[E0308]: mismatched types --> src/lib.rs:50:44`.
findings.implication: Put `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target aarch64-apple-darwin` in a pre-commit hook / Makefile target. It turns the ~10-minute CI round-trip for 'does it even compile on Windows' into 16 seconds locally. This is the single highest-leverage item in the whole strategy and it costs nothing.

findings.claim: Cross-target checking breaks on `--all-targets` if any dev-dependency has a C build script. criterion 0.8.2 pulls `alloca 0.4.0`, which fails with `failed to find tool "lib.exe"` (Windows) and a cc `-arch arm64` failure (macOS). divan 0.1.21 has a pure-Rust tree (clap, regex-lite, rustix, condtype) and does not.
findings.evidence: `cargo tree -i alloca` → `alloca v0.4.0 └── criterion v0.8.2 [dev-dependencies]`. `cargo clippy --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --all-targets` → `error occurred in cc-rs: failed to find tool "lib.exe"`. Plain `cargo check --target <both triples>` (lib+bin, no dev-deps) → EXIT=0 on both. `cargo tree` for divan 0.1.21 shows no cc/C deps.
findings.implication: Cross-check `--lib --bins` only (that IS the shipping code), or move benches into a separate workspace member excluded from the cross-check, or use divan 0.1.21 instead of criterion. Do not let a benchmark dependency cost you the Windows compile canary.

findings.claim: Wine 9.0 + mingw-w64 are installed on this box, a Windows .exe cross-builds in ~11 s, and driving it through a Linux PTY faithfully reproduces the Windows-only key-Release double-input bug.
findings.evidence: `cargo build --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` → `winsmoke.exe` (15.9 MB) in 10.74 s. Driven via pexpect 4.9.0 + pyte 0.8.2 under `wine-9.0`: with the `if k.kind != KeyEventKind::Press { return None }` guard, typing "hi" then Ctrl-S wrote `hi`; with the guard removed and nothing else changed, the same run wrote `hhii`. Wine 9.0's kernel32.dll/kernelbase.dll export CreatePseudoConsole/ClosePseudoConsole/ResizePseudoConsole (verified with `strings`).
findings.implication: Add a `make winsmoke` target: cross-build to x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, run under Wine in a PTY, assert file-on-disk contents and clean exit. It catches the highest-frequency class of Windows-only editor bugs (double-typed characters, key-modifier mismatches) in ~15 s on the dev box, before CI ever runs.

findings.claim: Wine is NOT a rendering oracle. Under Wine the same binary's screen came back with raw SGR sequences leaked as literal text and wrongly wrapped box borders.
findings.evidence: pyte screen rows captured under Wine included `'39m'`, `';48;5;4m[+]1'`, `'[39m'`, `'15;48;5;4m2'`, and the bottom border split across two rows as `'└─────────────────────────'` / `'  ─────────────────┘'`. The identical native Linux binary rendered a clean 12x46 grid.
findings.implication: Never assert on screen content from a Wine run — you will chase Wine bugs, not jio bugs. Wine tests assert only on side effects: process exited 0, file bytes on disk, no panic on stderr. Screen assertions stay on Linux TestBackend + Linux PTY.

findings.claim: portable-pty 0.9.0 hardcodes `PSUEDOCONSOLE_INHERIT_CURSOR | PSEUDOCONSOLE_RESIZE_QUIRK | PSEUDOCONSOLE_WIN32_INPUT_MODE` in `CreatePseudoConsole` with no opt-out. INHERIT_CURSOR makes ConPTY emit `ESC[6n` at startup and block waiting for a cursor-position reply.
findings.evidence: src/win/psuedocon.rs:83-90 passes exactly those three flags; `PSEUDOCONSOLE_PASSTHROUGH_MODE` is defined but `#[allow(dead_code)]` and unused. Microsoft's CreatePseudoConsole doc: with INHERIT_CURSOR 'the calling application should be prepared to respond to the request for the cursor state ... Failure to do so may cause the calling application to hang.' A 3-second timeout was later added (microsoft/terminal#17688). winpty-rs 1.0.6's own docs independently warn 'backends such as ConPTY may hang waiting for the response of such requests'.
findings.implication: A naive portable-pty harness on windows-latest will stall ~3 s per spawned process, or hang outright on older images. Your Windows PTY harness MUST scan the raw byte stream for `\x1b[6n` before feeding vt100 and write back `\x1b[1;1R`. Budget this as harness code you have to write blind and debug only through CI logs.

findings.claim: vt100 0.16.2's `Callbacks` trait has no DSR / cursor-position-report hook, so the ESC[6n auto-reply must be implemented by sniffing raw bytes upstream of the parser.
findings.evidence: vt100-0.16.2/src/callbacks.rs `pub trait Callbacks` exposes only audible_bell, visual_bell, resize, set_window_icon_name, set_window_title, copy_to_clipboard. No dsr/cpr/device_status method.
findings.implication: Structure the reader thread as: read chunk -> scan for `\x1b[6n` -> if found, write `\x1b[1;1R` back to the pty writer -> then `parser.process(chunk)`. Write this on day one even though you can only test the Linux half; it is dead code on Unix and load-bearing on Windows.

findings.claim: ConPTY does not passthrough VT faithfully: it re-serializes SGR lossily (rewrites `[49m`/`[39m` to `[m`), drops DCS entirely, and can deliver OSC out of order. Screen bytes from a Windows PTY are therefore not comparable to a Unix PTY.
findings.evidence: microsoft/terminal#362 (ConPTY translating [49m to [m), #17313 (DCS not passed to 3rd-party terminals), #17314 (OSC received out-of-order), #12166 (ConPTY modifies escape sequences passed to process input).
findings.implication: Do NOT share golden screen snapshots between the Linux and Windows PTY tiers — `insta` will fail on Windows for reasons that are not bugs in jio. Windows PTY assertions must be substring/predicate-based ('screen contains "hello"', 'cursor is on row 1'), never full-grid snapshots. Only the Linux tier gets .snap files.

findings.claim: crossterm 0.29.0 emits BOTH `KeyEventKind::Press` and `KeyEventKind::Release` on Windows unconditionally, while on Unix (without the kitty protocol) it emits only Press. Every un-guarded key handler double-applies on Windows.
findings.evidence: crossterm-0.29.0/src/event/sys/windows/parse.rs:223-227 and 286-290: `let kind = if key_event.key_down { KeyEventKind::Press } else { KeyEventKind::Release };` with no filtering. Confirmed end-to-end under Wine: removing the guard turned "hi" into "hhii" on disk.
findings.implication: Day-one unit test: feed a synthetic `KeyEvent { kind: Release }` into the pure `crossterm::event::KeyEvent -> jio::Key` decoder and assert it yields `None`. That test runs on all 3 OSes as an ordinary `cargo test`, needs no PTY, and catches the bug in microseconds. This is the archetype for the whole strategy: pull the OS-divergent decision into a pure function.

findings.claim: ratatui 0.30.2 `TestBackend`'s `Display` impl — what `insta::assert_snapshot!(term.backend())` serializes — renders SYMBOLS ONLY and drops every style. A syntax-highlighting color regression will not fail such a snapshot.
findings.evidence: ratatui-core-0.1.2/src/backend/test.rs: `impl fmt::Display for TestBackend { write!(f, "{}", buffer_view(&self.buffer)) }` and `fn buffer_view` only calls `c.symbol()`. My snapshot of a status bar with `.bg(Color::Blue).fg(Color::White)` came back as `" [+] | cur 29                 "` with no style info.
findings.implication: Write a ~20-line `styled_view(&Buffer) -> String` that emits a text grid, a parallel style-mask grid (one legend letter per distinct Style), and a legend. I built and ran it; output is human-readable and diffs beautifully. Use it for any test whose subject is color/attribute. Working code is at /home/user/jio/notes/scratch/testing-harness/tests/styled_snap.rs.

findings.claim: TestBackend's snapshot flags double-width overwrites, which makes CJK/emoji width regressions cheap to catch without a PTY.
findings.evidence: My snapshot of `"中文abc\n👨‍👩‍👧‍👦x"` produced `"│中文abc     │" Hidden by multi-width symbols: [(2, " "), (4, " ")]` and `"│👨‍👩‍👧‍👦x         │" Hidden by multi-width symbols: [(2, " ")]`. ratatui-core's own test asserts this format for a ZWJ family emoji.
findings.implication: One snapshot test with a CJK + ZWJ-emoji + combining-mark fixture is your entire Unicode-width regression suite. It is fast, deterministic, and identical on all 3 OSes.

findings.claim: A full PTY E2E harness on Linux works today and is fast: spawn the real binary, type, save, verify file on disk, quit — 60 ms. Resize stress including a 1x1 terminal survives. All verified against portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2.
findings.evidence: tests/pty.rs: `e2e_type_and_save ... ok ... finished in 0.06s`, final screen captured and file content asserted `== "hello"`. tests/resize.rs: resized master to (1,1), (3,5), (60,200), (24,80) with `pair.master.resize(...)` + `parser.screen_mut().set_size(...)`, writing a keystroke after each; `resize_does_not_crash_and_reflows ... ok ... 0.52s`. Whole 8-test suite: 2524 ms wall.
findings.implication: PTY E2E is cheap enough to run on every PR on Linux. The 1x1 resize case is the classic ratatui layout-panic trigger and costs half a second — make it test #10 on day one.

findings.claim: PTY tests are parallel-safe when each lives in its own `tests/*.rs` file, because cargo compiles one binary per file and the child owns the pty, not the test process. No `serial_test` needed.
findings.evidence: My 3 PTY tests (pty.rs, resize.rs, osc52.rs) are separate integration targets and ran concurrently under default `cargo test` with no interference; total wall 2.5 s vs. sum-of-parts 0.80 s.
findings.implication: One file per PTY scenario. Avoid the trap of putting them all in one file with `--test-threads=1`, which is what most projects end up doing and what makes PTY suites slow.

findings.claim: OSC 52 clipboard writes are fully observable inside the PTY harness via `vt100::Callbacks::copy_to_clipboard`, with no GUI, no X server, and no OS clipboard.
findings.evidence: Implemented `\x1b]52;c;<base64>\x07` on Ctrl-Y in the probe binary; harness with `Parser::new_with_callbacks` captured `["amlvLWNsaXAtcGF5bG9hZA=="]` and base64-decoded it to exactly `jio-clip-payload`. Test `osc52_clipboard_is_observable_in_ci ... ok ... 0.22s`.
findings.implication: Make OSC 52 the PRIMARY clipboard path in jio, with the native OS clipboard as an opt-in fallback. That converts clipboard from 'untestable in CI on any OS' into 'a 40-line deterministic test'. It also happens to be the right product decision for an editor used over SSH.

findings.claim: The native OS clipboard is largely untestable on GitHub-hosted runners. Windows runners run in session 0 with no GUI; Linux runners have no DISPLAY (X11-backed crates like arboard will fail).
findings.evidence: GitHub community discussion #176432: Windows runners have 'no access to GUI/Hardware (headless, with limited admin rights)' and 'GitHub runners run in session 0'. On this box `DISPLAY` is empty and Xvfb is installed but not running; ubuntu-24.04 runner image ships xvfb 2:21.1.12 but no display session by default.
findings.implication: Budget the native-clipboard code path as MANUAL-TEST-ONLY and design it so a failure degrades to OSC 52 rather than crashing. On Linux CI you can wrap the whole job in `xvfb-run -a` to get an X11 clipboard test, but that only validates Linux — do not pretend it says anything about macOS or Windows.

findings.claim: insta 1.48.0 refuses to write snapshots when `CI` is set: a brand-new snapshot fails the test and produces neither a `.snap` nor a `.snap.new` file.
findings.evidence: Ran `CI=true cargo test --test styled_snap brand_new` on a fresh `assert_snapshot!("never-seen-before-value")` → `snapshot assertion for 'brand_new_snapshot_in_ci' failed in line 49`, `test result: FAILED`, and `ls tests/snapshots/` showed no brand_new file and no `.snap.new`. Locally, `INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test` writes the file.
findings.implication: Snapshot workflow is safe by default: `INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test` (or `cargo insta review`, cargo-insta 1.48.0) locally, plain `cargo test` in CI. No extra config needed. Do commit `.gitattributes` with `*.snap text eol=lf` — otherwise git's autocrlf on the Windows runner will rewrite snapshot line endings and every snapshot test will fail for a non-reason.

findings.claim: proptest 1.11.0 differential testing (rope vs naive `Vec<char>`) is the single best value-per-line test for a text buffer: 43 lines, 500 randomized command sequences of up to 200 ops, 0.73 s.
findings.evidence: tests/prop.rs asserts `core.text.to_string() == naive.text()`, `core.cursor == naive.cur`, and `core.cursor <= core.text.len_chars()` after replaying the same random `Cmd` stream against ropey 1.6.1 and a `Vec<char>` reference. `rope_matches_naive ... ok ... 0.77s` with `cases: 500`. Full source at /home/user/jio/notes/scratch/testing-harness/tests/prop.rs.
findings.implication: Write this on day one, before the rope is even finished. The naive `Vec<char>` reference is 12 lines and is the specification. Extend the `Cmd` strategy as you add commands; the test grows for free and it is the only thing that will catch rope chunk-boundary bugs at 4 KiB / CRLF / grapheme-cluster edges.

findings.claim: Real performance numbers on this exact 4-vCPU box: ropey 1.6.1 loads a 64 MiB buffer in 79.2 ms (808 MiB/s); insert+delete a char at the midpoint of a 64 MiB rope takes 343 ns per pair. Large fixtures are generated in-memory at bench time and never committed.
findings.evidence: criterion 0.8.2: `buffer/load_64MiB time: [78.720 ms 79.165 ms 79.648 ms] thrpt: [803.54 MiB/s 808.44 MiB/s 813.01 MiB/s]`; `insert_char_mid_64MiB time: [342.20 ns 343.27 ns 344.34 ns]`. Fixture built by a deterministic `fixture(mb: usize) -> String` generator.
findings.implication: Never commit large fixtures — a 20-line generator function gives you reproducible 1/16/64/256 MiB inputs and keeps the repo tiny. Cache generated fixtures under `target/` or an actions/cache key so CI does not regenerate them every run.

findings.claim: Wall-clock benchmark gating on GitHub-hosted runners is not reliable enough to fail CI. Instruction-count measurement is the only credible CI gate, and neither valgrind nor tmux is preinstalled on the runner images.
findings.evidence: CodSpeed: 'measuring in hosted CI runners is a particularly challenging task, mostly because of noisy neighbors leaking through virtualization layers'; they cite sub-1% false-positive rate only with instruction-count simulation and a 1.5% gate. codspeed-criterion-compat 5.0.1 exists on crates.io. Ubuntu2404 runner readme: xvfb present, valgrind absent, tmux absent, Rust 1.98.0. macos-15 runner readme: Python 3.14.7, Node 22.23.2, Cargo 1.98.0, tmux absent. My own criterion run showed 9% outliers on an idle 4-vCPU box.
findings.implication: Do NOT gate PRs on criterion wall-clock deltas — you will get weekly false alarms and start ignoring them. Instead: (a) a plain `#[test]` with a 10x-generous budget assertion (e.g. 'open 64 MiB in < 2 s') that only fires on catastrophic regressions, and (b) either iai-callgrind 0.16.1 with `apt-get install valgrind` on a nightly schedule, or CodSpeed (free for OSS) if you want per-PR numbers.

findings.claim: tmux 3.4 works as a second, independent headless terminal-emulator harness on Linux/macOS, with symbolic key names and colour-preserving capture — but it is NOT preinstalled on either GitHub runner image and does not exist on Windows.
findings.evidence: `tmux -f /dev/null new-session -d -s jio -x 46 -y 12 "<binary> /tmp/t.txt"`, `tmux send-keys -t jio "hello"`, `tmux capture-pane -p -t jio` returned a clean 12x46 grid; `capture-pane -p -e` returned `^[[38;5;15m^[[48;5;4m [+] | cur 5` (SGR preserved); `send-keys C-s` wrote the file; `send-keys C-q` ended the session. Neither the Ubuntu2404 nor macos-15 runner readme lists tmux.
findings.implication: Worth exactly one CI job on Linux (`apt-get install -y tmux`, ~5 s) as a cross-check that your own vt100-based emulation is not forgiving a VT bug a real emulator would show. Not worth `brew install tmux` on macOS. Multi-emulator matrices under xvfb (alacritty/kitty/xterm) are NOT worth it for a solo dev — they test the emulators, not jio.

findings.claim: A purpose-built PTY test harness for TUIs exists (termlens, portable-pty + vt100 + insta, MSRV 1.85) and it is explicitly Unix-only: 'Unix only for now (Linux + macOS in CI). The PTY layer (portable-pty) supports ConPTY, so Windows is planned, not designed out.'
findings.evidence: termlens README (github.com/vyncint/termlens). Its determinism API is `wait_until` (re-check predicate on every output chunk), `wait_frame` (requires DEC 2026 synchronized updates for exact frame boundaries), `wait_idle` (heuristic settle).
findings.implication: Two things. (1) A dedicated harness team shipped Linux+macOS and left Windows undone — treat that as the market's estimate of ConPTY difficulty and plan Windows PTY as smoke-only. (2) Steal the `wait_until`-on-every-chunk design instead of `sleep()`, and consider emitting DEC 2026 synchronized-update markers (`ESC[?2026h` / `ESC[?2026l`) around each frame in jio — it costs 2 lines in the render loop and gives your harness exact, non-flaky frame boundaries forever.

findings.claim: Helix's integration test shape is a `TestCase { in_text, in_selection, in_keys, out_text, out_selection, line_feed_handling }` driven by `test_key_sequence(app, in_keys, test_fn, should_exit)` against a real `Application` over a mock tokio event channel, with `parse_macro(in_keys)` turning a key string into events and an explicit `LineFeedHandling` axis for \n vs native line endings. Kakoune uses directory-per-test with `in`/`cmd`/`rc`/`env`/`enabled`/`script` files driven by a shell runner.
findings.evidence: helix-term/tests/test/helpers.rs (struct + signatures quoted verbatim); helix docs/CONTRIBUTING.md; kakoune/test/run.
findings.implication: Copy Helix's shape, not Kakoune's. Kakoune's shell-based runner is structurally Unix-only — that alone disqualifies it for jio. Note that Helix put `LineFeedHandling` directly in the TestCase struct: they hit the CRLF problem and made it a first-class test axis. Do the same from test #1.

findings.claim: A text-DSL for keystrokes is worth ~30 lines and pays for itself immediately. My `parse_keys` handles literal chars plus `<left> <right> <bs> <ret> <C-s> <C-q>` and drives both the pure-core tests and the snapshot tests from the same string.
findings.evidence: tests/snapshot.rs: `run("", "hello<bs><bs>p!")` asserts buffer == `"help!"`; `run("", "fn main() {<ret>    println!();<ret>}")` feeds the snapshot test. 41 lines total including both tests.
findings.implication: Keep the DSL in Rust (a `parse_keys(&str) -> Vec<Key>` function), NOT in external data files. A Rust function works identically on Windows, needs no runner script, no file-discovery, no CRLF handling for the test data itself, and gives you `#[test]` names and `cargo test <filter>` for free. Add `<S-...>`, `<A-...>`, `<esc>`, `<tab>` as you need them; make unknown key names `panic!` so typos fail loudly.

findings.claim: cargo-mutants 27.1.0 installs and runs but is disk- and CPU-hungry: at `-j4` it copies the source tree per worker and filled the remaining disk in under 2 minutes (`No space left on device`), burning 6m12s of CPU for 1m55s of wall time on a 388-line crate.
findings.evidence: `cargo mutants --no-times -j 4 -- --test prop --test snapshot` → `Error: write message to log / Caused by: No space left on device (os error 28)`; `real 1m55s user 6m12s sys 1m4s`. Disk went from 2.6 G free to exhausted.
findings.implication: Mutation testing is NOT a per-PR gate for a solo dev. Run it monthly, scoped to `jio-core` only (`--file 'src/core/**'`), with `-j1` or `--in-place`, on a schedule. Its real value is a one-time audit of whether your core tests are actually asserting anything — after which the marginal return drops sharply.

findings.claim: cargo-fuzz 0.13.2 requires a nightly compiler; nightly installs fine here (1.100.0-nightly, 2026-09-06). libFuzzer supports x86-64 Linux, x86-64 and aarch64 macOS, and (per the current README) Windows via MSVC AddressSanitizer, though older docs say Unix-only.
findings.evidence: `rustup toolchain install nightly` → `nightly-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu installed - rustc 1.100.0-nightly (5a2be9f5f 2026-09-06)`. cargo-fuzz README/rust-fuzz book: 'cargo-fuzz needs a nightly compiler'; platform support statement is inconsistent between the book and the README.
findings.implication: Fuzz on Linux only — the targets worth fuzzing (encoding/BOM detector, key-sequence parser, VT/CSI parameter parser, rope invariants under an Arbitrary-derived op stream) are all pure logic with no OS dependence. Three targets, run nightly on a schedule with a committed corpus + crash regression tests. Do not try to make cargo-fuzz work on the Windows runner.

findings.claim: GitHub runner images moved under you in 2026: macos-latest is macos-26 on Apple Silicon (arm64) as of Feb 2026, and windows-latest/windows-2025 roll to a Visual Studio 2026 image between June 8-15, 2026. Both images ship Rust/Cargo 1.98.0, while this dev box has 1.94.1.
findings.evidence: github.blog changelog 2026-02-26 (macos-26 GA) and 2026-05-14 (upcoming image migrations); actions/runner-images#14167 (macos-latest → macos-26 in June 2026); Ubuntu2404-Readme.md and macos-15-Readme.md both list Cargo 1.98.0 / Rust 1.98.0. Local: `rustc 1.94.1 (e408947bf 2026-03-25)`.
findings.implication: Two actions. (1) Pin runners explicitly (`macos-26`, `windows-2025`, `ubuntu-24.04`) so an image migration is a deliberate PR, not a mystery red build on a Monday. (2) Commit a `rust-toolchain.toml` — your local 1.94.1 is BEHIND the runners' 1.98.0, so you can write code that compiles locally and hits a new lint/deny in CI, or vice versa. Since macos-latest is arm64, your macOS cross-check target is `aarch64-apple-darwin` (which is what I verified), not x86_64.

findings.claim: insta 1.48.0 ships a `filters` feature (regex + strip-ansi-escapes) purpose-built for normalizing noisy snapshot input.
findings.evidence: insta-1.48.0/Cargo.toml `[features]` → `filters = ["regex", "strip-ansi-escapes"]`, plus `redactions`, `glob`, `json`, `ron`, `csv`.
findings.implication: Use `insta` filters to scrub absolute paths, tempdir names, timings, and stray ANSI from any snapshot that comes out of a PTY run. Without this, PTY-derived snapshots are unstable even within a single OS.

surveys.recommendation:
BOTTOM LINE: make the editor a pure state machine and put ALL cross-platform risk into a shell so thin you can read it in one screen. Then 90% of jio is testable identically on all three runners as boring `cargo test`, and PTY testing becomes a Linux luxury rather than a Windows dependency.

THE SEAM (this is the whole answer)
  bytes/events --[decode]--> Key --[keymap]--> Cmd --[Core::apply]--> (State', Vec<Effect>)
  State --[render]--> ratatui Buffer --[backend]--> bytes
Four pure functions. `Core::apply` returns *descriptions* of I/O (`Effect::WriteFile{path,bytes}`, `Effect::Quit`, `Effect::SetClipboard(String)`) and never performs it. The impure shell — enable_raw_mode, event::read, fs::write, terminal draw — should be 100-150 lines and is the ONLY code you cannot unit test. I built exactly this (47-line core, 57-line shell, 12-line render) and every tier below works against it today.

Workspace: `jio-core` (rope/cursor/undo/commands/keymap — zero platform deps, zero C build scripts), `jio-render` (Core -> Buffer, depends on ratatui-core only), `jio-platform` (fs/path/encoding/clipboard as pure-ish functions over paths and bytes; cfg-heavy but each function individually testable), `jio` (the bin). This mirrors helix-core / helix-view / helix-term, which is the shape that made Helix testable.

TESTING PYRAMID (by test count, and roughly by where your time goes)
  60%  Pure core: table-driven + keystroke-DSL tests over `jio-core`. Microseconds each. Runs on all 3 OSes.
  15%  Property/differential: proptest 1.11.0, rope vs naive `Vec<char>`; undo(redo(x))==x; cursor always on a grapheme boundary; save-then-load round-trips. Runs on all 3 OSes.
  12%  Render snapshots: ratatui 0.30.2 TestBackend + insta 1.48.0, plus the custom `styled_view` for anything colour-related. Runs on all 3 OSes.
   8%  Platform tier: `jio-platform` fs/path/line-ending/encoding tests. Plain `cargo test`, no terminal. THIS is where macOS and Windows coverage actually comes from — run it on all 3 runners.
   4%  PTY E2E: portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2. Linux = full (screen snapshots, resize, OSC 52). macOS = same tests, allowed to be substring-only. Windows = SMOKE ONLY, `continue-on-error: true` for the first month.
   1%  Scheduled: cargo-fuzz (Linux/nightly), cargo-mutants (monthly, jio-core only), benches.
Target: full per-PR suite under 60 s per runner. My 8-test proof-of-concept including 3 real PTY tests ran in 2.5 s, so this is achievable.

CI MATRIX
  every push: `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --lib --bins` + `--target aarch64-apple-darwin --lib --bins` LOCALLY via pre-commit (16 s + 8 s), so CI rarely sees a compile failure.
  PR job A (ubuntu-24.04): fmt, clippy -D warnings, full test suite incl. PTY, tmux cross-check, coverage.
  PR job B (macos-26): tiers 1-4 (`cargo test --workspace --exclude-pty-tier`) + PTY tier substring-only.
  PR job C (windows-2025): tiers 1-4 ONLY, plus one PTY smoke test marked continue-on-error.
  nightly: fuzz (Linux), iai-callgrind or CodSpeed, `cargo mutants` monthly.
Pin the runner labels. Commit `rust-toolchain.toml`. Commit `.gitattributes` with `*.snap text eol=lf` and `* text=auto eol=lf`.

WHAT I'D DO DIFFERENTLY FROM THE OBVIOUS PLAN
1. Make OSC 52 the primary clipboard. Verified: it is fully observable in a PTY test with zero GUI on any OS. Native clipboard becomes an optional fallback that degrades instead of crashing, and stops being a testing hole.
2. Emit DEC 2026 synchronized-update markers (`ESC[?2026h`/`ESC[?2026l`) around every frame. Two lines in the render loop; it gives your harness exact frame boundaries and kills an entire class of flake forever.
3. Add `make winsmoke`: cross-build to x86_64-pc-windows-gnu (11 s) and run it under Wine 9.0 in a PTY, asserting only on file bytes and exit status. It caught the Press/Release double-typing bug locally. Nobody does this; it works; it is nearly free.
4. Do NOT chase multi-emulator xvfb matrices (alacritty/kitty/xterm). One tmux cross-check on Linux gets you 90% of the value for 5 seconds of apt-get.
5. Do NOT gate PRs on criterion wall-clock. Use one generous budget `#[test]` for catastrophes and instruction-count benches on a schedule.

FIRST 10 TESTS, DAY ONE (in order)
 1. `rope_matches_naive` — proptest differential: replay a random `Cmd` stream against ropey and a `Vec<char>` reference; assert text, cursor, and `cursor <= len_chars()`. 43 lines, 0.73 s, and it is your buffer specification. (Working code: /home/user/jio/notes/scratch/testing-harness/tests/prop.rs)
 2. `key_release_is_ignored` — build a synthetic `crossterm::event::KeyEvent { kind: Release }`, assert the pure decoder returns `None`. Runs on all 3 OSes; this is THE Windows bug, verified by Wine.
 3. `keymap_table` — table-driven: every (KeyCode, KeyModifiers) pair you have bound maps to the expected `Cmd`, and unbound keys map to `None`. Grows for free.
 4. `dsl_edits_buffer` — `parse_keys("hello<bs><bs>p!")` -> assert buffer == `"help!"`. Establishes the keystroke DSL on day one so every later test is one line.
 5. `snapshot_screen` — TestBackend(30,8) + `insta::assert_snapshot!(term.backend())` of a 3-line file. Establishes the golden-screen workflow and the `.gitattributes`/`INSTA_UPDATE` conventions.
 6. `styled_snapshot` — same, but through `styled_view()` so colours are actually asserted. Prove to yourself on day one that plain TestBackend snapshots do not check styles.
 7. `cjk_and_emoji_widths` — snapshot a buffer with CJK, a ZWJ family emoji, and a combining mark; TestBackend reports `Hidden by multi-width symbols: [...]`. Your whole Unicode-width regression suite, in 8 lines.
 8. `line_ending_round_trip` — write a CRLF file, open, edit one line, save, assert the bytes still use CRLF and no line got converted; repeat for LF, for a mixed file, and for a file with no trailing newline. Plain `cargo test`, runs on all 3 runners. This is the highest-value platform test in the whole suite.
 9. `e2e_type_and_save` — portable-pty spawn of the real binary; type, Ctrl-S, poll the FILE ON DISK (never `sleep`), Ctrl-Q, assert clean exit. 63 lines, 60 ms. (Working code: .../tests/pty.rs)
10. `resize_does_not_crash` — resize the pty to (1,1), (3,5), (60,200), (24,80), writing a keystroke after each; assert the app is still alive and rendering. 35 lines, 0.52 s. The 1x1 case is the classic ratatui layout panic.

WHAT STAYS MANUAL, AND HOW TO COLLECT IT
Untestable in CI on any runner: native OS clipboard on macOS/Windows, real terminal-emulator quirks (Terminal.app, iTerm2, Windows Terminal, WezTerm, Ghostty, VS Code's terminal), IME/CJK input, true-colour and font/ligature rendering, high-DPI, mouse, bracketed paste from a real terminal, and anything involving a network filesystem or OneDrive/iCloud-synced paths. Ship three things on day one to make user reports actionable: (a) `jio --version` that also prints a `--system-info` dump — OS + version, arch, `$TERM`, `TERM_PROGRAM`/`TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION`, `COLORTERM`, detected terminal size, locale, whether kitty-keyboard/synchronized-updates/OSC-52 were negotiated, and the jio git SHA; (b) a panic hook that writes a scrubbed crash report to a temp file and prints the exact path plus a pre-filled issue URL (never auto-upload); (c) a GitHub issue template whose first required field is the `--system-info` paste and whose second is a keystroke script in your DSL — because if a user can express the repro as `"hello<bs><bs>p!"` you can turn their bug into test #61 in thirty seconds.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND
If a Windows PTY smoke test turns out to be green and fast on windows-2025 for two straight weeks, promote the Windows PTY tier from smoke to substring-assertion coverage. If it is flaky, delete it entirely rather than adding retries — a retried test is a test you have stopped believing, and the pure tiers already cover the behaviour.
risks: ConPTY startup stall/hang: portable-pty 0.9.0 hardcodes PSUEDOCONSOLE_INHERIT_CURSOR, so ConPTY emits ESC[6n and blocks for up to 3 s per spawn (or hangs outright on pre-Win11-24H2 images) unless your harness replies with a CPR. vt100 0.16.2 has no callback for this, so you must sniff raw bytes. You will debug this blind, through CI logs only.

Golden screen snapshots WILL diverge between Linux and Windows PTY runs for reasons that are not bugs: ConPTY rewrites [49m/[39m to [m, drops DCS, and can reorder OSC. If you share .snap files across the PTY tier you will get permanent red on Windows and eventually disable the job.

Git autocrlf on the Windows runner silently rewrites .snap and any fixture file to CRLF, breaking every snapshot test and every line-ending test for a reason that looks like a real failure. Without `.gitattributes` this bites on the very first Windows CI run.

The dev box is on rustc 1.94.1 while both GitHub runner images ship 1.98.0. Code that compiles clean locally can hit a new lint or a `deny`-level change in CI, and you cannot reproduce it. Only a committed rust-toolchain.toml closes this.

Cross-target `cargo check` silently stops working the moment a dev-dependency pulls a C build script — criterion 0.8.2 -> alloca 0.4.0 already does this (`failed to find tool "lib.exe"`). You will not notice you lost the Windows canary until CI catches something check should have.

Wine's console mangles rendering completely (raw SGR leaked into the grid, borders wrapped wrong). If you ever assert on Wine screen content, you will spend days fixing Wine bugs instead of jio bugs. Wine is for side effects only.

macOS runners are now Apple Silicon (macos-26, arm64). Any test with an implicit x86_64 assumption, and any cross-check that targets x86_64-apple-darwin instead of aarch64-apple-darwin, is validating the wrong thing.

windows-latest rolls to a VS 2026 image June 8-15 2026 and macos-latest moved to macos-26 in June 2026. Using `-latest` labels means your only Windows/macOS validation can change out from under you overnight with no PR.

PTY tests are inherently racy: any `sleep()` in the harness is a future flake, and CI runners are 3-4x slower and far more contended than this box, so timings that pass here at 60 ms can time out there. Every wait must be a predicate poll with a generous timeout that prints the full screen on failure.

Native clipboard is untestable on Windows (session 0, no GUI) and on Linux CI (no DISPLAY). If clipboard is a native-only code path, it ships unverified on two of three platforms — the exact scenario the whole strategy exists to prevent.

cargo-mutants at -j4 exhausted the disk on a 388-line crate in under 2 minutes (copies the tree per worker). On a real editor it will be far worse; treat disk and wall time as hard constraints and never put it in the PR path.

Wall-clock benchmark gating on hosted runners produces false alarms (I saw 9% outliers on an idle box). A perf gate you learn to ignore is worse than no perf gate, because it also masks the real regression when it finally arrives.

Atomic-save semantics diverge sharply per-OS and are the most dangerous untested area for a text editor: rename-over-open-file (Windows sharing violation), permission/ownership preservation (Unix), symlink following, ADS/reparse points, case-insensitive-but-case-preserving filesystems on macOS/Windows, and non-UTF8 paths. These ARE testable as plain `cargo test` on all 3 runners — but only if the save path is a pure function over paths and bytes rather than being inlined in the shell.

termlens, a purpose-built TUI PTY harness, is still Unix-only in 2026 with Windows explicitly 'planned, not designed out'. If a dedicated project has not shipped Windows PTY testing, the odds that your solo-dev harness gets it right blind are low. Plan for the Windows PTY tier to be deleted rather than fixed.
open_questions: Does portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 actually drive a crossterm/ratatui app end-to-end on windows-2025? I verified the code paths compile for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and that Wine's kernel32 exports the ConPTY entry points, but I cannot execute a real ConPTY here. This needs one throwaway CI run before any Windows PTY test is written.

With PSEUDOCONSOLE_WIN32_INPUT_MODE forced on by portable-pty, does writing plain bytes ("hello", "\x13") to the master still synthesize the right INPUT_RECORDs, or must the harness emit win32-input-mode sequences (ESC[Vk;Sc;Uc;Kd;Cs;Rc_)? Microsoft's spec is ambiguous on backward compatibility here and it decides whether a Windows PTY harness is 30 lines or 300.

Does the ESC[6n auto-reply workaround actually unblock ConPTY on windows-2025, and does the 3-second INHERIT_CURSOR timeout apply on that image (Windows 26100+ changed ClosePseudoConsole behaviour)? Measure spawn-to-first-frame latency in a probe workflow before committing to the tier.

Is jio's repo public? Everything above assumes free unlimited GitHub Actions minutes for public repos. If it is private, macOS runners bill at a 10x multiplier and Windows at 2x, which would push the macOS PTY tier off the per-PR path entirely.

Does arboard (or whatever clipboard crate is chosen) actually work on a windows-2025 runner in session 0? Session 0 does have a window station with a clipboard, so it may work despite the no-GUI constraint. Worth one probe job — if it works, the native clipboard tier is cheap; if not, OSC 52 is mandatory rather than merely preferable.

How much of Wine 9.0's ConPTY is real vs. stubbed? If CreatePseudoConsole is functional enough, a Wine + portable-pty harness could exercise the ConPTY path locally, which would collapse the biggest blind spot in the plan. My Wine test went through Wine's tty bridge, not through CreatePseudoConsole, so this is untested.

Do ratatui 0.30's TestBackend `assert_buffer_lines` / `assert_scrollback` APIs produce identical grids across the 3 OSes for the same widget tree? They should (pure computation), but line-ending and unicode-width crate version differences could theoretically diverge. One cheap CI run confirms or kills the assumption that render snapshots can be shared across runners.

For performance gating, is CodSpeed (free for OSS, sub-1% false positives with a 1.5% gate) worth the third-party dependency versus iai-callgrind 0.16.1 + apt-installed valgrind on a nightly schedule? The latter is self-hosted and Linux-only; the former is hosted and gives per-PR feedback.

grounding.summary:
Empirical ground-truth run on the headless Ubuntu 24.04 box (rustc 1.94.1, cargo 1.94.1, 4 vCPU, 15 GB RAM) on 2026-09-07. Every number below is real command output from /tmp/claude-0/rust-tui-eval/.

Headlines:

1. THE CORE STACK IS HEALTHY AND CHEAP. crossterm 0.29.0 + ratatui 0.30.2 + ropey 1.6.1 + unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 + unicode-width 0.2.2 + anyhow 1.0.104 + toml 1.1.5 + serde 1.0.229 resolves clean (191 packages in Cargo.lock, 84 actually compiled on Linux), clean release build 23.8s, 981 KB binary. A 168-line toy editor on crossterm+ratatui+ropey compiled FIRST TRY against the ratatui 0.30 API: 14.3s clean release, 1.07s incremental release rebuild, 0.15s warm `cargo check`, 76 crates, 1.14 MB unstripped / 909 KB stripped / 636 KB with opt-level="z"+lto+codegen-units=1+panic=abort+strip.

2. ratatui 0.30 IS A WORKSPACE SPLIT, NOT A MONOLITH. `ratatui 0.30.2` is a facade over `ratatui-core 0.1.2`, `ratatui-widgets 0.3.2`, `ratatui-crossterm 0.1.2`, `ratatui-macros 0.7.2`, and there is now a fourth backend, `termina`, alongside crossterm/termion/termwiz. Backends live at `ratatui::backend::{Backend, TestBackend, CrosstermBackend}`; `ratatui::{init, restore, run, try_init}` exist but are crossterm-feature-gated.

3. THE macOS/WINDOWS "NO HARDWARE" PROBLEM IS MOSTLY SOLVABLE ON THIS BOX. I built a real Mach-O arm64 AND x86_64 macOS binary of the toy from Linux with cargo-zigbuild 0.23.4 + `pip install ziglang` (zig 0.16.0), no macOS SDK, in ~10s each. More important: `cargo zigbuild --release --target aarch64-apple-darwin` built the FULL heavy stack (tree-sitter C + tree-sitter-rust grammar C + syntect + arboard + notify + portable-pty + nucleo + encoding_rs + chardetng) in 54.8s, and the macOS-only code paths genuinely compiled — objc2, objc2-app-kit, objc2-core-foundation, objc2-core-graphics, objc2-foundation (arboard's macOS clipboard) and fsevent-sys (notify's FSEvents backend), 126 rlibs. Windows-GNU builds the same full stack with the already-installed mingw in 51.0s, pulling clipboard-win, crossterm-winapi, windows-sys.

4. WINE CAUGHT A REAL WINDOWS-ONLY BUG THAT CI WOULD HAVE SHIPPED. Running the cross-built .exe under wine-9.0 in a pty, the toy died instantly: `Error: Keyboard progressive enhancement not implemented for the legacy Windows API.` Root cause verified in crossterm-0.29.0/src/event.rs:495-542: `PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags` and `PopKeyboardEnhancementFlags` hard-code `is_ansi_code_supported() -> false` on Windows, so `execute!` routes to `execute_winapi()` which unconditionally returns `ErrorKind::Unsupported` — even on Windows Terminal where ANSI works fine. Also `crossterm::terminal::sys::windows::supports_keyboard_enhancement()` is `Ok(false)` unconditionally. Guarding on `supports_keyboard_enhancement().unwrap_or(false)` fixed it and the guarded .exe then ran under wine, rendered, took keys, and exited 0 on Ctrl-Q.

5. TESTING WITHOUT A TERMINAL WORKS THREE DIFFERENT WAYS, ALL VERIFIED. (a) ratatui `TestBackend` + `Buffer::with_lines` + `assert_eq!` gives a readable side-by-side diff; `term.get_cursor_position()` works. (b) insta 1.48.0 snapshots of the buffer work end to end (write, re-run, pass). (c) A pty driver (Python `pty.fork` + TIOCSWINSZ) runs the REAL binary headlessly and lets you assert on the emitted escape sequences — I verified `\x1b[?1049h/l` (alt screen), `\x1b[?2004h/l` (bracketed paste), `\x1b[>1u`/`\x1b[<1u` (kitty keyboard). Add qemu-user-static and you can run the full test suite for aarch64: `cargo test --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` → 5 tests, all pass, under qemu-aarch64.

6. ropey IS THE RIGHT ROPE AND IT IS NOT CLOSE. On a generated 100.07 MiB UTF-8 corpus (2.49 M lines, 91.2 M chars, 21.2 M non-ASCII bytes): ropey loads in 167ms with 125 MiB peak RSS via `from_reader`, 2.10 µs per random single-char insert, 147 ns per sequential insert. A flat `String` is 2.40 ms per random insert — 1143x slower. crop 0.4.3 is 2.88 µs/insert, jumprope 1.1.2 is 3.43 µs/insert with 194 MiB resident.

7. helix-core IS NOT REUSABLE. `cargo add helix-core` resolves to v0.0.0 whose entire lib.rs is `//! Placeholder` and whose description is "This package is a placeholder for the future helix-editor crate." `helix-stdx` does not exist on crates.io. Any Helix reuse means a git dependency on an MPL-2.0 workspace.

Everything I built is at /tmp/claude-0/rust-tui-eval/: toy/src/main.rs (the 235-line editor incl. tests), toy/tests/wide.rs (wide-char probe), ropebench/src/main.rs, tsdemo/src/main.rs, platcheck/ (cross-platform full-stack check), probe.sh (the survey harness), ptyrun.py (headless pty driver).

grounding.verdict:
TAKE THE STACK: crossterm 0.29.0 + ratatui 0.30.2 + ropey 1.6.1 + unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 + unicode-width 0.2.2 + anyhow 1.0.104 + toml 1.1.5 + serde 1.0.229. It resolves clean, builds in 14s from scratch and 1s incrementally, ships a 636 KB stripped binary, and every part of it is exercisable headlessly. Nothing in the survey argues against it.

Specific calls, in priority order:

ROPE: ropey, not crop, not jumprope, not String. 2.10 µs/random-insert vs crop 2.88 and jumprope 3.43, 125 MiB peak on a 100 MiB file, and char-indexed (which matches how you will address a text buffer for LSP UTF-16 conversion and grapheme walking; crop is byte-indexed, which is a different and more error-prone API shape). Always construct with `Rope::from_reader`, never `read_to_string` + `from_str` — measured 42% lower peak RSS and 30% faster. What would change my mind: if you decide to build on CRDT collaborative editing, jumprope's provenance (diamond-types) matters more than 1.6x on insert. Nothing else would.

CROSS-PLATFORM STRATEGY — this is where the research actually pays off, and the answer is NOT "CI only":
- Tier 1 (free, every commit, 4s each): `cargo check --target {x86_64,aarch64}-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target {x86_64,aarch64}-apple-darwin`, plus `cargo clippy --target`. Works right now with zero installs. Catches 80% of `#[cfg]` rot.
- Tier 2 (pip install ziglang + cargo-zigbuild, already on the box): actually LINK macOS arm64/x86_64 and aarch64 Linux binaries locally, tree-sitter C and objc2 clipboard code included, 55s for the full stack. This proves link-time symbol resolution, which `cargo check` cannot.
- Tier 3 (apt install wine64, qemu-user-static): actually RUN the Windows .exe and the aarch64 binary headlessly under a pty. This is the tier that earns its keep — wine caught the `PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags` Windows crash in one run, a bug that a `cargo check` matrix and a naive CI "cargo build --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc" would both have passed and that would have made jio fail to start on every Windows machine on day one.
- Windows MSVC linking is genuinely impossible here (aka.ms is proxy-blocked, so cargo-xwin cannot fetch the CRT). MSVC must be GitHub Actions. But windows-gnu + wine gives you a local proxy for behavioral testing, and MSVC-vs-GNU differences are mostly ABI/linking, not console behavior.

CONSEQUENCE FOR ARCHITECTURE: put every terminal-driver call behind a thin `term` module with a capability probe at startup (`supports_keyboard_enhancement()`, mouse, bracketed paste), and make the pty harness a first-class test target from commit one. The one Windows bug found today is the archetype of the whole class: crossterm silently degrades some commands to a WinAPI path that returns `Err(Unsupported)`, and there is no compile-time signal. If jio's terminal layer is a leaf module with a pty test, wine and qemu catch that class locally in seconds; if it is smeared through the render loop, you find out from a GitHub issue.

TESTING: ratatui TestBackend + insta 1.48.0 is a real, working golden-buffer harness — use it, but snapshot the `Buffer` Debug output, not a hand-rolled `symbol()` join, because wide-char continuation cells are literal spaces and a naive join silently produces the wrong string. Add proptest 1.11.0 for rope/cursor invariants (28 crates, cheap). Defer criterion 0.8.2 (53 crates, 158 MB target dir) to a separate `benches` workspace member — on a box that spent the whole session at 97-99% disk, that matters.

DEFER OR AVOID: gix 0.87.1 costs 148 crates and 68s of build time; do not take it for a status-line git indicator, shell out to `git` first. tower-lsp 0.20.0 (lsp-types 0.94.1) and async-lsp 0.2.4 (lsp-types 0.95.1) both drag you onto stale lsp-types while standalone is at 0.97.0 — if you want an LSP client, prefer tower-lsp-server 0.23.0 (maintained fork, 52 crates) or hand-roll JSON-RPC over lsp-types 0.97.0 and keep the type crate under your own control. termwiz 0.23.3 (90 crates) buys you nothing over crossterm unless you specifically want its terminal emulation; ratatui 0.30 supports it as a backend so the door stays open. syntect 5.3.0 MUST be taken as `default-features = false, features = ["default-fancy"]` or onig_sys breaks every cross-compile — but honestly tree-sitter 0.27.0 + tree-sitter-rust 0.24.2 (verified ABI 15 on both sides, incremental reparse working) is the better highlighting story and only costs 20 crates.

DO NOT PLAN ON REUSING HELIX CODE. helix-core on crates.io is a literal `//! Placeholder` stub at 0.0.0. Reuse means a git dependency on an MPL-2.0 workspace with no semver contract, no docs.rs, and no stability guarantee. Read Helix for ideas; do not link it.
surprises: ratatui 0.30 is no longer one crate. It is a facade over ratatui-core 0.1.2 / ratatui-widgets 0.3.2 / ratatui-crossterm 0.1.2 / ratatui-macros 0.7.2, and it now ships a FOURTH backend called `termina` alongside crossterm/termion/termwiz. Any tutorial, blog post, or remembered API from the 0.2x monolith era is describing a different crate layout. Backends are at `ratatui::backend::{Backend, TestBackend, CrosstermBackend}`; `ratatui::{init, restore, run, try_init, try_restore, DefaultTerminal}` exist but only under the crossterm feature.

THE BIG ONE: crossterm's kitty-keyboard commands are not merely no-ops on Windows, they are HARD ERRORS. crossterm-0.29.0/src/event.rs:495-542 gives both PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags and PopKeyboardEnhancementFlags a `#[cfg(windows)] is_ansi_code_supported() -> false`, which forces `execute!` down the WinAPI path, where `execute_winapi()` unconditionally returns `Err(ErrorKind::Unsupported)`. So the idiomatic `execute!(out, EnterAlternateScreen, PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags(...))?` — which is what most examples show — makes your editor fail to start on Windows, including on modern Windows Terminal where ANSI would work perfectly. Nothing about this is visible at compile time; `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` passes happily. I only found it because wine ran the binary.

You can build genuine macOS binaries on a Linux box with no macOS SDK and no Apple anything: `pip install ziglang` (zig 0.16.0) + the pre-installed cargo-zigbuild 0.23.4 produced a `Mach-O 64-bit arm64 executable` with platform=1, sdk=26.4, minos=13.0, linking /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib — and it compiled arboard's objc2/objc2-app-kit ObjC-bridge crates and notify's fsevent-sys along the way. The common wisdom that "macOS cross-compilation requires the SDK / osxcross" is wrong for pure-Rust-plus-cc-crate projects in 2026.

This box was already far more cross-capable than the brief implies: nine rustup targets pre-installed (including both apple-darwin and both windows-msvc), cargo-zigbuild AND cargo-xwin already in /root/.cargo/bin, and mingw's x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc in /usr/bin. `apt-get install` also works (I installed time, bc, qemu-user-static, wine64), and pip/npm reach their registries. The "no extra installs" framing is much softer than stated.

cargo-xwin is installed but useless here, and it fails for a network reason rather than a technical one: `HTTP GET https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/channel` → `CONNECT proxy failed: proxy server responded 403/403`. If the proxy allowlist ever gains aka.ms, MSVC cross-linking becomes possible on this box and the whole "Windows is CI-only" premise changes.

The `cc` crate + zig combination does NOT work if you hand-roll the CC shim: cc passes the raw Rust triple through and zig replies `error: unable to parse target query 'x86_64-pc-windows-gnu': UnknownOperatingSystem`. You must use `cargo zigbuild`, which installs its own translating wrappers. Similarly, using `zig cc` as a bare `linker=` for a musl target produces `duplicate symbol: _start` because zig's crt1.o collides with rustc's self-contained one — the fix, `-C link-self-contained=no`, is not something the cargo-zigbuild README leads with.

Snapshot-testing a TUI is subtly wrong by default for CJK. ratatui stores a double-width grapheme in cell x and a LITERAL SPACE in cell x+1, so `(0..w).map(|x| buf[(x,y)].symbol()).collect::<String>()` returns "日 本 語 ab  " — visually wrong, and it will happily bake that wrongness into an insta snapshot. ratatui's own Buffer Debug gets it right and even annotates it: `"日本語ab  ", // hidden by multi-width symbols: [(1, " "), (3, " "), (5, " ")]`.

helix-core is squatted by its own author as a 0.0.0 `//! Placeholder`, with the description "This package is a placeholder for the future helix-editor crate." Anyone who read a blog post saying "just use helix-core for the rope/transaction model" is describing a git dependency, not a crates.io one — and helix-stdx isn't on crates.io at all.

The LSP ecosystem is fragmented three ways right now: standalone lsp-types is at 0.97.0, tower-lsp 0.20.0 still pins 0.94.1, async-lsp 0.2.4 pins 0.95.1, and the maintained fork tower-lsp-server 0.23.0 has abandoned lsp-types entirely for its own `ls-types 0.0.6`. There is no single shared LSP type vocabulary to build against.

syntect's default feature set still drags in the C library Oniguruma (onig_sys 69.9.3) in 2026, and that single build script is what breaks every cross-compile of the stack. Nothing in the crate name or the usual quickstart hints at a C dependency.

A flat String buffer is not merely "slower", it is 1143x slower on this workload — 2.4 ms per single-char insert into a 100 MB file, i.e. ~400 keystrokes per second before the editor is unusable, and that is a release build with no other work happening. The gap is far wider than the usual "ropes are better for big files" hand-waving suggests.

grounding.summary: Built two ~160-line equivalent TUI editors (Rust ratatui 0.30.2 + crossterm 0.29.0; Go tcell v2.13.10) on the headless box, then drove both through real pseudo-terminals with three independent harnesses. PTY end-to-end testing is PROVEN feasible and NOT flaky here — 0 failures in 150+ runs across Python/pyte, Rust/portable-pty+vt100 and Go/creack-pty+vt10x, including under 4x CPU oversubscription with 4 parallel PTYs. The determinism trick is polling a predicate against the live emulated screen; fixed sleeps flake (10ms sleeps failed 56% of the time under load; 1ms failed 100% even idle). Go wins cross-compilation (7/7 targets from this box) and build speed (7.8s cold / 0.07s incremental vs 15.7s / 0.39s). Rust wins binary size (550KB vs 2.49MB), terminal-output efficiency (62 B/keystroke vs 139 B, size-independent), and — decisively for this project — CI reach: portable-pty 0.9.0 has a real ConPTY backend and the whole Rust test harness typechecks for windows-msvc and darwin, whereas creack/pty v1.1.24's start_windows.go is a compile-clean stub that returns ErrUnsupported at runtime. Two other CI-critical asymmetries found: tcell hard-fails when TERM is unset/dumb/unknown (crossterm does not consult terminfo at all and renders fine), and Rust's "can't cross-compile" folklore is wrong for windows-gnu (454KB .exe built in 14.3s, 4/4 reproducible, runs under wine). Key file paths: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-jio/16c10884-cbf0-5549-8678-28b34a054161/scratchpad/lab/{rs-toy/src/main.rs, go-toy/main.go, pty/harness.py, pty/flaky.py, rs-ptytest/src/lib.rs, rs-ptytest/tests/e2e.rs, go-ptytest/e2e_test.go}.

what_failed: RUST CROSS-LINK x86_64-pc-windows-msvc AND aarch64-pc-windows-msvc: `error: linker \`link.exe\` not found` / `note: the msvc targets depend on the msvc linker but link.exe was not found`. Unfixable on Linux without an MSVC toolchain. NOTE: `cargo check --release --target <msvc>` DOES succeed for both — you can typecheck the Windows code path locally, you just cannot link it.

RUST CROSS-LINK x86_64-apple-darwin AND aarch64-apple-darwin: `warning: invoking \"xcrun\" \"--sdk\" \"macosx\" \"--show-sdk-path\" to find MacOSX.sdk failed: No such file or directory (os error 2)` then `error: linking with \`cc\` failed: exit status: 1`. No macOS SDK, no Apple linker. `cargo check --target` for both: OK.

RUST CROSS-LINK aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu: `rust-lld: error: ...rcgu.o is incompatible with elf64-x86-64` and `libcompiler_builtins-*.rlib(lib.rmeta) is incompatible with elf64-x86-64` — rustc falls back to the host `cc`/lld, no aarch64 cross linker installed. aarch64-unknown-linux-musl fails the same way. `cargo check --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` from a CLEAN target dir: OK (my first check attempt reported a bogus 'could not parse/generate dep info' error only because it ran on artifacts left by the failed link).

RUST CROSS-LINK x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, FIRST ATTEMPT ONLY: `/usr/bin/x86_64-w64-mingw32-ld: cannot find -lwinapi_advapi32: No such file or directory` (winapi 0.3.9 comes in via crossterm 0.29 + crossterm_winapi 0.9.1). THIS WAS TRANSIENT — the winapi-x86_64-pc-windows-gnu-0.4.0/lib dir does contain all 1419 import libs, and after a `rm -rf target` the tuned profile (opt-level=z, lto, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, strip) built 4/4 times cleanly. I am flagging this explicitly because I initially concluded windows-gnu was broken and it is NOT. Correction stands: Rust CAN cross-build a working Windows exe from this box.

WINE CANNOT VALIDATE TUI RENDERING (both languages). wine-9.0 runs `rs-toy-win.exe --version` and `out-windows-amd64.exe --version` correctly (both print `jio-toy 0.1.0`), but driving the full TUI through wine+PTY produces mangled output at 60x12, 80x24 and 80x25. Rust/crossterm: box border and text rows collapse into each other and a literal `5;12H` leaks onto the screen (wine is eating the ESC prefix of CSI sequences). Go/tcell: total garbage — screen row 0 is `J[2 ... 6l` and nothing else renders. Wine is a smoke-test tool for startup/argv/non-TUI logic ONLY.

creack/pty v1.1.24 IS A WINDOWS STUB. /root/go/pkg/mod/github.com/creack/pty@v1.1.24/start_windows.go is `//go:build windows` and its entire body is `return nil, ErrUnsupported`. `GOOS=windows go vet ./...` on my Go PTY test suite returns OK — it compiles clean and then fails at runtime on a Windows runner. This is the single most dangerous finding for a Go choice.

tcell v2.13.10 HARD-FAILS ON BAD/ABSENT TERM. TERM=dumb -> `screen: terminal not cursor addressable`; TERM=unknown-term-xyz -> `screen: couldn't open terminfo ($TERM) file for unknown-term-xyz: exit status 1` (that 'exit status 1' is tcell shelling out to infocmp as a dynamic fallback); TERM unset entirely -> `screen: terminal entry not found: term not set`, 48 bytes written then exit. crossterm/ratatui renders a fully correct screen in all of those cases including TERM completely unset (757 bytes, verified via pyte). This box has only 41 terminfo files under /usr/share/terminfo.

NO EXECUTION OF FOREIGN-ARCH BINARIES BY DIRECT EXEC: binfmt_misc is not registered (/proc/sys/fs/binfmt_misc is empty), so `./out-linux-arm64` and `./out-windows-amd64.exe` give `cannot execute binary file: Exec format error`. You must invoke the emulator explicitly: `qemu-aarch64-static ./out-linux-arm64 --version` -> works, prints `jio-toy 0.1.0`.
docker is installed (29.3.1) but the daemon is NOT reachable — `docker info` fails. No container-based cross-testing.

NO X TERMINAL EMULATORS AT ALL: xterm, urxvt, alacritty, kitty, foot, gnome-terminal, konsole, st are all MISSING. Xvfb IS present but is useless with nothing to run in it. The GUI/Xvfb route to terminal testing is dead here; PTY is the only route.

NO CONTROLLING TTY: `tty` -> `not a tty`; opening /dev/tty raises `[Errno 6] No such device or address`; stdin is /dev/null and stdout is a file. TERM in this session is `linux`. /dev/pts is mounted with ptmxmode=000 so /dev/pts/ptmx is unusable, but the global /dev/ptmx is 0666 and `pty.fork()` works — this is why PTY testing works at all.

MEASUREMENT ARTIFACT I INITIALLY MIS-REPORTED: my first key->repaint benchmark showed Rust 6.4ms vs Go 36.9ms at 200x50. That gap was my Python predicate rebuilding the whole 200x50 pyte screen on every poll, plus spawning a fresh process per sample. With a cheap last-row-only predicate the two are equal (60x12: 0.63 vs 1.04ms; 200x50: 6.52 vs 6.44ms; 400x100: 25.6 vs 31.3ms — and at 400x100 the dominant cost is the Python harness, not either app). Do not quote the 36.9ms number.
A 400x100 pyte screen makes the naive `''.join(screen.display)` predicate so slow the test suite hangs (I had to kill a 600s run). If you use the Python route, poll only the rows you assert on.
