TMUX AS A THIRD HARNESS — VERIFIED WORKING HEADLESS: `tmux new-session -d -s jio2 -x 80 -y 24 <binary>` then `tmux send-keys -t jio2 'ABC'` then `tmux capture-pane -p -t jio2` returned the fully rendered screen including `│  1 ABChello world`. Language-agnostic, shell-only, no libraries. Weakness: no built-in wait-for-predicate, so you'd hand-roll a capture-pane polling loop.
grounding.verdict:
PTY end-to-end testing is DEFINITIVELY FEASIBLE on this headless box and is NOT inherently flaky — 0 failures in 180+ Python-route runs, 60/60 Rust-route and 60/60 Go-route under 4x CPU oversubscription with parallel PTYs. The entire flakiness question reduces to one rule: NEVER sleep, always poll a predicate against the emulated screen with a generous timeout. Fixed 10ms sleeps failed 56% of the time under load; the identical test with `wait_for(predicate)` failed 0%. Build the harness so the only timing knob is a 5s ceiling that a passing test never reaches (median full-drive time was 7-14ms idle, 38-40ms under load).

ON THE STACK, I recommend RUST + ratatui/crossterm, and the reason is specifically the CI constraint, not performance. Three verified facts drive this:

(1) The Rust harness (portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2) has a REAL ConPTY backend (src/win/conpty.rs) and the whole test crate `cargo check --tests` clean for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin. One test suite, three GitHub runners. The Go equivalent, creack/pty v1.1.24, has a start_windows.go whose entire body is `return nil, ErrUnsupported` — it passes `GOOS=windows go vet` and then fails at runtime. Choosing Go means writing a second, structurally different Windows test path (ActiveState/termtest v0.7.2 + termtest/conpty v0.5.0, or UserExistsError/conpty v0.1.4, both of which resolve through the proxy but which I could not exercise). For a project whose stated rule is "any design that cannot be verified in CI is a design that ships broken", a Windows test path that silently compiles and cannot run is the exact failure mode to avoid.

(2) crossterm never touches terminfo. It rendered a perfect screen with TERM unset, TERM=dumb and TERM=unknown-term-xyz. tcell hard-failed on all three, and its fallback shells out to infocmp. Bare CI runners and container steps routinely have TERM unset or dumb. That is a class of CI-only breakage you would spend days chasing.

(3) Size and wire efficiency: 550KB vs 2.49MB, and 62 vs 139 bytes per keystroke independent of terminal size. For an editor people run over SSH, the per-keystroke number is the one that matters, and crossterm is 2.2x tighter.

Go's advantages are REAL and I am not dismissing them. Cross-compilation is a rout: 7/7 targets from this box in ~8s each with zero cgo, versus Rust's 3/8 linking locally. Build speed is a rout: 7.8s cold and 0.07s incremental versus 15.7s and 0.39s (and 5.2s if you turn LTO on in the release profile — do not do that in the dev loop). And Rust's target/ dir hit 1.2 GB for a 156-line program versus 31 MB for the Go project.

But cross-compilation is worth much less here than the folklore suggests, for two reasons I verified: first, Rust DID cross-build a working 454KB Windows .exe (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, 14.3s, 4/4 reproducible, runs under wine) — my initial "windows-gnu is broken" reading was a transient registry-unpack race and I retract it. Second and more important, you have ubuntu/macos/windows GitHub runners anyway, and macOS release builds must be produced and signed on macOS regardless of what Linux can link. The thing local cross-compilation actually buys is a fast "did I break the Windows/macOS code path" signal — and `cargo check --target` gives you exactly that for msvc, darwin and aarch64-linux, in seconds, without linking.

CONCRETE RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) keep `lto` OUT of the dev profile and put the size tuning in a separate `[profile.dist]` — the 13x incremental penalty is the single worst thing about the Rust loop and it is entirely opt-in; (b) add a pre-push `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --target aarch64-apple-darwin` gate, since it catches platform-code-path breakage locally in seconds; (c) write the e2e harness ONCE in Rust (portable-pty + vt100, ~112 lines, see .../lab/rs-ptytest/src/lib.rs) so it runs on all three runners; (d) keep the Python/pyte harness (.../lab/pty/harness.py, 87 lines) as a fast local scratchpad — it is genuinely the quickest thing to prototype with and pyte is already installed — but do NOT make it the CI gate, because Python's `pty` module is Unix-only; (e) use ratatui's TestBackend (ratatui-core 0.1.2 backend/test.rs) for cheap unit-level screen assertions and reserve PTY tests for real input/escape-sequence/terminal-mode behavior.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND: if portable-pty's ConPTY backend turns out to be broken on a real windows-latest runner. That is the one load-bearing claim I could NOT verify from Linux — I proved it typechecks, not that it works. Run a hello-world PTY test on all three runners as literally the first CI job of this project; if Windows fails there, the Rust advantage collapses and Go + ActiveState/termtest becomes competitive again. I would also switch if the project turns out to be small enough that daily build latency dominates everything else.

WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY FROM LINUX (state this plainly to the owner): that ANY macOS or Windows binary actually runs correctly — wine proved only that `--version` works and then mangled every escape sequence in the real TUI, so it is a startup smoke test and nothing more; that crossterm's or tcell's Windows console rendering path works at all; that tcell's console_win.go sidesteps the TERM/terminfo problem on Windows (it probably does, since it uses the console API, but that is inference); what TERM value GitHub Actions runners actually set; and macOS terminfo availability. Everything on those platforms is CI-or-nothing.
surprises: "Rust can't cross-compile, that's Go's killer feature" is WRONG for Windows. `cargo build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` produced a 454,656-byte PE32+ exe in 14.27s from a fully clean target dir, 4/4 reproducible, and wine ran it (`jio-toy 0.1.0`). The mingw toolchain and 9 rustup std targets are ALREADY on this box. Rust's real cross-compile gap is msvc + apple-darwin + aarch64-linux, not "Windows".

tcell — the toolkit with the reputation for being the portable, batteries-included, works-everywhere choice — is MEASURABLY LESS CI-PORTABLE than crossterm. It hard-fails with TERM unset (`terminal entry not found: term not set`, 48 bytes then exit), TERM=dumb (`terminal not cursor addressable`), and any TERM missing from the local terminfo db (it shells out to infocmp and reports `exit status 1`). crossterm consults terminfo not at all and rendered a byte-perfect screen in every one of those cases. I expected the opposite.

Go's PTY-testing story is WORSE than Rust's, which inverts the usual "Go has better tooling" assumption. creack/pty v1.1.24 — the de-facto Go PTY library — ships a Windows file that compiles cleanly and returns ErrUnsupported at runtime. `GOOS=windows go vet ./...` says OK. That is a silent CI trap: green typecheck, red-at-runtime on windows-latest. portable-pty 0.9.0 ships an actual ConPTY implementation.

The vt100 crate has a whitespace trap that makes a WORKING ratatui app look broken while a tcell app looks fine. `vt100::Cell::contents()` returns "" for a cell that was never written; ratatui/crossterm skip writing blanks and just move the cursor, so a naive per-cell reconstruction collapses `│  1 hello world` into `│1helloworld`. My Rust e2e test failed on the Rust binary and passed on the Go binary for exactly this reason before I normalized empty->space. pyte does NOT have this problem, and vt100's own `Screen::contents()` is also fine — it is specifically the per-cell API. This would have cost a day if hit cold.

Go's binary is 4.5x LARGER than Rust's for the identical program (2,486,456 vs 550,816 bytes at each side's best flags), and even Rust's untuned default release build (931,832 B) beats Go's best by 2.7x. The usual framing is that Rust binaries are bloated.

Both toolkits do proper damage tracking — I initially measured tcell writing 2,454 bytes per keystroke at 200x50 and nearly reported that as a tcell flaw. It was MY code calling s.Clear() every frame. Removing one line dropped it to 139 bytes, constant in terminal size. Lesson worth passing on: `s.Clear()` in a tcell draw loop dirties every cell and defeats the diff.

wine is installed and DOES run both cross-built Windows binaries — but only for non-TUI work. Under a PTY it corrupts ANSI output badly enough that a literal `5;12H` appeared as text on the emulated screen, and tcell's output was pure garbage. I expected wine to be either unusable or usable; "runs the process fine, destroys the terminal protocol" is the worst of both and is exactly the shape of result that would produce false confidence if you only tested `--version`.

tmux 3.4 works fully headless with no display and no tty: `tmux new-session -d -x 80 -y 24 <tui>` + `send-keys` + `capture-pane -p` returned a correctly rendered screen. It is a legitimate zero-dependency third harness that nobody proposes, and it works from plain shell in CI.

Rust's LTO release profile costs 13x on the incremental loop (5.2s vs 0.39s debug) — the size win (931KB -> 550KB) is real but you pay it on every single edit if you put it in `[profile.release]` and then habitually build release. Go's equivalent loop is 0.07s.

The build-artifact footprint gap is far larger than the binary-size gap and runs the other way: 1.2 GB of Rust target/ across 8 cross-targets (148 MB for a single target) for a 156-line program, versus 31 MB for the entire Go project including seven cross-compiled binaries. That is a GitHub Actions cache-size problem, not a curiosity.

pyte 0.8.2, pexpect 4.9.0 and ptyprocess 0.7.0 were ALREADY installed on this box — the fastest PTY prototype needed zero installs. Meanwhile hyperfine had to be cargo-installed and failed once transiently before succeeding.

qemu-aarch64-static is present and runs cross-built aarch64 Linux binaries (`qemu-aarch64-static ./out-linux-arm64 --version` -> `jio-toy 0.1.0`), but binfmt_misc is unregistered so you must invoke it explicitly. That means arm64 Linux is the one non-native platform you CAN meaningfully test locally — and only for Go, since Rust cannot link aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu or -musl here.

contradictions.topic: Does termina solve Windows terminal handling, and did Helix prove it?
contradictions.position_a: language-choice and ui-paradigm: "Helix migrated its terminal backend from crossterm to termina specifically to drop legacy Windows Console API code and use ConPTY/VT uniformly" — language-choice marks this VERIFIED and draws the implication that adopting termina "eliminates the entire dual-codepath legacy-console problem — the single biggest Windows terminal pain — for free."
contradictions.position_b: prior-art-postmortems and rust-ecosystem: Helix ships TWO backends and selects by platform — `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies] crossterm = "0.28"`, termina everywhere else.
contradictions.who_is_right: prior-art and rust-ecosystem. language-choice's implication is false.
contradictions.why: I fetched helix-term/Cargo.toml on master today. Line 57: `tui = { ... features = ["termina", "crossterm"] }`. Lines 92-93: `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies]` / `crossterm = { version = "0.28", features = ["event-stream"] }` — a non-optional Windows dependency. helix-tui/Cargo.toml likewise carries crossterm only under cfg(windows). PR #13307 (which I also fetched) does state the ConPTY intent verbatim ("we tell terminals on Windows to 'speak VT'", "we will require Windows 10 ... 10.0.17763"), so the motivation is real — but ~12 months after that merge Helix still has not deleted its Windows crossterm path. The flagship user has NOT validated termina-only on Windows. Anyone adopting termina for jio would be doing so ahead of Helix, on the one platform the owner cannot test by hand. This inverts the strongest stated argument for termina.

contradictions.position_a: text-buffer-core: crop, because it is byte-indexed (matching tree-sitter/LSP/ripgrep), has LF+CRLF-only line semantics matching LSP, and measured lowest memory (1.054 vs 1.153 bytes/byte), fastest load (45 vs 71 ms), fastest localized edits (140 vs 168 ns).
contradictions.position_b: rust-ecosystem, language-choice and grounding-agent-1: ropey 1.6.1, because it is what Helix ships, is best-documented, and measured FASTER: grounding measured ropey 2.097 µs/random-insert vs crop 2.882 µs on a 100 MiB file, and ropey's `from_reader` gave 125 MiB peak RSS vs crop's 208 MiB.
contradictions.who_is_right: text-buffer-core is right on the architectural argument; grounding-agent-1's memory number is a harness artifact and should not be used against crop.
contradictions.why: The two performance datasets do not actually conflict: text-buffer-core itself measured ropey faster on UNIFORMLY RANDOM inserts (136 vs 178 ms/100k) and crop faster on LOCALIZED inserts (140 vs 168 ns). grounding-agent-1 only measured the random case, so it reproduced the same direction and then over-generalized to "ropey is decisively the right rope." Real typing is localized. Separately, grounding's 208 MiB crop peak is because their harness used `read_to_string` + `Rope::from`; crop has `RopeBuilder`, and text-buffer-core measured streaming a 64 MiB file through it in 91 ms. That is a measurement of the harness, not the crate. The genuinely decisive argument is text-buffer-core's: ropey 1.x's `insert(char_idx, ...)` and tree-sitter's all-byte `InputEdit` are both `usize`, so a byte/char mixup compiles and works on ASCII and fails only on CJK/emoji — the exact bug class that is undiscoverable without hardware. BUT text-buffer-core understates the counterweight it found itself: crop is ~320 stars, effectively bus-factor 1, versus ropey with Helix as a shipping cross-platform user. The right resolution is neither survey's: pick either behind the `Buffer` newtype text-buffer-core proposes, and treat the choice as reversible.

contradictions.topic: Is portable-pty + vt100 a genuine cross-platform CI harness?
contradictions.position_a: rust-ecosystem: "The complete headless end-to-end test harness works today ... Both cross-check to x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin from this Linux box" — marked VERIFIED, recommended as the DEFAULT PICK with "identical test code runs on all three GitHub runners." ui-paradigm similarly marks VERIFIED that it "genuinely works on Windows runners."
contradictions.position_b: headless-testing: portable-pty 0.9.0 hardcodes `PSUEDOCONSOLE_INHERIT_CURSOR`, which makes ConPTY emit `ESC[6n` and block (~3s timeout, or hang on older images) unless the harness replies; vt100 0.16.2 has no DSR callback, so the reply must be byte-sniffed upstream of the parser. ConPTY also rewrites SGR (`[49m`→`[m`), drops DCS, and reorders OSC, so screen snapshots are not portable. Verdict: Windows PTY = smoke only. grounding-agent-2 adds that creack/pty's Windows file is a runtime stub and that it "proved it typechecks, not that it works."
contradictions.why: "Cross-checks" and "the source contains a ConPTY backend" are compile-time facts. Neither rust-ecosystem nor ui-paradigm executed anything on Windows — nobody in this entire research set has. headless-testing read the actual flag constants in portable-pty's `src/win/psuedocon.rs`, cross-referenced microsoft/terminal#17688 and the CreatePseudoConsole doc's explicit hang warning, and independently corroborated with winpty-rs's own README. It also cites termlens — a purpose-built TUI PTY harness that shipped Linux+macOS and left Windows undone. When a dedicated project declines to do this, a solo dev writing it blind through CI logs should not assume it will work. This matters because the Windows PTY tier is the tier meant to substitute for owning a Windows machine.

contradictions.topic: How much can Wine substitute for a Windows machine?
contradictions.position_a: language-choice: "wine 9.0 runs the cross-built Windows binaries with byte-identical output ... You can catch most Windows logic bugs locally in seconds" (edprobe.exe printed an identical 9-line Unicode table).
contradictions.position_b: grounding-agent-2: driving the real TUI through Wine+PTY produced mangled output at 60x12, 80x24 and 80x25 — a literal `5;12H` leaked onto the screen for the Rust/crossterm app, and the Go/tcell app rendered pure garbage. "wine is a smoke-test tool for startup/argv/non-TUI logic ONLY."
contradictions.who_is_right: Both, on different axes — but language-choice's "byte-identical output" is misleading evidence for a TUI project.
contradictions.why: language-choice's edprobe.exe printed plain stdout text; it never exercised alternate screen, raw mode, or CSI sequences, so "byte-identical" says nothing about the code path that matters. grounding-agent-2 drove an actual ratatui app and Wine ate the ESC prefixes. However, grounding-agent-2 undersells it too: Wine found two REAL Windows bugs in this research set — grounding-agent-1 caught crossterm's `PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags` returning a hard `ErrorKind::Unsupported` on Windows (which would make jio fail to start on every Windows machine, and which `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` passes happily), and headless-testing caught the `KeyEventKind::Release` double-typing bug ("hi" → "hhii"). Correct framing: Wine is a high-value canary for input decoding, startup, and file/path logic, and worthless as a render oracle. Never assert on Wine screen content.

contradictions.topic: How to compute display width for emoji/ZWJ sequences
contradictions.position_a: rust-ecosystem: "DEFAULT PICK: unicode-segmentation for grapheme clusters + unicode-width called PER GRAPHEME, never per char" — evidenced by a ZWJ family emoji having `str.width() == 2` but sum-of-char-widths == 8.
contradictions.position_b: ui-paradigm: measured the same ZWJ family sequence as unicode-width=2, tmux 3.4=5, vt100 0.16.2=6. "jio's cursor column arithmetic will be wrong on some real terminal ... no matter which width table it picks."
contradictions.who_is_right: ui-paradigm. rust-ecosystem's advice is correct as far as it goes but its framing ("DEFAULT PICK", problem solved) is wrong.
contradictions.why: Per-grapheme width is strictly better than per-char, so rust-ecosystem's rule should be adopted. But it yields 2 for a sequence that tmux renders as 5 cells and vt100 as 6 — i.e. the "correct" answer disagrees with the two emulators actually measured. ui-paradigm's structural mitigations are the part that survives: model in grapheme clusters, treat cell width as a per-terminal rendering hint, and re-emit an absolute `CSI row;col H` at the start of every painted line so a width disagreement corrupts one line instead of desynchronising the screen. rust-ecosystem's version of this advice would produce an editor that is confidently misaligned and has no recovery mechanism.

contradictions.topic: MSRV floor in the proposed CI workflow
contradictions.position_a: ci-build-release: its recommended ci.yml contains an `msrv` job pinned to `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.85.0` running `cargo check --locked --all-features`.
contradictions.position_b: ui-paradigm states ratatui 0.30 has MSRV 1.86; rust-ecosystem states ratatui 0.30.2 MSRV 1.88.
contradictions.who_is_right: rust-ecosystem. The proposed MSRV job is broken as written, and ui-paradigm's number is stale for the version it recommends.
contradictions.why: I queried the crates.io sparse index directly today: ratatui 0.30.0 declares rust_version 1.86.0, but 0.30.1 and 0.30.2 declare 1.88.0. A 1.85.0 MSRV job fails on the first push. crop 0.4.3 is 1.85, termina 0.4.0 is 1.71, crossterm 0.29.0 is 1.63 — so ratatui is the binding constraint at 1.88. Nobody reconciled the MSRV number across surveys. Related internal inconsistency in the same survey: its ci.yml uses `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` while its own risk list says to commit a `rust-toolchain.toml`; those two conflict, and the toolchain file wins silently.

unsupported_claims: language-choice, marked VERIFIED: "termina ... hands you uniform ConPTY/VT behavior across all three OSes, erasing the largest Windows terminal problem before you write a line." Nothing was executed on Windows, and Helix — the cited proof — still carries `[target.'cfg(windows)'.dependencies] crossterm = "0.28"` on master today (I fetched it). The cited evidence (a merged PR description + `cargo add termina --dry-run`) supports "this was the intent", not "the problem is erased."

language-choice, marked VERIFIED: "macOS is NOT a CI-only build target for Rust — only a CI-only *test* target." The evidence is `file` output on cross-built Mach-O binaries. Not one macOS binary produced in this entire research effort was ever executed, anywhere. The survey's own risk list concedes zig's LLD links against libSystem stubs and that subtle dyld/TLS/weak-symbol differences can produce binaries that link cleanly and crash on a real Mac. "Builds" is being reported at the confidence level of "works."

ci-build-release, marked VERIFIED: "Cross-compiled aarch64-apple-darwin binaries from zig DO carry a valid ad-hoc LC_CODE_SIGNATURE, so they will exec on Apple Silicon." The load-command parse is verified; "so they will exec" is unexecuted inference. A present LC_CODE_SIGNATURE is necessary, not sufficient — this is exactly the claim their own `smoke` job exists to test, and it was written as settled.

ci-build-release, marked VERIFIED: "Rust release builds are already bit-reproducible across build directories, WITHOUT any flags." Two builds of one trivial crate with no build scripts, no C dependencies, and no absolute-path deps. Generalizing this to jio — which will have tree-sitter `cc` build scripts emitting object files, and possibly `--remap`-sensitive panic locations — is not supported by the experiment run.

rust-ecosystem, marked VERIFIED: "The complete headless end-to-end test harness works today and is pure Rust ... Both cross-check to x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin from this Linux box." It works on Linux. `cargo check --target` is a typecheck; it cannot detect the ConPTY `ESC[6n` stall that headless-testing found by reading portable-pty's source constants.

ui-paradigm, marked VERIFIED: "This is jio's tier-2 CI layer and it genuinely works on Windows runners: your test process becomes the terminal emulator, so conhost's limitations do not apply." The evidence is a source read of `psuedocon.rs` declaring `CreatePseudoConsole`. Presence of an API call is not evidence of working behaviour, and the same file contains the hardcoded INHERIT_CURSOR flag that headless-testing identified as a hang risk.

rust-ecosystem's "DEFAULT PICK: gen-lsp-types 0.11.0" is presented as the mature replacement for a stale crate, with no stability caveat. I checked the index: gen-lsp-types 0.1.0 was published 2026-04-19 and 0.11.0 on 2026-07-28 — twelve releases in 100 days, all pre-1.0 (so every minor bump may break). lsp-types 0.97.0 (2024-06-04) is genuinely frozen, which the survey got right, but swapping a frozen dependency for one shipping a potentially-breaking release every ~9 days is a different problem, not a smaller one, for a solo dev.

text-buffer-core's headline "crop wins on the metrics that matter for an editor" is partly contradicted by its own data: under uniformly random inserts it measured ropey faster (136 ms vs 178 ms per 100k), and grounding-agent-1 independently reproduced that direction (2.097 µs vs 2.882 µs). The claim is defensible only for localized editing, which the survey does say — but the summary line drops the qualifier.

prior-art-postmortems attributes Raph Levien's CRDT verdict at "high" confidence to a GitHub issue comment it admits it could not render, sourced only from a search snippet. The retrospective quotes it fetched as raw markdown are solid; the CRDT quote specifically is second-hand and should be labelled medium.

ci-build-release's Homebrew/Gatekeeper/Azure-signing findings are marked "high" but rest on secondary sources (eclecticlight.co, appleinsider, forum answers) for behaviour that changes with every macOS point release. The specific claim that "macOS 15 Sequoia removed the Control-click bypass" and the Azure Artifact Signing eligibility rules for an EU self-employed individual are both load-bearing for a spending decision and neither was confirmed against a primary Apple/Microsoft source.
gaps: THE UX MODEL. Nobody was assigned it and nobody answered it: is jio modal (vim/helix/kakoune), selection-first (kakoune/helix), or modeless (nano/micro)? This is upstream of the buffer design — selection-first requires `Selection { ranges: SmallVec<[Range;1]> }` and multi-cursor from commit one, modeless requires a single cursor and a completely different command surface. It also collides with a hard terminal constraint ui-paradigm verified: on GNOME Terminal (the Ubuntu/Fedora default, no kitty protocol) Ctrl+Shift and Ctrl+digit are simply not expressible, Tab==Ctrl+I and Enter==Ctrl+M. Modal keymaps exist largely BECAUSE of that. A modeless jio will run out of chords on the majority Linux terminal. Decide this before the rope.

LICENSING — completely absent from every survey except incidental mentions. The repo has exactly one file (Readme.md) and NO LICENSE, which legally means all-rights-reserved: nobody can contribute, fork, or package it, and Homebrew/distro packaging is blocked. Separately, unresolved copyleft exposure: nucleo 0.5.0 is MPL-2.0, tree-house is Helix-licensed (MPL territory), termina is dual MIT-OR-MPL-2.0 (take MIT explicitly), ropey 1.6.1 is MIT-only while ropey 2.0 is MIT-OR-Apache-2.0 — and Rust convention is dual MIT/Apache-2.0. Nobody proposed a license for jio itself or checked the aggregate obligations.

NAMING AND TRADEMARK — nobody raised it. Two concrete blockers I verified today: (1) the crates.io name `jio` is ALREADY TAKEN — version 0.0.0, published 2024-08-15 — so `cargo publish` and `cargo install jio` are unavailable without a crates.io name dispute. (2) "JIO" is a registered, judicially recognised well-known trademark of Reliance Industries (multiple US registrations; Indian courts have granted injunctions), and Reliance has demonstrably pursued individual developers over `jio`-prefixed names. Also unchecked: Homebrew formula name collision, Scoop/WinGet name collision, and the `jio` binary name on PATH. This is cheap to resolve now and expensive to resolve after a release.

SECURITY / WORKSPACE TRUST. Not mentioned once. An editor that runs LSP servers, loads tree-sitter grammars, and reads per-project config is an arbitrary-code-execution surface: cloning a hostile repo and opening it launches whatever `.jio/config.toml` names. VS Code needed Workspace Trust for exactly this. Also unaddressed: tree-sitter C grammars are memory-unsafe code parsing untrusted input inside a memory-safe editor, and Helix's dynamic grammar loading (dlopen of a .so from a user directory) is a second vector. Decide the trust model before the plugin/LSP work, not after.

WHAT IS IN v0.1? No survey produced a feature list or an effort estimate. prior-art came closest (Kibi is 2,652 lines, kilo 1,308, Helix 107,479) but nobody wrote down what jio must do to be called done. Without this there is no way to evaluate whether any of the recommended subsystems belong in v1.

TREE-SITTER: YES OR NO. language-choice explicitly calls this "THE swing factor" for the language decision (drop it and Go becomes competitive) and it was never decided. It also gates cross-compilation: rust-ecosystem verified that any C dependency kills the 16-second local `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` canary, and ci-build-release verified that a single macOS-framework-linking crate kills Linux→macOS zigbuild entirely. Whether jio has C dependencies is therefore an architecture decision, not a feature decision.

DOES THE OWNER KNOW RUST? language-choice names the borrow checker versus an editor's cyclic data model (buffers ↔ views ↔ cursors ↔ undo) as "the single biggest schedule risk" in its own recommendation, and notes Helix works around it with one giant Editor struct plus integer indices while Zed had to invent GPUI's Entity<T> system. Unanswered. If the answer is no, Go's 33x faster warm rebuild becomes a much stronger argument than any survey allowed.

CRASH/DURABILITY POLICY. crossplatform-pitfalls proposes a vim-style WAL journal fsynced every ~200 keystrokes, with swap-file recovery UX, as the price of defaulting to in-place save. text-buffer-core separately proposes lossless invalid-byte escaping to Plane-16 PUA. Nobody costed either, nobody reconciled them, and nobody asked whether v0.1 needs crash recovery at all.

MINIMUM SUPPORTED PLATFORM CONTRACT. Windows 10 1809 / build 17763 was proposed independently by four surveys (portable-pty hard-fails below it with no winpty fallback; termina and WezTerm require it; Kibi requires 1703 for VT). macOS deployment target is unresolved (zig stamped minos 13.0, rustc's default is 11.0, and nothing in CI asserts it). Linux glibc floor is unresolved (2.28 via zigbuild vs 2.35 from ubuntu-22.04 vs musl-static). These need to be written down as a tested contract before the first release, not discovered from bug reports.

CONFIG AND KEYMAP FORMAT. Every survey assumes a TOML config and a declarative keymap (prior-art makes the command-registry-first argument well), but nobody designed the schema, the merge/override semantics, or where it lives per-OS. crossplatform-pitfalls flags a related landmine nobody resolved: `directories` 6.0.0 maps config_dir to Roaming AppData on Windows and ~/Library/Application Support on macOS, and TUI users expect XDG. Changing this after release is user-hostile.

ACCESSIBILITY. Raised once (ui-paradigm: AccessKit 0.25.0 is the only real answer and it requires a GUI) and then dropped. If screen-reader support is ever a requirement, it retroactively invalidates the TUI-only decision, so it needs an explicit yes/no now.
biggest_risks: SCOPE CREEP — by far the largest risk, and the one the research itself creates. The union of the eight recommendations is: a rope behind a swappable trait, Helix's full ChangeSet/Selection algebra, a WAL crash journal, vim's backupcopy heuristic with hidden probe files, a five-stage encoding-detection ladder with Plane-16 lossless byte escaping, ReplaceFileW/renamex_np platform save paths, tree-sitter with vendored C grammars, an LSP client on a hand-rolled JSON-RPC transport, gix (148 crates), a three-tier PTY test pyramid, an 8-target release matrix with universal2 lipo and a smoke job, Homebrew and Scoop taps, release-plz, cargo-mutants, and cargo-fuzz. That is comfortably a year before jio can edit a file, and prior-art's own evidence says this is what kills projects: xi died of novelty points, Helix has not cut a release in 14 months while chasing a plugin system, Ox and Zee simply stopped. Kibi is a cross-platform editor in 2,652 lines. The correct v0.1 is closer to Kibi than to any recommendation in this digest.

macOS IS BUILD-VERIFIED AND EXECUTION-UNVERIFIED, EVERYWHERE. Not one macOS binary produced in this research was ever run. cargo-zigbuild links against zig's libSystem stubs with a zig-chosen minos of 13.0, not Apple's linker against a real SDK, and no macOS emulator exists (no darling). Every macOS runtime bug will surface as a red CI job with no local repro and no debugger. Compounding it: Gatekeeper quarantine means "download and run" is simply false for a browser-downloaded tarball without a $99 Apple account, so the mitigation (curl|sh + Homebrew formula) is also a distribution constraint.

THE WINDOWS TEST TIER IS THE LEAST-PROVEN PART OF THE PLAN AND IT IS THE PART DOING THE MOST WORK. It is supposed to substitute for owning a Windows machine, yet: portable-pty hardcodes INHERIT_CURSOR (3s stall or hang without a byte-sniffed CPR reply that vt100 cannot help you write); ConPTY rewrites SGR, drops DCS and reorders OSC so snapshots can't be shared; GitHub's windows runners host conhost, not Windows Terminal, so the terminal your users actually run is never exercised; and termlens, a dedicated TUI PTY harness, shipped Linux+macOS and left Windows undone. Meanwhile crossterm's `PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags` returns a hard error on Windows and `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` passes it — that entire bug class is invisible to the compiler.

SILENT DATA LOSS IN THE SAVE/ENCODING PATH. crossplatform-pitfalls found three verified file-destroying defaults: `encoding_rs::Encoding::encode()` silently emits UTF-8 when the encoding is UTF_16LE/BE (`UTF_16LE.output_encoding() == UTF-8`), and replaces unmappable characters with the literal ASCII `🙂`; `tempfile::NamedTempFile` + persist downgrades 0664→0600, drops xattrs, breaks hard links, replaces symlinks with regular files, and as a non-root user succeeds over a 0444 file and resets it to 0644. Every one of these is a plausible first implementation, none produces an error, and none is visible while developing on Linux with ASCII files. This is the risk most likely to produce "jio ate my file" rather than "jio crashed."

NAME AND LICENSE ARE UNRESOLVED AND BOTH GET MORE EXPENSIVE WITH EVERY COMMIT. crates.io `jio` is taken (0.0.0, 2024-08-15). "JIO" is a well-known registered trademark with a documented history of enforcement against individual developers. The repo has no LICENSE, so it is currently all-rights-reserved and legally unpackageable and uncontributable. Renaming after a release means broken install instructions, a dead Homebrew tap, and a dead Scoop bucket.

TERMINAL WIDTH DIVERGENCE IS UNFIXABLE AND UNCATCHABLE. unicode-width 0.2.2, tmux 3.4 and vt100 0.16.2 disagree on 7 of 12 test strings (ZWJ family: 2 vs 5 vs 6). Whichever table jio's snapshots encode will be green in CI and wrong on some user's terminal for emoji, combining marks and Indic text — the CJK/Unicode correctness the project cares about. No CI tier catches this class at all.

PRE-1.0 DEPENDENCY CHURN ON THE EXACT COMPONENTS THAT CANNOT BE HAND-TESTED. ratatui-termina 0.1.0 pins termina 0.3.3 while termina is at 0.4.0 (two copies in one lockfile, verified); gen-lsp-types went 0.1.0 → 0.11.0 in 100 days; ropey 2.0 is a beta still renaming enum variants; crop is bus-factor 1; async-lsp pins lsp-types 0.95.1 against a top-level 0.97.0; tree-sitter grammar crates drag conflicting runtime versions (tree-sitter-toml 0.20.0 pulls tree-sitter 0.20.10). Each of these produces a mismatched-types error at a distance, and the ones on the Windows path are debuggable only through CI logs.

SOLO-DEVELOPER ATTENTION DECAY. prior-art's strongest empirical finding: Ox last committed 2025-03-13, Zee 2025-02-06, Xray archived outright. The failure mode is a 6-month gap, not a wrong data structure. Everything that lengthens the time to a first shippable, installable binary — and most of this digest does — increases this risk directly.

TOOLCHAIN AND RUNNER DRIFT AGAINST A DEV BOX THAT CANNOT BE UPGRADED FREELY. The box is rustc 1.94.1; both GitHub runner images ship 1.98.0. Without a committed rust-toolchain.toml, PRs fail on lints that cannot be reproduced locally. Meanwhile the runner labels themselves moved in 2026 (macos-latest → macOS 26 arm64, windows-latest → VS2026, macos-14 fully unsupported by Nov 2 2026, Intel macOS gone entirely by Aug 2027), so a floating label can change the only validation channel between two identical pushes.

THE FREE-CI ASSUMPTION IS LOAD-BEARING AND SINGLE-POINT. I confirmed the repo is public and that standard runners (including macos-15-intel, macos-26-intel, windows-11-arm, ubuntu-24.04-arm) are free and unlimited on public repos. If jio ever goes private, macOS bills at 10x and the entire validation strategy collapses. There is also no second machine anywhere: an extended Actions outage means zero artifacts for any platform.
convergent_conclusions: Rust, and a TUI, and one process. Every survey that considered alternatives reached this independently: Electron/Node SEA is 124.8 MB for hello-world; Tauri's Linux webview is a system webkit2gtk dependency and is unrunnable headless; eframe/egui is 38x the binary, 345 crates, a 5-minute build, and would not execute on this box without apt-installing X libraries; Zig 0.16.0's std.Io rewrite still has Ghostty unmigrated; Go loses on cgo-to-macOS with tree-sitter. A GUI is also the one shape that cannot be exercised at all in this environment.

No process/RPC boundary between core and frontend, and no CRDT in v1. Raph Levien's own retrospective (fetched verbatim as raw markdown, twice, by two researchers) says the frontend/core process split "was not a good idea" and that async "is a complexity multiplier" — the features that broke were scroll and resize-with-wrap, i.e. exactly jio's day-one features. Neovim's durable boundary is a dumb grid-of-cells presentation protocol, and VS Code's is around untrusted extensions. Both are at the edges, not the model.

Some rope, not a String, not Vec<String>, not a naive piece table. Independently measured: String is 2.4 ms/insert at 64 MiB (1143x slower than a rope in one measurement); Vec<String> costs 85 bytes/line overhead and 1.3 ms to insert a line mid-file; a naive non-tree piece table degenerated to 399,399 pieces and 379 µs/edit after 200k random edits. Any of ropey/crop is ~60-3000 ns and therefore not the bottleneck.

The core must be a pure state machine with an injectable event stream, and the terminal must sit behind a trait. Helix's `Application::event_loop_until_idle(&mut rx_stream)` driven by `parse_macro("ihello<esc>")` was independently identified by prior-art, headless-testing and ui-paradigm as the single most copyable artifact. This is what makes macOS/Windows correctness testable as ordinary `cargo test` on all three runners, and it is what makes the crossterm→termina decision reversible later.

ratatui 0.30.2's TestBackend + insta 1.48.0 is the primary test tier: fully headless, byte-identical across OSes, milliseconds, and it already annotates double-width overwrites ("Hidden by multi-width symbols"), which makes one CJK/ZWJ fixture the entire Unicode-width regression suite. Verified working by three independent agents. Two caveats also converged: TestBackend's Display drops all styles (write a styled_view helper), and a naive per-cell symbol join is wrong because ratatui writes a literal space in the continuation cell.

portable-pty 0.9.0 + vt100 0.16.2 is the right E2E harness shape, and predicate-polling — never fixed sleeps — is the entire answer to PTY flakiness. Independently: 0 failures in 180+ Python-route runs and 60/60 in each of the Rust and Go routes under 4x CPU oversubscription with parallel PTYs, while fixed 10 ms sleeps failed 56% of the time under load and 1 ms sleeps failed 100% even idle.

A bare PTY is not a terminal: it answers no capability queries. Reproduced three ways (script(1), python pty.fork, and stdout-redirected-inside-tmux) — the probe emits `ESC[?u ESC[c` and times out, while the same binary in a tmux pane returns promptly. Consequences agreed on: probe against /dev/tty (never stdout), with a hard ~100 ms timeout, gated behind an is-terminal check, plus a regression test that pipes stdout and asserts no stall. crossterm's own `supports_keyboard_enhancement()` has a hardcoded 2000 ms timeout that will hang startup in tmux/CI/dumb terminals.

Keep the repo public and pin explicit runner labels. I confirmed against github/docs today that standard runners are free and unlimited on public repos and that the label set includes macos-15-intel, macos-26-intel, windows-11-arm and ubuntu-24.04-arm. Every survey that looked also concluded: never use macos-latest/windows-latest, because both migrated in mid-2026 and macos-14 is unsupported from Nov 2026.

`cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` and `--target aarch64-apple-darwin` work on this box today for pure-Rust code (8-16 s, targets already installed) and catch cfg-gated type errors a native check cannot — headless-testing proved this by injecting an error that only the cross-check found. Universally endorsed as the cheapest high-value technique available, and the reason to feature-gate every C dependency so the canary stays green.

`pip install ziglang` + cargo-zigbuild unlocks Linux→macOS and Linux→aarch64 cross-builds including tree-sitter's C grammars and arboard's objc2 stack (Mach-O arm64 with platform 1 / minos 13.0 verified by two agents). Corollary all agreed on: MSVC cannot be linked here (aka.ms is proxy-blocked for cargo-xwin), so windows-msvc belongs on a native windows runner and windows-gnu is the local proxy.

Line endings and encodings are I/O-boundary concerns, and only that. Normalize to LF in the buffer, record the original style + BOM + detected encoding on the Document, re-emit on save; keep the rope UTF-8-only; make LineEnding a first-class type from day one (Helix spends 328 lines on it and put LineFeedHandling directly in its TestCase struct). Also universally flagged: commit a `.gitattributes` (`* text=auto eol=lf`, `*.snap text eol=lf`, fixtures `binary`) or git's autocrlf on the Windows runner will make line-ending tests pass or fail for the wrong reason.

Defer extensibility; ship a command registry and a declarative keymap instead. Helix — 46.1k stars, many contributors — has had its Steel plugin PR open since 2023-10-31 (491 commits, 700+ comments) and has cut no release since 25.07.1 in July 2025. xi blocked features behind plugin-API redesigns. The cheap form (route every user action through an internal command vocabulary now, pick a scripting runtime much later, if ever) costs almost nothing and is the actual Neovim/Emacs lesson.

Cursor movement is per grapheme cluster, not per char, and clipboard should be OSC 52-first with internal registers always available. The clipboard point converged from two directions: arboard fails on any headless box (X11 timeout, ~1 s stall), native clipboard is untestable on Windows runners (session 0) and Linux runners (no DISPLAY), whereas OSC 52 is fully observable in a PTY test via vt100's copy_to_clipboard callback — turning the single least-testable subsystem into a 40-line deterministic test. It is also the right answer for an editor used over SSH.
